chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: The law is a pillar of a civilised society; it shapes and is shaped by the society in which it operates and is, in turn, a product of its history and its institutions.

The law is a pillar of a civilised society; it shapes and is 
shaped by the society in which it operates and is, in turn, a product of its history and 
its institutions.

chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: In Australia, that inheritance comprised a common law legal system and a democratic and parliamentary system of government.
text_raw:
In Australia, that inheritance comprised a common law legal system and a democratic 
and parliamentary system of government.

chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: The inherited law and those political and legal institutions, developed over a millennium, needed adaptation to this land, some 20,000 kilometres from the model of law and government in 18th-century Britain.
text_raw:
The inherited law and those political and legal 
institutions, developed over a millennium, needed adaptation to this land, some 20,000

chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: Laying Down the Law charts the evolution of those changes since European settlement and the gradual reconciliation of that introduced system with the existing legal and cultural systems of Australia’s indigenous peoples.
text_raw:
Laying Down 
the Law charts the evolution of those changes since European settlement and the gradual 
reconciliation of that introduced system with the existing legal and cultural systems of 
Australia’s indigenous peoples.

chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: From these beginnings emerged a federal system of parliaments and executive government to make laws, the establishment of a multi-tiered system of courts and tribunals to interpret and apply those laws, and a complex and sophisticated regulatory system to develop standards and maintain a watchful eye over the operations of its institutions.
text_raw:
From these beginnings emerged a federal system of parliaments and executive 
government to make laws, the establishment of a multi-tiered system of courts and tribunals 
to interpret and apply those laws, and a complex and sophisticated regulatory system to 
develop standards and maintain a watchful eye over the operations of its institutions.

chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: Laying Down the Law provides a succinct account of that history and of those institutions.
text_raw: Laying Down the Law provides a succinct account of that history and of those institutions.

chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: From its inception, the text has taken account of the need to e ﬃciently introduce students of law to the knowledge and the skills needed to navigate their legal studies.

students of law to the knowledge and the skills needed to navigate their legal studies.

chapter_title: Part 6: The Essential Legal Toolkit 607
text: This involves inculcating key substantive and procedural principles of the common law system, such as the doctrine of precedent which ensures consistency within the hierarchy of Australian courts, and to the processes that protect the less advantaged within the criminal justice system.
text_raw:
This 
involves inculcating key substantive and procedural principles of the common law system, 
such as the doctrine of precedent which ensures consistency within the hierarchy of

text: 5 Introduction This book oﬀers students an introduction to the foundational knowledge and skills needed for their further study of law, as well as a resource that can be used throughout these studies and beyond.

Introduction
This book oﬀers students an introduction to the foundational knowledge and skills needed 
for their further study of law, as well as a resource that can be used throughout these 
studies and beyond.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 1 LAYING THE FOUNDATIONS
text: In Part/uni00A01, /f_irst Chapter/uni00A01 explores reasons for studying law; provides an overview of the major legal systems in the world, focusing on common law (Australia’s legal system), and civil law systems; their foundations, including the Western legal tradition; and the convergence of these major systems; and includes a brief introduction to legal theory, ways to categorise laws, and a warning about technical legal language.

33
• asserted that the Crown had no power to suspend the operation of law;

text: Introduction The Australian legal system is made up of key governmental institutions that make, interpret, administer and enforce laws, at the federal, state and territory levels.
text_raw:
Introduction
The Australian legal system is made up of key governmental institutions that make, 
interpret, administer and enforce laws, at the federal, state and territory levels.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: These institutions are guided by written constitutions, such as the Australian Constitution,2 and fundamental constitutional principles.

institutions are guided by written constitutions, such as the Australian Constitution,2 and 
fundamental constitutional principles.

international context.

text: 56 LAYING DOWN THE LAW The second feature, one that is peculiar to a parliamentary system of government, is a particular overlap of personnel and powers among the branches of government (more so in the United Kingdom than Australia).
text_raw:
56
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
The second feature, one that is peculiar to a parliamentary system of government, is 
a particular overlap of personnel and powers among the branches of government (more 
so in the United Kingdom than Australia).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: In establishing the federal government, the Australian Constitution required the judiciary to be separate in personnel and powers from the other two branches, the legislature and the executive, which overlap, as they do in the British government in Westminster.
text_raw:
In establishing the federal government, the 
Australian Constitution required the judiciary to be separate in personnel and powers from 
the other two branches, the legislature and the executive, which overlap, as they do in 
the British government in Westminster.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: The judiciary is comprised only of judges, who are charged with exercising judicial power, and only judicial power in that role at the federal level: see/uni00A03.24–3.26.

federal level: see/uni00A03.24–3.26.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 3 THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: Each branch of government has diﬀerent powers and responsibilities, and diﬀerent personnel, with some important quali/f_ications. • The legislature, comprised of elected Members of Parliament, is designed primarily to make law, speci/f_ically to enact legislation. • The primary role of the judiciary, the judges, is to be the arbiter of disputes and, in doing so, provide authoritative guidance on the meaning of the laws. • The executive branch is by far the largest and most amorphous branch of government, as it is made up of numerous oﬃcers, departments and institutions whose primary role is to execute or administer the laws.
text_raw:
Each branch of government has diﬀerent powers and responsibilities, 
and diﬀerent personnel, with some important quali/f_ications. 
• The legislature, comprised of elected Members of Parliament, is designed 
primarily to make law, speci/f_ically to enact legislation. 
• The primary role of the judiciary, the judges, is to be the arbiter of disputes 
and, in doing so, provide authoritative guidance on the meaning of the laws. 
• The executive branch is by far the largest and most amorphous branch of 
government, as it is made up of numerous oﬃcers, departments and institutions 
whose primary role is to execute or administer the laws.

Australian legal institutions
The principal legal institutions in Australia are parliaments, which pass legislation and 
monitor delegated legislation; the courts, which interpret those laws in their application 
to individual disputes; and the executive, which administers those laws.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: 83 Introduction As discussed in previous chapters, on settlement Australia received English laws and subsequently developed a legal and justice system in the English common law tradition under which Australia’s First Nations and their pre-existing customary laws were largely ignored.
text_raw:
83
Introduction
As discussed in previous chapters, on settlement Australia received English laws and 
subsequently developed a legal and justice system in the English common law tradition 
under which Australia’s First Nations and their pre-existing customary laws were largely 
ignored.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: In this chapter, we consider in more detail how the Australian legal system has treated First Nations Australians.
text_raw:
In this chapter, we consider in more detail how the Australian legal system has 
treated First Nations Australians.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: It took the Australian legal system around 200/uni00A0 years to belatedly recognise native/uni00A0 title.

It took the Australian legal system around 200/uni00A0 years to belatedly recognise 
native/uni00A0 title.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: The dispossession and discrimination suﬀered by Australia’s First Nations have resulted in social disadvantage and criminalisation, but governments have struggled to /f_ind a response that has not worsened the situation.
text_raw:
The dispossession and discrimination suﬀered by Australia’s First Nations 
have resulted in social disadvantage and criminalisation, but governments have struggled 
to /f_ind a response that has not worsened the situation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: Through the 19 th a n d 2 0th centuries many Australian governments instituted protection regimes in which Chief Protectors took control over all aspects of the lives of First Nations people, frequently taking children away from their families.
text_raw:
Through the 19 th a n d 2 0th 
centuries many Australian governments instituted protection regimes in which Chief 
Protectors took control over all aspects of the lives of First Nations people, frequently 
taking children away from their families.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: This paternalistic approach fell out of favour in the second half of the 20 th century , with growing appreciation of First Nations peoples’ rights and the recognition of native title.
text_raw:
This paternalistic approach fell out of favour in 
the second half of the 20 th century , with growing appreciation of First Nations peoples’ 
rights and the recognition of native title.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: However, at the beginning of the 21st century the Commonwealth Government, still struggling to address First Nations disadvantage, returned to paternalism with its Northern Territory Intervention, and some states implemented similar schemes.
text_raw:
However, at the beginning of the 21st century 
the Commonwealth Government, still struggling to address First Nations disadvantage, 
returned to paternalism with its Northern Territory Intervention, and some states 
implemented similar schemes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: There is little evidence that these are having a positive impact on the lives of aﬀected First Nations Australians.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: In particular, given the disruptive impact of colonisation on First Nations Australians, it should not be required that ‘the acknowledgment of traditional laws and the observance of traditional customs have continued substantially uninterrupted since sovereignty’.26 Rather, it must be acknowledged that ‘traditional laws and customs may adapt, evolve or otherwise develop’.27 Further, references in the NTA to a ‘traditional physical connection’ with the land or waters, which may be open to a more stringent interpretation, should be deleted.28 As Patrick Keane, then Chief Justice of the Federal Court, noted extrajudicially, a/uni00A0key practical issue regarding native title is ‘how [its] economic value … can be unlocked and managed for the future’.29 The terms of reference of the NTA review by the ALRC included the question of ‘the capacity of native title to support Indigenous economic development and generate sustainable long-term bene/f_its for Indigenous Australians’.30 The ALRC recommended that the NTA be amended to expressly recognise that ‘native title rights and interests … may comprise a right that may be exercised for any purpose, including commercial or non-commercial purposes’.31 In Akiba the High Court recognised that there was a long history of the T orres Strait Islander claimants /f_ishing for the purpose of trade and exchange.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 94 Over the succeeding decades, the courts exercised increasing jurisdiction over First Nations defendants, even regarding incidents that involved only First Nations people.68 In R/uni00A0v Paddy and Wills69 in 1886, for example, counsel for the defendants admitted that they had killed another Aboriginal man, but argued that the defendants were ignorant of the law and that it was natural for the defendants to kill a man of a diﬀerent tribe.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
94
Over the succeeding decades, the courts exercised increasing jurisdiction over First 
Nations defendants, even regarding incidents that involved only First Nations people.68 In 
R/uni00A0v Paddy and Wills69 in 1886, for example, counsel for the defendants admitted that they 
had killed another Aboriginal man, but argued that the defendants were ignorant of the 
law and that it was natural for the defendants to kill a man of a diﬀerent tribe.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: PROTECTION REGIMES During the 19 th century the practice developed of subjecting Aboriginal people to diﬀerential treatment within a broader colonial legal framework.
text_raw:
PROTECTION REGIMES
During the 19 th century the practice developed of subjecting Aboriginal people to 
diﬀerential treatment within a broader colonial legal framework.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: Aboriginal people were drawn within comprehensive protection regimes where Protection Boards exerted almost total control over all aspects of their lives.
text_raw:
Aboriginal people were 
drawn within comprehensive protection regimes where Protection Boards exerted almost 
total control over all aspects of their lives.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: One tragic aspect of this was that many First Nations children were forcibly removed from their families and communities to be placed in institutions or with non-Aboriginal foster parents.71 This severely damaged the children and their families — the ‘Stolen Generations’ — and has had a lasting impact on later generations.
text_raw:
One tragic aspect of this was that many First 
Nations children were forcibly removed from their families and communities to be placed 
in institutions or with non-Aboriginal foster parents.71 This severely damaged the children 
and their families — the ‘Stolen Generations’ — and has had a lasting impact on later 
generations.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: Along with their dispossession of traditional lands and the destruction of their culture, this continues to contribute to First Nations peoples’ alienation and disadvantage.
text_raw:
Along with their dispossession of traditional lands and the destruction of their 
culture, this continues to contribute to First Nations peoples’ alienation and disadvantage.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: Another consequence of the ‘absolutist welfare control’72 of the protection system was that criminal conduct by Aboriginal people was often not dealt with by the criminal justice system.
text_raw:
Another consequence of the ‘absolutist welfare control’72 of the protection system 
was that criminal conduct by Aboriginal people was often not dealt with by the criminal 
justice system.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: Instead, extra-judicial and often brutal punishments were handed down administratively by the Chief Protector.
text_raw:
Instead, extra-judicial and often brutal punishments were handed down 
administratively by the Chief Protector.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: An example is the methods of Reverend William Mackenzie who ‘ruled’ Aurukun, a mission on the Cape Y ork Peninsula, for four decades from 1925:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: Mackenzie’s punishments were harsh, unorthodox, and arbitrary — they included the use of banishment, corporal punishment, including /f_logging and beating, use of his /f_ists, use of the ‘electro magnet’, binding the mouth to stop verbal abuse and swearing.73 As noted in 3.44, following the Second World War there was, in Australia as elsewhere, an increasing awareness of human rights, particularly those of the First Nations peoples of colonies and former colonies.
text_raw:
Mackenzie’s punishments were harsh, unorthodox, and arbitrary — they included the use 
of banishment, corporal punishment, including /f_logging and beating, use of his /f_ists, use of 
the ‘electro magnet’, binding the mouth to stop verbal abuse and swearing.73
As noted in 3.44, following the Second World War there was, in Australia as elsewhere, 
an increasing awareness of human rights, particularly those of the First Nations peoples 
of colonies and former colonies.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: This was accompanied by a shift away from the paternalistic ‘protection’ approach to indigenous peoples.
text_raw:
This was accompanied by a shift away from the 
paternalistic ‘protection’ approach to indigenous peoples.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: As a consequence, Aboriginal people were no longer outside the criminal justice system.
text_raw:
As a consequence, Aboriginal 
people were no longer outside the criminal justice system.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: The rise in protection regimes at the beginning of the 20 th century had led to a decline in the Aboriginal prison population.
text_raw:
The rise in protection 
regimes at the beginning of the 20 th century had led to a decline in the Aboriginal 
prison population.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: But with the fall of the protection regimes in the last quarter of the 20th century, the Aboriginal prison population increased alarmingly.
text_raw:
But with the fall of the protection regimes in the last quarter of the 
20th century, the Aboriginal prison population increased alarmingly.

EQUALITY UNDER THE LAW
This issue — whether the sentencing court should or should not consider a First 
Nations oﬀender’s cultural background — highlights the distinction between formal 
and substantive equality.136 It may be objected that provisions that require sentencing 
courts to take account of the traditional culture of First Nations oﬀenders 137 introduce 
an inequality as they refer to a consideration that is not applicable to other oﬀenders.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: For the criminal justice system to provide First Nations people with substantive equality, it is necessary to take into account the reasons for their ‘entrenched disadvantage … [including] historical factors such as dispossession and exclusion from traditional lands, the impact of past government policies of assimilation and child removal, and the breakdown of cultural authority and traditional law’.143 Provisions like s/uni00A016AA(1) of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth), which prevent these factors from being considered, deny First Nations people substantive equality.

For the 
criminal justice system to provide First Nations people with substantive equality, it is 
necessary to take into account the reasons for their ‘entrenched disadvantage … [including] 
historical factors such as dispossession and exclusion from traditional lands, the impact of 
past government policies of assimilation and child removal, and the breakdown of cultural 
authority and traditional law’.143 Provisions like s/uni00A016AA(1) of the Crimes Act 1914 (Cth), 
which prevent these factors from being considered, deny First Nations people substantive 
equality.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 116 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS, ALIENS AND THE CONSTITUTION While politicians, experts, and First Nations leaders were considering constitutional change to better recognise First Nations Australians, the High Court was presented with ‘two special cases’ regarding their position under the Constitution in its current form.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
116
FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS, ALIENS AND THE CONSTITUTION
While politicians, experts, and First Nations leaders were considering constitutional 
change to better recognise First Nations Australians, the High Court was presented with 
‘two special cases’ regarding their position under the Constitution in its current form.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: 233 In Love and Thoms, the two plaintiﬀs, citizens of Papua New Guinea and New Zealand respectively, had had their visas cancelled following their conviction of criminal oﬀences and were facing deportation under migration and citizenship legislation.
text_raw:
233 
In Love and Thoms, the two plaintiﬀs, citizens of Papua New Guinea and New Zealand 
respectively, had had their visas cancelled following their conviction of criminal oﬀences 
and were facing deportation under migration and citizenship legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: This legislation had been made under the Commonwealth Parliament’s power to legislate with respect to ‘aliens’.234 The men argued that, in application to them, the legislation was not supported by the aliens power in the Constitution because they are First Nations Australians.
text_raw:
This legislation 
had been made under the Commonwealth Parliament’s power to legislate with respect to 
‘aliens’.234 The men argued that, in application to them, the legislation was not supported 
by the aliens power in the Constitution because they are First Nations Australians.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: While they had not been born in Australia and held foreign citizenship, Mr Love and Mr Thoms claimed to be members of the Kamilaroi people and Gunggari people respectively.
text_raw:
While 
they had not been born in Australia and held foreign citizenship, Mr Love and Mr Thoms 
claimed to be members of the Kamilaroi people and Gunggari people respectively.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: By a majority of 4:3235 the High Court accepted the men’s claim that First Nations Australians could not be considered ‘aliens’ under the Constitution.
text_raw:
By a majority of 4:3235 the High Court accepted the men’s claim that First Nations 
Australians could not be considered ‘aliens’ under the Constitution.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: The central meaning of ‘alienage’ is ‘lack of relationship with a country’.236 However, First Nations Australians have a connection with land and waters that is unique … It is a connection which existed and persisted before and beyond settlement, before and beyond the assertion of sovereignty and before and beyond Federation.
text_raw:
The central meaning 
of ‘alienage’ is ‘lack of relationship with a country’.236 However, First Nations Australians 
have 
a connection with land and waters that is unique … It is a connection which existed and 
persisted before and beyond settlement, before and beyond the assertion of sovereignty and 
before and beyond Federation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 4 FIRST NATIONS AUSTRALIANS AND THE AUSTRALIAN LEGAL SYSTEM
text: It is older and deeper than the Constitution.237 The connection to country recognised by the majority is broader than native title, which in many cases has been extinguished.
text_raw:

The connection to country recognised by the majority is broader than native title, 
which in many cases has been extinguished.

text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 134 ‘Genuine’ steps The obligation to minimise the cost of civil litigation under model litigant rules has motivated consistent moves in recent years to settle matters prior to a hearing.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
134
‘Genuine’ steps
The obligation to minimise the cost of civil litigation under model litigant rules 
has motivated consistent moves in recent years to settle matters prior to a hearing.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: 147 Introduction As a society, we mostly rely on ‘voluntary’ compliance with laws, but there will always be breaches and disputes.
text_raw:
147
Introduction
As a society, we mostly rely on ‘voluntary’ compliance with laws, but there will always 
be breaches and disputes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Accompanying the laws, made by the various branches of government to regulate behaviour, are legal institutions set up to encourage, enable and enforce compliance, and to resolve disputes.
text_raw:
Accompanying the laws, made by the various branches of 
government to regulate behaviour, are legal institutions set up to encourage, enable 
and enforce compliance, and to resolve disputes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The most well-known institutions for resolving disputes are courts of law.
text_raw:
The most well-known institutions for 
resolving disputes are courts of law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Courts decide claims, usually by adversarial hearings that involve elaborate rules of procedure and result in enforceable judgments.
text_raw:
Courts decide claims, usually by adversarial hearings 
that involve elaborate rules of procedure and result in enforceable judgments.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: There are, however, other dispute-resolution institutions, such as tribunals, and alternative dispute resolution mechanisms such as conciliation, mediation and arbitration.
text_raw:
There are, 
however, other dispute-resolution institutions, such as tribunals, and alternative dispute 
resolution mechanisms such as conciliation, mediation and arbitration.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: There is also a raft of institutions that operate in various areas of regulation, not in response to legal disputes, but to prevent them from arising.
text_raw:
There is also a 
raft of institutions that operate in various areas of regulation, not in response to legal 
disputes, but to prevent them from arising.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Mostly situated in the executive branch of government, these regulatory agencies engage with persons involved in speci/f_ic industries and activities, to encourage and enable their compliance.
text_raw:
Mostly situated in the executive branch of 
government, these regulatory agencies engage with persons involved in speci/f_ic industries 
and activities, to encourage and enable their compliance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Regulators’ eﬀorts are often backed up by the power to prosecute a matter to a court or tribunal as a last resort.
text_raw:
Regulators’ eﬀorts are often 
backed up by the power to prosecute a matter to a court or tribunal as a last resort.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The focus in law schools and law texts is often on dispute resolution by courts and tribunals, but students should keep in mind alternative methods of dispute resolution, and wider regulatory frameworks designed to enable compliance without litigation.
text_raw:
The 
focus in law schools and law texts is often on dispute resolution by courts and tribunals, 
but students should keep in mind alternative methods of dispute resolution, and wider 
regulatory frameworks designed to enable compliance without litigation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: This chapter introduces students to the procedures and mechanisms by which legal compliance is encouraged and enforced, and legal disputes are resolved.
text_raw:
This chapter introduces students to the procedures and mechanisms by which legal 
compliance is encouraged and enforced, and legal disputes are resolved.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The legal system, in pursuing compliance and enforcement, may intervene in diﬀerent ways and to diﬀering degrees.
text_raw:
The legal system, 
in pursuing compliance and enforcement, may intervene in diﬀerent ways and to diﬀering 
degrees.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Much of the chapter focuses on the most formal and interventionist mechanism: civil and criminal litigation in the courts.
text_raw:
Much of the chapter focuses on the most formal and interventionist mechanism: 
civil and criminal litigation in the courts.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: We begin, in the next section, by outlining the range of procedural laws that govern court litigation, ranging from who has standing through to which party pays litigation costs.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

LAYING DOWN THE LAW
148
If you buy a car, the manufacturer, distributor and retailer should all have complied with 
work health and safety laws in respect of their workers, and safety standards and consumer 
protection laws relating to the goods and services they provide.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: A central institution is the judiciary/uni00A0— the court system — which has constitutional responsibility for interpreting the law as it applies to individual cases.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: In relation to the courts, a large body of procedural law has been developed, with rules about when a court can be called on to resolve a dispute; who can seek its intervention; how the process is commenced; how the parties may gather evidence, including from each other; and how the court conducts itself in resolving the dispute.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: There are also other dispute-resolution institutions and mechanisms, governed by diﬀerent procedures, such as tribunals and alternative dispute resolution (ADR), which includes mediation, conciliation and arbitration.

text: Further, in designing legislative responses to identi/f_ied social problems, Parliament commonly now also establishes regulatory agencies with responsibility for identifying and prosecuting possible breaches of the rules, as well as promoting compliance to avoid the need for litigation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 150 PROCEDURE Beyond the question of who can initiate legal action, there are rules governing other aspects of the process.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
150
PROCEDURE
Beyond the question of who can initiate legal action, there are rules governing other 
aspects of the process.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The law can prescribe how the process is to be initiated, including the speci/f_ic forms to be used and submitted to the agency or court; the steps that must be taken to ‘serve’ the documents on the other party so they know they are the subject of legal action; the fees that need to be paid to the court or agency to start the process; and time limits for commencing proceedings.
text_raw:
The law can prescribe how the process is to be initiated, including 
the speci/f_ic forms to be used and submitted to the agency or court; the steps that must 
be taken to ‘serve’ the documents on the other party so they know they are the subject of 
legal action; the fees that need to be paid to the court or agency to start the process; and 
time limits for commencing proceedings.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Once proceedings are commenced, a number of steps are taken before the case reaches court.
text_raw:
Once proceedings are commenced, a number of steps are taken before the case 
reaches court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The parties will exchange pleadings outlining their opposing claims.
text_raw: The parties will exchange pleadings outlining their opposing claims.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: This may have the eﬀect of narrowing the issues.
text_raw:
This 
may have the eﬀect of narrowing the issues.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The parties might agree on some matters relating to the dispute (for example, that there was a contract), joining issue on other points (such as whether there was a breach, or the extent of the harm suﬀered).
text_raw:
The parties might agree on some matters 
relating to the dispute (for example, that there was a contract), joining issue on other 
points (such as whether there was a breach, or the extent of the harm suﬀered).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The court may also give the parties the opportunity to gather evidence from each other through the inspection and copying of documents (‘discovery’) and the asking of questions (‘interrogatories’).
text_raw:
The court 
may also give the parties the opportunity to gather evidence from each other through 
the inspection and copying of documents (‘discovery’) and the asking of questions 
(‘interrogatories’).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Many of the legal rules that are referred to as civil and criminal procedure relate more speci/f_ically to the hearing process in that they address speci/f_ic questions such as how witnesses can be called and examined, the types of evidence that are not admissible at trial, and how factual uncertainty is resolved.
text_raw:
Many of the legal rules that are referred to as civil and criminal procedure relate 
more speci/f_ically to the hearing process in that they address speci/f_ic questions such as how 
witnesses can be called and examined, the types of evidence that are not admissible at trial, 
and how factual uncertainty is resolved.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Further procedural rules govern limited rights to appeals.
text_raw:
Further procedural rules govern limited rights to 
appeals.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: These are explored at 6.29ﬀ as aspects of the adversarial trial.
text_raw: These are explored at 6.29ﬀ as aspects of the adversarial trial.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: There are also many rules about how the costs of litigation are to be born.
text_raw: There are also many rules about how the costs of litigation are to be born.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Costs may include the court fees, lawyer fees and litigation expenses such as the fee for transcription of the hearing, and paying experts to provide evidence.
text_raw:
Costs may 
include the court fees, lawyer fees and litigation expenses such as the fee for transcription 
of the hearing, and paying experts to provide evidence.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The general rule in civil litigation is ‘loser pays’; however, the court, in making orders regarding costs, has a discretion to consider many factors, although not the impecuniosity of the losing party.
text_raw:
The general rule in civil litigation 
is ‘loser pays’; however, the court, in making orders regarding costs, has a discretion to 
consider many factors, although not the impecuniosity of the losing party.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: 9 In criminal matters a successful defendant may obtain costs, 10 and, more rarely, in a narrow range of circumstances, costs may be awarded against an unsuccessful defendant.11 As discussed at 6.37ﬀ, litigation can be very expensive for parties, raising concern about access to justice, and giving rise to reforms to introduce cheaper dispute-resolution mechanisms.
text_raw:
9 In criminal

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: ALTERNATIVES TO COURTS Before we examine the trial process, it is worth remembering that courts are used only as the last resort for resolving disputes.
text_raw:
ALTERNATIVES TO COURTS
Before we examine the trial process, it is worth remembering that courts are used only as 
the last resort for resolving disputes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Even where litigation is commenced, parties generally seek to resolve their dispute through negotiation, with or without external assistance, and often reach a settlement agreement before trial.
text_raw:
Even where litigation is commenced, parties generally 
seek to resolve their dispute through negotiation, with or without external assistance, and 
often reach a settlement agreement before trial.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Growing concerns about costs, delays and access to justice in courts have encouraged exploration of alternative, less adversarial methods of dispute resolution.
text_raw:
Growing concerns about costs, delays 
and access to justice in courts have encouraged exploration of alternative, less adversarial 
methods of dispute resolution.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: A great deal of litigation is now heard, less formally and more cheaply, by tribunals.
text_raw:
A great deal of litigation is now heard, less formally and 
more cheaply, by tribunals.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Courts and tribunals encourage, and in some cases order, parties to engage in negotiations and ADR.
text_raw:

parties to engage in negotiations and ADR.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

text: 151 Further, many regulatory agencies have been established, not only to investigate and litigate legal disputes, but to use a range of regulatory tools to prevent them and encourage compliance.
text_raw:
151
Further, many regulatory agencies have been established, not only to investigate 
and litigate legal disputes, but to use a range of regulatory tools to prevent them and 
encourage compliance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Agencies such as the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission, for example, are empowered primarily to enable, encourage and monitor compliance; enforcement through court prosecution is rarely needed.
text_raw:
Agencies such as the Fair Work Ombudsman and the Australian 
Competition and Consumer Commission, for example, are empowered primarily to 
enable, encourage and monitor compliance; enforcement through court prosecution is 
rarely needed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The regulatory tools granted to such agencies can include powers to set standards; provide guidance; undertake inspections; conduct audits and investigations of organisations, industries or speci/f_ic complaints; issue compliance notices; monitor disclosures; and engage with regulated actors to improve compliance with the law.
text_raw:
The regulatory tools granted to such agencies can include powers to set 
standards; provide guidance; undertake inspections; conduct audits and investigations 
of organisations, industries or speci/f_ic complaints; issue compliance notices; monitor 
disclosures; and engage with regulated actors to improve compliance with the law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Used responsively and strategically, such tools can be more eﬃcient and eﬀective than the power to prosecute a handful of individual cases through expensive court processes.
text_raw:
Used 
responsively and strategically, such tools can be more eﬃcient and eﬀective than the 
power to prosecute a handful of individual cases through expensive court processes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The adversarial trial Perhaps the best-known mechanism for resolving disputes, familiar from numerous courtroom dramas on the stage and screen, is the adversarial trial.
text_raw:
The adversarial trial
Perhaps the best-known mechanism for resolving disputes, familiar from numerous 
courtroom dramas on the stage and screen, is the adversarial trial.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: But despite its familiarity and archetypal status, the adversarial trial is, in some respects, an unnatural and problematic solution to the problem of legal con/f_lict.
text_raw:
But despite its familiarity 
and archetypal status, the adversarial trial is, in some respects, an unnatural and problematic 
solution to the problem of legal con/f_lict.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Concerns with the adversarial trial have given rise to eﬀorts to divert disputes away from the courts, and to an increasing array of ADR processes: see 6.49–6.53.
text_raw:
Concerns with the adversarial trial have given 
rise to eﬀorts to divert disputes away from the courts, and to an increasing array of ADR 
processes: see 6.49–6.53.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The trial is described as adversarial because, rather than conducting an investigation into disputed events, the court adjudicates a contest between the opposing litigants as adversaries.
text_raw:
The trial is described as adversarial because, rather than conducting an investigation 
into disputed events, the court adjudicates a contest between the opposing litigants as 
adversaries.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The parties put to one side the matters that are undisputed and agreed upon, and focus on the matters that are genuinely in dispute.
text_raw:
The parties put to one side the matters that are undisputed and agreed upon, 
and focus on the matters that are genuinely in dispute.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Each party gathers and presents evidence in an eﬀort to persuade the court to accept their version of events with respect to those issues.
text_raw:
Each party gathers and presents 
evidence in an eﬀort to persuade the court to accept their version of events with respect 
to those issues.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Most commonly, the parties are contesting the facts and how the law applies to those facts; however, purely legal issues also may arise.
text_raw:
Most commonly, the parties are contesting the facts and how the law 
applies to those facts; however, purely legal issues also may arise.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The court has ultimate authority over the dispute, but it seeks to remain above the fray.
text_raw:
The court has ultimate authority over the dispute, but it seeks to remain above 
the fray.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The court should generally not call or examine witnesses.12 The court’s primary role/uni00A0 is to ensure that the contestants play by the rules, and even then, the court may require prompting by one party before it considers enforcing a rule against another,13 thus the familiar trope of counsel interrupting opposing counsel’s examination of a witness with the declaration: ‘Objection, your Honour!’ ACCUSATORIAL CRIMINAL TRIAL The criminal trial is the mechanism for resolving disputes about the guilt of a defendant (‘the accused’) or group of defendants (‘the co-accused’ or ‘co-defendants’).

GOALS OF THE ADVERSARIAL TRIAL
Accuracy and individual autonomy
On one view, the adversarial system is designed to advance the goal of accurate dispute 
resolution.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Factual accuracy has been described as a ‘fundamental’ 28 and ‘paramount’ 29 goal of the trial.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Giving the parties control over the proceedings is said to serve this goal, since the parties know the dispute and ‘each side [will] strive as hard as it can in a keenly partisan spirit, to bring to the court’s attention the evidence favourable to that side’.30 On another view, however, the adversarialist spirit of proceedings has the potential to disrupt the court’s pursuit of factual accuracy.31 A lawyer will not ‘concede the existence of facts if they are inimical to his client and he thinks they cannot be proved by his adversary’.32 The evidence that is placed before the court is likely to be the ‘partisan and coerced residue/uni00A0… culled by the parties with a view not so much to establishing the whole truth as to winning the case’.33 Indeed, critics have suggested that the common law system’s attraction to adversarialism prioritises values other than factual accuracy.

text: All Australian states have introduced this exception to double jeopardy68 but it has so far been virtually unused.69 This is a little surprising given that the strength of the presumption of innocence and the demanding requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt imply that a signi/f_icant proportion of acquitted defendants may in fact be guilty.

All Australian states have introduced 
this exception to double jeopardy68 but it has so far been virtually unused.69 This is a little 
surprising given that the strength of the presumption of innocence and the demanding 
requirement of proof beyond reasonable doubt imply that a signi/f_icant proportion of 
acquitted defendants may in fact be guilty.

text: Further, it is far easier for a defendant to appeal against a conviction than it is for the prosecution to appeal against an acquittal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The asymmetries increase the risk of mistaken acquittals, but these are viewed as less harmful than wrongful convictions.

viewed as less harmful than wrongful convictions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

corrected on appeal.

text: Expert witnesses owe a duty to the court similar to that of prosecutors: ‘An expert witness is not an advocate for a party and has a paramount duty, overriding any duty to the party … to assist the court impartially on matters relevant to the area of expertise of the witness.’81 And yet they too may get caught up in the contest, losing sight of their duty.

Expert witnesses owe a duty to the court similar to that of prosecutors: 
‘An expert witness is not an advocate for a party and has a paramount duty, overriding 
any duty to the party … to assist the court impartially on matters relevant to the area 
of expertise of the witness.’81 And yet they too may get caught up in the contest, losing 
sight of their duty.

text: He identi/f_ied himself with the prosecution and plainly demonstrated his bias in favour of the prosecution.’82 Similar comments about a prosecution expert witness were made in a recent appeal in the New South Wales Court of Criminal Appeal, Wood v The Queen: ‘Rather than remaining impartial and oﬀering his independent expertise to the Court’, ‘A/Prof Cross [the prosecution’s expert witness] took upon himself the role of investigator and became an active participant in attempting to prove that the applicant had committed murder’.83 Unreliable and biased expert evidence has also been identi/f_ied as major factor in the cases on the National Registry of Exonerations in the United States; other leading causes are witnesses making false accusations, oﬃcial misconduct, mistaken identi/f_ication and false confessions.84 It is diﬃcult to determine how often wrongful convictions occur.

A major goal for litigation is to provide an eﬃcient way of resolving disputes that gains 
general acceptance among the community.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

text: In most cases, the parties will not have the necessary knowledge or skills to engage in the adversarial contest themselves: ‘a/uni00A0trial is a battle and the lawyer the client’s champion’.92 Some lawyers may see an advantage in using certain technical rules in game-playing strategies that create delays and additional costs.93 Clearly, not everyone engaged in a legal dispute will be able to aﬀord a lawyer: ‘Y ou can’t pay $500 per hour when you earn $500 per week.’94 Y ou have to be very wealthy — or in some cases have your insurance company exercise the right of subrogation and take over the litigation on your behalf — to contemplate going to trial, which could easily cost $100,000 in legal fees.95 Even if you win (which cannot be guaranteed) and the losing party is ordered to pay your costs,96 you may still end up out of pocket.

Unsurprisingly, in view of the costs issue, most civil disputes do not go to court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Even where litigation is commenced, the vast majority of disputes settle prior to trial.
text_raw: Even where litigation is commenced, the vast majority of disputes settle prior to trial.

text: Considerable time and eﬀort will already have been spent by the parties in ensuring readiness for trial and the court will have scheduled time for trial; late settlement wastes the court’s resources and delays other cases.

text: The New South Wales Government, for example, recently noted that ‘73 per cent of serious criminal cases end with the defendant pleading guilty, yet 23 per cent of guilty pleas are not entered until the day of trial’.111 It introduced reforms to encourage early guilty pleas, promising that this would reduce expenditure on ‘police, courts and lawyers on both sides’, as well as reducing stress for victims of crime.112 Under the scheme, which commenced on 30/uni00A0April 2018, criminal defendants charged with indictable oﬀences will receive a reduction in their sentence for pleading guilty, with the size of the discount (up to 25%) depending on the earliness of the guilty plea.113 As with civil procedure reforms, the scheme requires greater case management by courts, earlier exchange of information by the parties, and mandatory case conferencing.

INQUISITORIAL AND INFORMAL PROCESSES
Another major advantage of tribunals over courts — and this is not limited to their 
administrative review function — is that they generally operate with less formality than 
courts, and so are cheaper and quicker.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The stated objective of the Administrative Appeals Tribunal Act 1975 (Cth), for example, is to ‘provid[e] a mechanism of review that [among other things] … is accessible; and … is fair, just, economical, informal and quick’.127 Fees for tribunal matters are generally less than for courts.

employed by the AAT134 include the following:

issues, discuss the future conduct of the matter, and to explore whether an 
agreed outcome is possible.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

or directing the parties to reach a particular outcome.

the dispute and the various options available.

Distinction between matters of fact and matters

An important conceptual distinction emerging from the preceding sections is that 
between fact and law.145 In a jury trial, this distinction draws the boundary between the 
responsibilities of the judge, the tribunal of law, and those of the jury, the tribunal of 
fact.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Judicial review of administrative decisions is generally con/f_ined to errors of law; one of the features of administrative tribunals is that they provide merits review, including any factual matters.

decisions is generally con/f_ined to errors of law; one of the features of administrative

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: In some situations, the distinction between fact and law is easily seen.
text_raw: In some situations, the distinction between fact and law is easily seen.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Consider, for example, the issue of identity in a murder trial.
text_raw:
Consider, for 
example, the issue of identity in a murder trial.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: As a matter of law, for the accused to be guilty of murder, generally it must have been the accused rather than someone else who performed the act that caused the death of the victim.
text_raw:
As a matter of law, for the accused to be guilty 
of murder, generally it must have been the accused rather than someone else who performed 
the act that caused the death of the victim.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Determining who performed the fatal act — for example, whether to believe the prosecution’s eyewitness evidence/uni00A0— is clearly a question of fact for the jury.
text_raw:
Determining who performed the fatal act — for 
example, whether to believe the prosecution’s eyewitness evidence/uni00A0— is clearly a question 
of fact for the jury.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: There are cases, however, where the issue of identity presents greater legal complexity.
text_raw:
There are cases, however, where the issue of identity presents greater legal 
complexity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: For example, the prosecution may allege that the murder was part of a joint criminal enterprise for which the defendant should be held responsible even though he did not pull the trigger.
text_raw:
For example, the prosecution may allege that the murder was part of a joint 
criminal enterprise for which the defendant should be held responsible even though he did 
not pull the trigger.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The scope of the joint criminal enterprise doctrine is quite controversial, having reached the High Court on several occasions.146 The legal requirements for joint criminal enterprise will be determined by the trial judge on the basis of legal materials.
text_raw:
The scope of the joint criminal enterprise doctrine is quite controversial, 
having reached the High Court on several occasions.146 The legal requirements for joint 
criminal enterprise will be determined by the trial judge on the basis of legal materials.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: The trial judge will then instruct the jury as to the legal requirements regarding identity and joint criminal enterprise.
text_raw:
The 
trial judge will then instruct the jury as to the legal requirements regarding identity and joint 
criminal enterprise.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 6 GOING TO LAW: LEGAL DISPUTE RESOLUTION PROCESSES
text: Whether these requirements are satis/f_ied will then be a question of fact for the jury, determined based on their consideration of the evidence.

Whether these requirements are satis/f_ied will then be a question of fact 
for the jury, determined based on their consideration of the evidence.

text: [W]hen the Justices sitting as a Full Court are divided in opinion as to the decision to be given on any question, the question shall be decided according to the decision of the majority, if there is a majority but if the Court is equally divided in opinion — (a) in the case where a decision of a Justice of the High Court (whether acting as a Justice of the High Court or in some other capacity), a decision of the Supreme Court of a State or T erritory or a Judge of such a Court, a decision of the Federal Court of Australia or a Judge of that Court or a decision of the Family Court of Australia or a Judge of that Court is called in question by appeal or otherwise, the decision appealed from shall be afﬁrmed; and (b) in any other case, the opinion of the Chief Justice, or if he is absent the opinion of the Senior Justice present, shall prevail.

[W]hen the Justices sitting as a Full Court are divided in opinion as to the decision to 
be given on any question, the question shall be decided according to the decision of the 
majority, if there is a majority but if the Court is equally divided in opinion —
(a) in the case where a decision of a Justice of the High Court (whether acting as a Justice 
of the High Court or in some other capacity), a decision of the Supreme Court of

Australia or a Judge of that Court or a decision of the Family Court of Australia or a 
Judge of that Court is called in question by appeal or otherwise, the decision appealed

chapter_title: CHAPTER 7 CASE LAW AND PRECEDENT
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 222 Those with a taste for fairytales seem to have thought that in some Aladdin’s cave there is hidden the Common Law in all its splendour and that on a judge’s appointment there descends on him knowledge of the magic words Open Sesame.137 Now it seems that most, if not all, judges and legal commentators reject the fairytale and accept that judges do make law.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
222
Those with a taste for fairytales seem to have thought that in some Aladdin’s cave there 
is hidden the Common Law in all its splendour and that on a judge’s appointment there 
descends on him knowledge of the magic words Open Sesame.137
Now it seems that most, if not all, judges and legal commentators reject the fairytale 
and accept that judges do make law.

text: T o a greater or lesser extent, this will present the court with a ‘judicial dilemma’.140 T o comply with the existing rule opens the court to criticism that it is out of step with community values or social developments, while to change the law invites the charge that the court is undermining certainty and breaching the separation of powers by ‘usurping the role of the legislature’.141 Given the way the doctrine of precedent operates, judges higher in the court hierarchy will have greater scope to depart from precedents than lower courts. ‘The ultimate function of developing the law must lie for the most part in the hands of an ultimate appellate court’.142 And, as Phillips and Farah Constructions illustrate, the High/uni00A0Court has guarded its privileged position jealously (notwithstanding that, on another occasion, it suggested that intermediate appellate courts are serve as ‘courts of last resort for all practical purposes’).143 Lower courts, particularly trial courts, are more likely to feel constrained by what appear to be inappropriate precedents.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS
text: In particular the chapter discusses: • the special factors considered by the High/uni00A0Court in determining whether it will overrule itself, and how these vary depending on whether the case concerns common law, legislation or the Australian Constitution; • the circumstances in which other courts in the Australian federal, state and territory hierarchies will overrule themselves; • whether and in what circumstances a court in a hierarchy is bound by a decision of another court in the same hierarchy; • the precedential value of decisions by courts in another court hierarchy; • the precedential value of decisions in another Australian court hierarchy regarding the common law of Australia, Commonwealth legislation or national scheme legislation; • the meaning of expressions commonly used in the practice of precedent such as ‘plainly wrong’ and ‘judicial comity’; • the practice of precedent in tribunals; and • the precedential value of decisions from other common law jurisdictions with particular attention to decisions of the House of Lords and the Privy Council.

text: For example, it is clear that the rationes of appeal decisions of the High/uni00A0Court are binding on all other courts.70 However, a decision of a single justice of the High/uni00A0Court is not binding because a single justice of the High/uni00A0Court does not have appellate jurisdiction.71 Similarly, the District Court of New/uni00A0South/uni00A0Wales in its civil jurisdiction is not strictly bound by decisions of single judges of the Supreme Court because there is no avenue of appeal from the former to the latter.72 This leaves the question whether courts should be bound by their own prior decisions.

text: The sections/uni00A0following explore further how the doctrine of precedent deals with situations where an Australian court is faced with precedents from other Australian court hierarchies which either deal with the same law — common law or Commonwealth legislation — or diﬀerent legislation in identical or similar terms.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS
text: PRECEDENT ACROSS DIFFERENT AUSTRALIAN APPEAL HIERARCHIES According to the ordinary operation of the doctrine of precedent, whether a precedent is strictly binding is determined by reference to the appeal hierarchy.
text_raw:
PRECEDENT ACROSS DIFFERENT AUSTRALIAN APPEAL 
HIERARCHIES
According to the ordinary operation of the doctrine of precedent, whether a precedent is 
strictly binding is determined by reference to the appeal hierarchy.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS
text: Unless the precedent comes from a court that has the power, on appeal, to overturn the decision of the present court, the precedent will not be strictly binding.
text_raw:
Unless the precedent 
comes from a court that has the power, on appeal, to overturn the decision of the present 
court, the precedent will not be strictly binding.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS

refer to contrary legislation or a binding precedent will not, in itself, render the court’s 
decision per incuriam.

Overview of the doctrine of precedent in 
Australian courts
The foregoing discussion has been somewhat lengthy , but a consistent pattern of principles 
has/uni00A0emerged across the various jurisdictions that may be summarised as follows: 
• The High/uni00A0Court is not self-bound, but will depart from its own decisions with 
reluctance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS
text: There are no set principles as to when the High/uni00A0Court will reconsider the law, although it will often apply the considerations in John and Imbree. • Other Australian courts are bound by courts higher in the same hierarchy. • Australian courts do not consider themselves bound by their own decisions, but will depart from one only when they consider the decision ‘plainly wrong’.
text_raw:
There are no set principles as to when the High/uni00A0Court will reconsider 
the law, although it will often apply the considerations in John and Imbree.
• Other Australian courts are bound by courts higher in the same hierarchy.
• Australian courts do not consider themselves bound by their own decisions, but 
will depart from one only when they consider the decision ‘plainly wrong’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS

interpretation of uniform national legislation.

DECISIONS FROM OTHER COMMON LAW JURISDICTIONS
In modern Australia, no decision of any foreign court is binding on Australian courts.

text: There are several interrelated reasons why decisions of the House of Lords, although never part of the Australia court hierarchy, have been given so much weight.
text_raw:
There are several interrelated reasons why decisions of the House of Lords, although 
never part of the Australia court hierarchy, have been given so much weight.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 8 PRECEDENT IN AUSTRALIAN COURTS
text: Of course, while the House of Lords ‘never has been’ 279 part of the Australian court hierarchy, the Privy Council was, and there was considerable overlap between the personnel of the two courts to the point where, on one view, there was a ‘convergence’ between them.280 This may be taken as an explanation for the ‘special position of decisions of the House of Lords given in the period in which appeals lay from this country to the Privy Council’.281 In Parker v/uni00A0 South/uni00A0 Australian Housing Trust (‘SAHT’)282 King/uni00A0 CJ provided another reason for the respect accorded to decisions of the House of Lords — its ‘position … as the ultimate court of appeal of the country in which the common law had its genesis and experienced its formative development’.283 It should be remembered that on settlement, so far as was applicable to the new colonies, Australia received English common law developed by the British courts headed by the House of Lords: see/uni00A02.58ﬀ.

text: The chapter covers: • the historical development and ambit of ‘legislation’, from initially being secondary to case law as the source of law, to the point of being the dominant source today; • the weight of and interaction between legislation and case law: legislation prevails over case law, but judges still interpret the law; • the parliamentary processes by which a statute is made; • key questions relating to legislation, including when it commences, is amended, revives, ceases to exist or is repealed, and when it can commence retrospectively; • the powers of the Commonwealth Parliament to disallow the legislation of the territories; • the formal structure of a statute and the signi/f_icance attached to each element; • the use and value of interpretation legislation (statutes passed in each jurisdiction providing default rules for the operation of legislation, and common terms found in legislation); • the drafting of legislation and the recent emphasis on ‘plain language’ over the ornate language previously associated with ‘legalese’; • diﬀerent types of legislation and their signi/f_icance, including forms of legislation in the Australian territories; • the nature of delegated legislation — that is, legislation made by someone authorised under an Act, rather than through the parliamentary process — including how it is made, and rules concerning its disallowance, amendment and repeal; and • quasi-delegated legislation and its signi/f_icance.

text: Terminology There are two forms of legislation: statutes or Acts (made by Parliament) and delegated or subordinate legislation (made by oﬃce-holders or bodies to whom Parliament has delegated law-making power).

There are two forms of legislation: statutes or Acts (made by Parliament) and delegated 
or subordinate legislation (made by oﬃce-holders or bodies to whom Parliament has 
delegated law-making power).

text: VALUE OR WEIGHT OF LEGISLATIVE RULES As questions can arise in relation to the common law as to which precedent to apply (that is, which precedent carries the most ‘weight’ or has the most value: see/uni00A0Chapter/uni00A08), so too in relation to statute law the issue can arise as to which legislative rule should be applied to certain circumstances.
text_raw:
VALUE OR WEIGHT OF LEGISLATIVE RULES
As questions can arise in relation to the common law as to which precedent to apply 
(that is, which precedent carries the most ‘weight’ or has the most value: see/uni00A0Chapter/uni00A08), 
so too in relation to statute law the issue can arise as to which legislative rule should 
be applied to certain circumstances.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEGISLATION
text: This issue can arise in three key contexts: later and earlier legislation on the same topic; statutes and subordinate laws on the same topic; and legislation made by Parliaments of the Commonwealth, the states and the territories on the same topic.

legislation made by Parliaments of the Commonwealth, the states and the territories on 
the same topic.

an earlier Act or subordinate law on the same topic in the same jurisdiction repeals the

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEGISLATION
text: Purposes The purposes of this Act are— (a) to apply the Legal Profession Uniform Law as a law of Victoria; and (b) to provide for certain local matters to complement that Law; and (c) to repeal the Legal Profession Act/uni00A02004; and (d) to make transitional arrangements; and (e) to make consequential amendments to other Acts.
text_raw:
Purposes 
The purposes of this Act are— 
(a) to apply the Legal Profession Uniform Law as a law of Victoria; and 
(b) to provide for certain local matters to complement that Law; and 
(c) to repeal the Legal Profession Act/uni00A02004; and 
(d) to make transitional arrangements; and 
(e) to make consequential amendments to other Acts.

have refused to look at prior cases when interpreting it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: 72 ConsoLiDATions A consolidating Act brings together the original statute law on a topic and the subsequent amendments.
text_raw:
72
ConsoLiDATions
A consolidating Act brings together the original statute law on a topic and the subsequent 
amendments.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: This is done by Parliament repealing the initial and amending Acts and re-enacting their provisions in a single statute.
text_raw:
This is done by Parliament repealing the initial and amending Acts and 
re-enacting their provisions in a single statute.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Unlike reprinting, the process is, therefore, a formal one.
text_raw:
Unlike reprinting, the process is, therefore, 
a formal one.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The principal reason for consolidating legislation is convenience; it enables people to find the law on a topic more quickly.
text_raw:
The principal reason for consolidating legislation is convenience; it enables 
people to find the law on a topic more quickly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: In the past, Victoria regularly consolidated its legislation, but the last consolidation was in 1958.
text_raw:
In the past, Victoria regularly consolidated 
its legislation, but the last consolidation was in 1958.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Consolidation of all the legislation of a jurisdiction is a formidable task and is therefore rare; it is more common to find consolidations of the legislation on a specific topic.
text_raw:
Consolidation of all the legislation 
of a jurisdiction is a formidable task and is therefore rare; it is more common to find 
consolidations of the legislation on a specific topic.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The courts have developed some special rules for interpreting consolidating Acts.
text_raw: The courts have developed some special rules for interpreting consolidating Acts.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: There is an initial presumption that a consolidating Act does not amend an existing statute or the common law.
text_raw:
There is an initial presumption that a consolidating Act does not amend an existing statute 
or the common law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Where, however, the words of a consolidating Act clearly indicate that an amendment has been made to a statute, or a change effected in the common law, the presumption does not apply.
text_raw:
Where, however, the words of a consolidating Act clearly indicate 
that an amendment has been made to a statute, or a change effected in the common law, 
the presumption does not apply.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The courts do not rely, for interpretation purposes, on pre-consolidation versions of the Act.
text_raw:
The courts do not rely, for interpretation purposes, on 
pre-consolidation versions of the Act.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The term ‘consolidated’ legislation is also used at times for Acts published online that include all current amendments within them — such Acts are not the result of ‘consolidation’ by an Act of Parliament, but rather are a type of ‘reprint’: see 9.72.

325
REPRinTED ACTs
In all Australian jurisdictions, amended Acts are routinely reprinted as an alternative to

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The original Act is reprinted to incorporate the text of amendments which have been made.
text_raw:
The original Act is reprinted to incorporate the

text: Reprints are carried out by, or under the authority of, the government printer.

text: There are no special principles of interpretation for reprinted Acts.

text: The principal difference between a reprinted Act and a consolidation is that the former is not passed by Parliament.

text: Laws reflective of this history applicable in the Australian Capital T erritory include: • Imperial Acts and New South Wales Acts in force prior to establishment of T erritory on 1 January 1911;75 • New South Wales laws in force after self-government, for example, the Crimes Act 1900 (NSW) (as it applies in the Australian Capital T erritory);76 • Commonwealth ordinances passed for the T erritory prior to 1989; • Commonwealth Acts which apply nationally and those passed specifically for the T erritory, for example, Captain’s Flat (Abatement of Pollution) Agreement Act 1975 (Cth); and • Commonwealth Acts and instruments which prevail over the Acts made by the Legislative Assembly to the extent to which they are inconsistent.77 Since self-government all Australian Capital Territory enactments are known as Acts or legislative instruments.

Laws reflective of this history applicable in the Australian Capital T erritory include:
• Imperial Acts and New South Wales  Acts in force prior to establishment of

• New South Wales laws in force after self-government, for example, the Crimes

text: 327 noRTHERn TERRiT oRY The Acts applicable in the Northern T erritory reflect the fact that the Northern T erritory was, until 1911, part of South Australia.
text_raw:
327
noRTHERn TERRiT oRY
The Acts applicable in the Northern T erritory reflect the fact that the Northern T erritory 
was, until 1911, part of South Australia.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The legislation applicable in the Northern T erritory is, accordingly: • South Australian legislation applicable in the T erritory, to continue in force until substitute laws are passed;78 • Imperial laws formerly part of the law in South Australia; • Ordinances for the T erritory made by the Commonwealth prior to self- government in 1978, now called Acts;79 • Commonwealth Acts made specifically for the T erritory since 1978, and those Acts of the Commonwealth that apply nationally.
text_raw:
The legislation applicable in the Northern 
T erritory is, accordingly:
• South Australian legislation applicable in the T erritory, to continue in force until 
substitute laws are passed;78
• Imperial laws formerly part of the law in South Australia;
• Ordinances for the T erritory made by the Commonwealth prior to self-
government in 1978, now called Acts;79
• Commonwealth Acts made specifically for the T erritory since 1978, and those 
Acts of the Commonwealth that apply nationally.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Since 1978, the Northern Territory Legislative Assembly has made Acts and authorised delegated legislation, generally in the form of regulations.
text_raw:
Since 1978, the Northern Territory Legislative Assembly has made Acts and authorised 
delegated legislation, generally in the form of regulations.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The Northern Territory of Australia Index to Legislation, formerly published twice yearly, included a chronological list of South Australian Acts in force in the Northern T erritory.
text_raw:
The Northern Territory of Australia Index to Legislation, formerly published twice yearly, 
included a chronological list of South Australian Acts in force in the Northern T erritory.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: No list of United Kingdom Acts in force has been drawn up.
text_raw: No list of United Kingdom Acts in force has been drawn up.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Under s 18 of that Act, Commonwealth laws applied to the T erritory only when specified to do so.
text_raw:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Laws passed for the T erritory were called ordinances.
text_raw: Laws passed for the T erritory were called ordinances.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The Norfolk Island Legislative Assembly was replaced in 2015 by an elected Norfolk Island Regional Council, and New South Wales law became applicable to the T erritory.81 The result is that the Commonwealth is responsible for providing national and state level services to Norfolk Island; its Regional Council provides for local government services.
text_raw:
The Norfolk Island Legislative 
Assembly was replaced in 2015 by an elected Norfolk Island Regional Council, and New 
South Wales law became applicable to the T erritory.81 The result is that the Commonwealth 
is responsible for providing national and state level services to Norfolk Island; its Regional 
Council provides for local government services.
