chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 328 Delegated legislation This is legislation made by office-holders or bodies other than Parliament.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
328
Delegated legislation
This is legislation made by office-holders or bodies other than Parliament.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The most frequently specified delegates are the Governor-General or a Governor, a Minister or a local government body.
text_raw:
The most 
frequently specified delegates are the Governor-General or a Governor, a Minister or a 
local government body.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Delegated legislation is known variously as regulations, rules, by- laws, orders, statutory instruments, subordinate law, subsidiary legislation, notices, orders in council, ordinances and proclamations.
text_raw:
Delegated legislation is known variously as regulations, rules, by-
laws, orders, statutory instruments, subordinate law, subsidiary legislation, notices, orders 
in council, ordinances and proclamations.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Commonly too such legislation is referred to as a legislative instrument.
text_raw:
Commonly too such legislation is referred 
to as a legislative instrument.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: An example of a form of delegated legislation appears in 9.95.84 There are several reasons for framing rules as delegated legislation.
text_raw:
An example of a form of delegated legislation appears 
in  9.95.84 There are several reasons for framing rules as delegated legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Matters of administration are best left for the executive arm of government, to reduce the pressure on parliamentary time; delegated legislation is more appropriate where technical matters or matters of detail are involved; and when facts which are the subject of the legislation are likely to change rapidly, it is more sensible to deal with them in a form of legislation that can be changed with relative ease.
text_raw:
Matters of 
administration are best left for the executive arm of government, to reduce the pressure 
on parliamentary time; delegated legislation is more appropriate where technical matters 
or matters of detail are involved; and when facts which are the subject of the legislation 
are likely to change rapidly, it is more sensible to deal with them in a form of legislation 
that can be changed with relative ease.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Some jurisdictions have Acts specific to delegated legislation in addition to their interpretation Acts.85 Delegated legislation is not made by the parliamentary enactment process.
text_raw:
Some jurisdictions have Acts specific to delegated 
legislation in addition to their interpretation Acts.85
Delegated legislation is not made by the parliamentary enactment process.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Methods for making delegated legislation may be prescribed by the statute which authorises the particular form of delegated legislation.
text_raw:
Methods 
for making delegated legislation may be prescribed by the statute which authorises the 
particular form of delegated legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Thus local government Acts contain provisions for making by-laws, and Acts constituting the courts provide for the making of rules of court.
text_raw:
Thus local government Acts contain provisions 
for making by-laws, and Acts constituting the courts provide for the making of rules of 
court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: 329 Regulations — the most common form of delegated legislation — are made by a process involving drafting, signature, notification and tabling in Parliament.
text_raw:
329
Regulations — the most common form of delegated legislation — are made by 
a process involving drafting, signature, notification and tabling in Parliament.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Once the instrument is drafted it must be signed by the Governor-General or Governor, generally on the advice of the Executive Council.
text_raw:
Once the 
instrument is drafted it must be signed by the Governor-General or Governor, generally 
on the advice of the Executive Council.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The next step is to publish, usually in the government Gazette, the text of the legislation or a notice that it has been made.
text_raw:
The next step is to publish, usually in the 
government Gazette, the text of the legislation or a notice that it has been made.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Finally, it is tabled in Parliament and, unless there is a motion for disallowance within a specified number of sitting days, the formal procedures for its making are complete.
text_raw:
Finally, 
it is tabled in Parliament and, unless there is a motion for disallowance within a specified 
number of sitting days, the formal procedures for its making are complete.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Failure to table the regulation in Parliament means it is void.
text_raw:
Failure to 
table the regulation in Parliament means it is void.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: 87 In all jurisdictions it is also quite common for a statute to specify a two-step procedure: signature by the relevant Minister and notification in the Gazette, no tabling in Parliament being required.
text_raw:
87 In all jurisdictions it is also quite 
common for a statute to specify a two-step procedure: signature by the relevant Minister 
and notification in the Gazette, no tabling in Parliament being required.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: PARLiAMEnTARY sCRUTinY AnD C onsULTATion Parliamentary control generally involves scrutiny of the principal forms of delegated legislation by a committee of members.
text_raw:
PARLiAMEnTARY sCRUTinY AnD C onsULTATion
Parliamentary control generally involves scrutiny of the principal forms of delegated 
legislation by a committee of members.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Guidelines — typical of which are those devised for use by the Senate Standing Committee for the Scrutiny of Delegated Legislation88 — are used to ensure that subordinate laws do not, for example, unduly trespass on individual rights, deal with matter more suitable for inclusion in an Act, or authorise the making of unreviewable decisions that affect people.
text_raw:
Guidelines — typical of which are those devised 
for use by the Senate Standing Committee for the Scrutiny of Delegated Legislation88 — 
are used to ensure that subordinate laws do not, for example, unduly trespass on individual 
rights, deal with matter more suitable for inclusion in an Act, or authorise the making of 
unreviewable decisions that affect people.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Subordinate laws which breach the guidelines are recommended for disallowance or may be required to be redrafted.
text_raw:
Subordinate laws which breach the guidelines 
are recommended for disallowance or may be required to be redrafted.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: An alternative and more radical approach to the scrutiny of subordinate laws has been adopted in some jurisdictions.
text_raw:
An alternative and more radical approach to the scrutiny of subordinate laws has 
been adopted in some jurisdictions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Additional steps, involving preparation of a regulatory impact statement and consultation with the public, occur before subordinate legislation is made, and this process is mandatory in some jurisdictions.89 QUAsi-DELEgATED LEgisLATion Increasingly, government departments and agencies are resorting to policy as a form of subordinate instrument.
text_raw:
Additional steps, involving preparation of a regulatory 
impact statement and consultation with the public, occur before subordinate legislation is 
made, and this process is mandatory in some jurisdictions.89
QUAsi-DELEgATED LEgisLATion
Increasingly, government departments and agencies are resorting to policy as a form 
of subordinate instrument.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Policy is not strictly delegated legislation and only some policy instruments require compliance with comparable formalities such as tabling in Parliament.
text_raw:
Policy is not strictly delegated legislation and only some 
policy instruments require compliance with comparable formalities such as tabling in 
Parliament.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The rules sometimes take the form of ‘quasi-legislative’ instruments and have been dubbed ‘soft law’.
text_raw:
The rules sometimes take the form of ‘quasi-legislative’ instruments and 
have been dubbed ‘soft law’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Commonly, soft law appears in the form of codes of practice, manuals, circulars and other policies.
text_raw:
Commonly, soft law appears in the form of codes of 
practice, manuals, circulars and other policies.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Unlike the more orthodox forms of delegated legislation, such as regulations, legislative instruments and statutory rules, these instruments have generally not been required to be numbered or published and are hard to find.
text_raw:
Unlike the more orthodox forms of 
delegated legislation, such as regulations, legislative instruments and statutory rules, 
these instruments have generally not been required to be numbered or published 
and are hard to find.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: However, amendments to the Freedom of Information Act 1982 (Cth) emphasise that information produced by government is a national resource.
text_raw:
However, amendments to the Freedom of Information Act 1982 
(Cth) emphasise that information produced by government is a national resource.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: A consequence is that presumptively such information should be publicly available unless there is a demonstrated reason to the contrary.
text_raw:
A consequence is that presumptively such information should be publicly available 
unless there is a demonstrated reason to the contrary.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Consequently, much of this material is now available, or at least notified, on agency websites under the Freedom of Information Publication Scheme or disclosure logs.
text_raw:
Consequently, much of this 
material is now available, or at least notified, on agency websites under the Freedom 
of Information Publication Scheme or disclosure logs.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Comparable developments are occurring in some of the states and territories.
text_raw:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 330 A deficiency is that quasi-delegated legislation and soft law, other than disallowable instruments, are not required to be scrutinised by parliamentary committees to ensure that they comply with standards designed to protect individual rights.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
330
A deficiency is that quasi-delegated legislation and soft law, other than disallowable 
instruments, are not required to be scrutinised by parliamentary committees to ensure that 
they comply with standards designed to protect individual rights.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The distinction between delegated legislation and disallowable instruments has been largely avoided under the Legislation Act 2003 (Cth), which defines instruments that are legislative instruments and those that are not.
text_raw:
The distinction between 
delegated legislation and disallowable instruments has been largely avoided under the 
Legislation Act 2003 (Cth), which defines instruments that are legislative instruments and 
those that are not.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: CoMMEnCEMEnT oF DELEgATED LEgisLATion As with Acts, default rules as to the commencement of delegated legislation vary between the jurisdictions.

As with Acts, default rules as to the commencement of delegated legislation vary between 
the jurisdictions.

text_raw:

Amendment
Delegated legislation can be amended by later statutes or later delegated legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Amendment by statute is rare.96 Repeal As with amendment, delegated legislation can be repealed by subsequent statutes or delegated legislation, although repeal by statute is infrequent.
text_raw:
Amendment by statute is rare.96 
Repeal
As with amendment, delegated legislation can be repealed by subsequent statutes or 
delegated legislation, although repeal by statute is infrequent.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: The repeal may be express or implied.
text_raw:
The repeal may be express 
or implied.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Delegated legislation is impliedly repealed if it is inconsistent with a later Act or delegated legislation.
text_raw:
Delegated legislation is impliedly repealed if it is inconsistent with a later Act 
or delegated legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: Automatic repeal Automatic repeal can occur in several ways.
text_raw:
Automatic repeal
Automatic repeal can occur in several ways.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: If an Act (or relevant sections of an Act) which authorises delegated legislation is repealed, any delegated legislation made under the Act is usually automatically repealed, although some jurisdictions provide for it to continue if not inconsistent with the repealing Act.97 The second type of automatic repeal is a more recent mechanism designed to ensure that subordinate laws do not become outdated.
text_raw:
If an Act (or relevant sections of an Act) 
which authorises delegated legislation is repealed, any delegated legislation made under 
the Act is usually automatically repealed, although some jurisdictions provide for it to 
continue if not inconsistent with the repealing Act.97 
The second type of automatic repeal is a more recent mechanism designed to 
ensure that subordinate laws do not become outdated.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: In the Commonwealth, New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria, delegated legislation ceases to operate after a fixed period (for example, 7 or 10 years) from the date it is made, unless exempt.98 Such sunset provisions are a form of automatic repeal.
text_raw:
In the Commonwealth, New 
South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, Tasmania and Victoria, delegated legislation 
ceases to operate after a fixed period (for example, 7 or 10 years) from the date it is made, 
unless exempt.98 Such sunset provisions are a form of automatic repeal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 9 LEgisLATion
text: This statutory device, which is designed to ensure that the continuation of the delegated legislation is justified, and that it does not remain in force indefinitely, has had a marked impact on the volume of subordinate legislation.

liabilities incurred under the delegated legislation are not disturbed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: 339 Introduction This chapter considers the common law rules and statutory rules relating to the interpretation of statutes.
text_raw:
339
Introduction
This chapter considers the common law rules and statutory rules relating to the 
interpretation of statutes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: It covers: • why interpretation of legislation is a key area of law; • the goal of interpretation, which is to give effect to the intention of Parliament in drafting the legislation, as determined by the courts on the basis of the text of the legislation, rather than other sources; • the historical common law rules taken by judges to interpreting statutes, including the literal approach, golden rule and purposive approach — these rules, which emphasised the primacy of the text, are now largely of historical interest in light of changes in interpretation legislation and common law approaches; • the provisions of interpretation legislation that require courts to prefer interpretations that give effect to the purpose of legislation; • different ways of determining purpose; and • the common law ‘modern approach’ of using ‘context’ to interpret legislation, including its purpose.
text_raw:
It covers:
• why interpretation of legislation is a key area of law;
• the goal of interpretation, which is to give effect to the intention of Parliament 
in drafting the legislation, as determined by the courts on the basis of the text of 
the legislation, rather than other sources;
• the historical common law rules taken by judges to interpreting statutes, including 
the literal approach, golden rule and purposive approach — these rules, 
which emphasised the primacy of the text, are now largely of historical interest 
in light of changes in interpretation legislation and common law approaches;
• the provisions of interpretation legislation that require courts to prefer 
interpretations that give effect to the purpose of legislation;
• different ways of determining purpose; and
• the common law ‘modern approach’ of using ‘context’ to interpret legislation, 
including its purpose.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: Legislation, as noted in Chapter 9 , is the most frequently encountered source of rules of law.
text_raw:
Legislation, as noted in Chapter 9 , is the most frequently encountered source 
of rules of law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: To the extent that the rules in legislation are in fixed verbal form, the interpretation of legislation is less problematic than the interpretation of case law.
text_raw:
To the extent that the rules in legislation are in fixed verbal form, 
the interpretation of legislation is less problematic than the interpretation of case law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: Nevertheless, legislation is frequently complex and its meaning can sometimes be difficult to determine.
text_raw:
Nevertheless, legislation is frequently complex and its meaning can sometimes be 
difficult to determine.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: Unsurprisingly, therefore, lawyers spend much of their time interpreting legislation in order to decide how it applies in particular circumstances.
text_raw:
Unsurprisingly, therefore, lawyers spend much of their time 
interpreting legislation in order to decide how it applies in particular circumstances.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: To do so requires an appreciation of the rules devised by the courts for the interpretive task.
text_raw:
To do so requires an appreciation of the rules devised by the courts for the interpretive 
task.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: In 2001 Chief Justice Spigelman, of the Supreme Court of New South Wales, wrote that ‘[t]he law of statutory interpretation has become the most important single aspect of legal practice.
text_raw:
In 2001 Chief Justice Spigelman, of the Supreme Court of New South Wales, 
wrote that ‘[t]he law of statutory interpretation has become the most important single 
aspect of legal practice.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: Applying that assumption to legislation in particular, it seems reasonable to suggest that most Australian judges accept the proposition that clarity of meaning on the face of a legislative provision is an attainable objective for a legislative drafter.5 In his short judgment in Secretary, Department of Health v Harvey,6 from which this chapter’s epigraph is taken, Meagher JA made the unexceptional assumption that his responsibility was to determine the meaning of the relevant Act and to apply it to the issue(s) under consideration.
text_raw:
Applying that assumption to legislation in particular, 
it seems reasonable to suggest that most Australian judges accept the proposition that 
clarity of meaning on the face of a legislative provision is an attainable objective for a 
legislative drafter.5
In his short judgment in Secretary, Department of Health v Harvey,6 from which this 
chapter’s epigraph is taken, Meagher  JA made the unexceptional assumption that his 
responsibility was to determine the meaning of the relevant Act and to apply it to the 
issue(s) under consideration.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: In the process of establishing what legislation means, two related interpretive techniques are regularly employed.
text_raw:
In the process of establishing what legislation means, two 
related interpretive techniques are regularly employed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: The first is to seek to discover the purpose of a provision, as that may be informative.
text_raw:

what we do now … In constitutional, statutory and contractual interpretation there does

Although this chapter concentrates on the literal and purposive approaches to

and sections should be interpreted in context is also considered.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: Summary of principles Here are the key principles covered in this chapter: • The goal of interpretation is to give effect to the ‘intention of Parliament’ as revealed primarily by the text of the statute — other expressions of parliamentary intent are regarded as extrinsic materials: see 10.6. • Historically, the focus of interpretation was the ‘literal rule’, which gave effect to the words of the statute according to their ordinary meaning, regardless of what that result might produce: see 10.9–10.10.
text_raw:
Summary of principles
Here are the key principles covered in this chapter:
• The goal of interpretation is to give effect to the ‘intention of Parliament’ as 
revealed primarily by the text of the statute — other expressions of parliamentary 
intent are regarded as extrinsic materials: see 10.6.
• Historically, the focus of interpretation was the ‘literal rule’, which gave effect 
to the words of the statute according to their ordinary meaning, regardless of 
what that result might produce: see  10.9–10.10.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon

text_raw:
(a) The ‘golden rule’, which allowed departure from the words of the statute to 
correct an error or where the result was absurd: see 10.11–10.12.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon

text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 342 The goal of interpretation As Higgins J stated in the famous High Court case ‘Engineers’ Case’,8 ‘the fundamental rule of interpretation, to which all others are subordinate, is that a statute is to be expounded according to the intent of parliament that made it’.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
342
The goal of interpretation
As Higgins J stated in the famous High Court case ‘Engineers’ Case’,8 ‘the fundamental rule 
of interpretation, to which all others are subordinate, is that a statute is to be expounded 
according to the intent of parliament that made it’.

text: As the High Court has stated on many occasions, ‘the task of statutory construction must begin with consideration of the text itself’.10 Thus, it has been noted that ‘the intention of Parliament is somewhat of a fiction’.11 As former Chief Justice Robert French has said:

text: 343 LITERAL APPRo ACH In the Engineers’ Case, Higgins J defined and explained the literal approach (or rule, as he called it):
text_raw:
343
LITERAL APPRo ACH
In the Engineers’ Case, Higgins J defined and explained the literal approach (or rule, as he 
called it):

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: The fundamental rule of interpretation, to which all others are subordinate, is that a statute is to be expounded according to the intent of the Parliament that made it; and that intention has to be found by an examination of the language used in the statute as a whole.
text_raw:
The fundamental rule of interpretation, to which all others are subordinate, is that a 
statute is to be expounded according to the intent of the Parliament that made it; and that 
intention has to be found by an examination of the language used in the statute as a whole.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: The question is, what does the language mean; and when we find what the language means, in its ordinary and natural sense, it is our duty to obey that meaning, even if we think the result to be inconvenient or impolitic or improbable.13 Stated in this form, the literal approach would have excluded the possibility of applying any other approach, however unsatisfactory the result.
text_raw:
The question is, what does the language mean; and when we find what the language means, 
in its ordinary and natural sense, it is our duty to obey that meaning, even if we think the 
result to be inconvenient or impolitic or improbable.13
Stated in this form, the literal approach would have excluded the possibility of applying 
any other approach, however unsatisfactory the result.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: It is now accepted that this approach complements the purposive approach.
text_raw:
It is now accepted that this 
approach complements the purposive approach.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: PURPosIVE APPRo ACH The common law purposive approach to interpretation of legislation is applied by determining the purpose of Parliament in passing the legislation or the particular provision in question, and adopting an interpretation of the words that is consistent with that purpose.
text_raw:
PURPosIVE APPRo ACH
The common law purposive approach to interpretation of legislation is applied by 
determining the purpose of Parliament in passing the legislation or the particular 
provision in question, and adopting an interpretation of the words that is consistent with 
that purpose.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: This approach has its origins in the so-called mischief rule which was set out in 1584 in Heydon’s Case.27 In this case all of the judges met [a]nd it was resolved by them, that for the sure and true interpretation of all statutes in general (be they penal or beneficial, restrictive or enlarging of the common law), four things are to be discerned and considered:– (1st.) What was the common law before the making of the Act.
text_raw:
This approach has its origins in the so-called mischief rule which was set

general (be they penal or beneficial, restrictive or enlarging of the common law), four 
things are to be discerned and considered:–
(1st.) What was the common law before the making of the Act.

text: A ‘purposive’ approach founders in the shallows of a multitude of obscure, uncertain and even apparently conflicting purposes.35 If we reflect on the nature of the purposive approach it will be clear that we have all used it, usually intuitively, to interpret documents.
text_raw:
A ‘purposive’ 
approach founders in the shallows of a multitude of obscure, uncertain and even apparently 
conflicting purposes.35
If we reflect on the nature of the purposive approach it will be clear that we 
have all used it, usually intuitively, to interpret documents.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: It often comes down to a conviction that our interpretations may be closer to the original intentions of a document’s author(s) if we go beyond the surface meanings of the words, seek to establish the underlying intentions of the author(s), and then strive for interpretations that give effect to those intentions.
text_raw:
It often comes down 
to a conviction that our interpretations may be closer to the original intentions of 
a document’s author(s) if we go beyond the surface meanings of the words, seek to 
establish the underlying intentions of the author(s), and then strive for interpretations 
that give effect to those intentions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon

text: The present matters are two actions by the Maritime Services Board of New South Wales (which I will call ‘the MSB’) to recover as a debt substantial sums of money from two shipowners … under s 7E(3) … The parties asked me to determine as a separate issue, before the trial of the actions, and pursuant to the Supreme Court Rules 1970, Pt 31, r 2, the meaning and effect of the words in s 7E(3) ‘the total amount of those expenses and liabilities’ … The critical question in the present case is whether … the plaintiff is entitled to recover from the relevant defendant sums representing the wages payable to permanent employees, some of whom were diverted from other tasks for the purpose of assisting in the clean-up of the spillage of oil, overhead expenses relating to them, and the cost of using its equipment which would or may have been employed for other purposes.

The present matters are two actions by the Maritime Services Board of 
New South Wales (which I will call ‘the MSB’) to recover as a debt substantial sums of

as a separate issue, before the trial of the actions, and pursuant to the Supreme Court

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: Each defendant conceded that it was liable to reimburse the plaintiff for moneys which it has paid or liabilities which it has incurred to third parties (eg outside contractors, etc) but claimed that the expressions ‘expenses and liabilities’ (s 7E) … did not go beyond this … In the present case it would, in my opinion, require clear words to bring about the result that, in every case where the MSB contracted out the whole or part of the work of cleaning up the results of oil pollution, it could recover from the owner of the vessel from which the oil was discharged in respect of all moneys paid out by it pursuant to such a contract, but could recover nothing (except perhaps overtime payments if any were made) where it diverted its own men and materials from other tasks and used them in the clean-up operation.

Section 138 of 
the Act provides that the term ‘working out the meaning of an Act’ means:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: (a) resolving an ambiguous or obscure provision of the Act; or (b) confirming or displacing the apparent meaning of the Act; or (c) finding the meaning of the Act when its apparent meaning leads to a result that is manifestly absurd or is unreasonable; or (d) finding the meaning of the Act in any other case.

(a) resolving an ambiguous or obscure provision of the Act; or

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: As Mason J stated, to read the section in isolation from the enactment of which it forms a part is to offend against the cardinal rule of statutory interpretation that requires the words of a statute to be read in their context … Problems of legal interpretation are not solved satisfactorily by ritual incantations which emphasize the clarity of meaning which words have when viewed in isolation, divorced from their context.
text_raw:
As 
Mason J stated, 
to read the section in isolation from the enactment of which it forms a part is to offend 
against the cardinal rule of statutory interpretation that requires the words of a statute to 
be read in their context … Problems of legal interpretation are not solved satisfactorily 
by ritual incantations which emphasize the clarity of meaning which words have when 
viewed in isolation, divorced from their context.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon
text: The modern approach to interpretation insists that the context be considered in the first instance, especially in the case of general words, and not merely at some later stage when ambiguity might be thought to arise.63 But what is meant by ‘context’?
text_raw:
The modern approach to interpretation 
insists that the context be considered in the first instance, especially in the case of general 
words, and not merely at some later stage when ambiguity might be thought to arise.63
But what is meant by ‘context’?

In statutory interpretation, ‘context’ may 
have essentially three meanings.

construction in which a term appears.

chapter_title: Chapter  12. The third is context ‘in its widest sense’, which was discussed in the
text: [T]he modern approach to statutory interpretation (a) insists that the context be considered in the first instance, not merely at some later stage when ambiguity might be thought to arise, and (b) uses ‘context’ in its widest sense to include such things as the existing state of the law and the mischief which, by legitimate means such as those just mentioned, one may discern the statute was intended to remedy … Instances of general words in a statute being so construed by their context are numerous.
text_raw:
[T]he modern approach to statutory interpretation (a) insists that the context be considered 
in the first instance, not merely at some later stage when ambiguity might be thought to 
arise, and (b) uses ‘context’ in its widest sense to include such things as the existing state 
of the law and the mischief which, by legitimate means such as those just mentioned, one 
may discern the statute was intended to remedy … Instances of general words in a statute 
being so construed by their context are numerous.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 10 APPRo ACHEs To InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon

Rather, his Lordship was saying that in the absence of any one of

appear in the statute.

operate in a particular way, even if the words used would not, on a literal construction, 
so apply or operate.

text: At issue in Lowe was whether the term ‘relies’ in statutory provisions of the Jury Directions Act 2013 (Vic) that required a mandatory direction to the jury where the prosecution ‘relies’ on evidence of incriminating conduct should be ‘read down’ — that is, given a narrower reading — as if the provision stated ‘explicitly relies’.

relies’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The chapter concentrates on the principles governing the permissible uses of extrinsic materials in the interpretive process, including: • how judges have used different kinds of extrinsic materials, including parliamentary documents and international agreements; • the common law ‘modern approach’ to using extrinsic materials as part of the wider context of the legislation, in particular to determine the mischief that the legislation addresses; and • the statutory provisions in interpretation legislation that provide for the use of extrinsic materials to confirm the meaning of the legislation, or determine the meaning where there is ambiguity or an absurd result.
text_raw:
The chapter concentrates on the principles 
governing the permissible uses of extrinsic materials in the interpretive process, including:
• how judges have used different kinds of extrinsic materials, including 
parliamentary documents and international agreements; 
• the common law ‘modern approach’ to using extrinsic materials as part of the 
wider context of the legislation, in particular to determine the mischief that the 
legislation addresses; and 
• the statutory provisions in interpretation legislation that provide for the use of 
extrinsic materials to confirm the meaning of the legislation, or determine the 
meaning where there is ambiguity or an absurd result.

Summary of principles
The following principles are discussed in this chapter:
• Extrinsic materials are materials outside a statute that can shed light on the 
statute’s contents and purpose.
• Both common law and statutory provisions permit the use of extrinsic materials 
to assist in statutory interpretation.

text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
368
• Historically, common law principles only allowed limited use of extrinsic 
materials: see 11.4–11.11.
• Under the common law ‘modern approach’ to statutory interpretation, extrinsic 
materials form part of the context of a statute, and may be consulted to assist in 
its interpretation, including to determine the law prior to the statute and the 
‘mischief’ the statute is intended to address: see 11.12–11.19. 
• Under interpretation legislation, except in South Australia, reference to extrinsic 
materials is also permitted (though not required) either:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (a) to confirm the meaning is the ordinary meaning; or (b) to determine the meaning of a provision where a ‘threshold test’ is met: namely, that, when read in light of the statute’s purpose, a provision is ambiguous or obscure, or the ordinary meaning leads to an absurd or unreasonable result: see 11.21–11.26. • The Australian Capital T erritory and Victorian provisions are not subject to these specific limitations: see 11.27 and 11.28, respectively.
text_raw:

(b) to determine the meaning of a provision where a ‘threshold test’ is met: namely,

text: HISTORICAL APPROACH TO PARLIAMENTARY AND RELATED MATERIALS The traditional common law rule on the use of parliamentary materials was quite restrictive; as recently as 1977, in Commissioner for Prices and Consumer Affairs (SA) v Charles Moore (Aust) Pty Ltd,3 the High Court had affirmed the common law rule that the courts would not refer to reports of parliamentary debates for any purpose as an aid to the construction of a statute.
text_raw:
HISTORICAL APPROACH TO PARLIAMENTARY AND RELATED 
MATERIALS
The traditional common law rule on the use of parliamentary materials was quite 
restrictive; as recently as 1977, in Commissioner for Prices and Consumer Affairs (SA) v Charles 
Moore (Aust) Pty Ltd,3 the High Court had affirmed the common law rule that the courts 
would not refer to reports of parliamentary debates for any purpose as an aid to the 
construction of a statute.

370

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The effect of s 4(1) was that ‘refugee’ in the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) had to be interpreted in accordance with art 31 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (‘Vienna Convention’),19 which sets out the following principles for the interpretation of international treaties:
text_raw:
The effect of s 4(1) was that ‘refugee’ in the Migration Act 1958 (Cth) had 
to be interpreted in accordance with art 31 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties 
(‘Vienna Convention’),19 which sets out the following principles for the interpretation of 
international treaties:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: 1 A treaty shall be interpreted in good faith in accordance with the ordinary meaning to be given to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and purpose.

to be given to the terms of the treaty in their context and in the light of its object and

text: 2 The context for the purpose of the interpretation of a treaty shall comprise, in addition to the text, including its preamble and annexes:

to the text, including its preamble and annexes:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Interpretive assistance may be gained from extrinsic sources (Art 32) in order to confirm the meaning resulting from the application of Art 31, or to determine the meaning when interpretation according to Art 31 leaves the meaning ‘ambiguous or obscure’ or ‘leads to a result which is manifestly absurd or unreasonable’.26 Article 32 thus allows recourse to supplementary materials to aid in the interpretation of treaties in similar circumstances to where Australian interpretation legislation allows recourse to extrinsic materials in the interpretation of domestic statutes: see 11.21ff.

Interpretive assistance may be gained from extrinsic sources (Art 32) in order to 
confirm the meaning resulting from the application of Art 31, or to determine the meaning 
when interpretation according to Art 31 leaves the meaning ‘ambiguous or obscure’ or 
‘leads to a result which is manifestly absurd or unreasonable’.26

of treaties in similar circumstances to where Australian interpretation legislation allows 
recourse to extrinsic materials in the interpretation of domestic statutes: see  11.21ff.

text: MODERN APPROACH TO STATUTORY INTERPRETATION Notwithstanding the statutory limitations on the consideration of extrinsic materials in the interpretation of legislation discussed in 11.21ff, the common law ‘modern approach’ to interpretation permits the use of those materials in circumstances in which their consideration is not sanctioned by those statutory provisions.

MODERN APPROACH TO STATUTORY INTERPRETATION
Notwithstanding the statutory limitations on the consideration of extrinsic materials in the 
interpretation of legislation discussed in 11.21ff, the common law ‘modern approach’ to 
interpretation permits the use of those materials in circumstances in which their consideration 
is not sanctioned by those statutory provisions.

text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 374 High Court authority supports the continued application of the ‘modern approach’ to consideration of a statute’s context in its interpretation.49 Nonetheless, there still remains some caution with regard to the usefulness of extrinsic materials.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
374
High Court authority supports the continued application of the ‘modern approach’ to 
consideration of a statute’s context in its interpretation.49 
Nonetheless, there still remains some caution with regard to the usefulness of extrinsic 
materials.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Thus, in Attorney General of New South Wales v Melco Resorts & Entertainment Ltd,50 the New South Wales Court of Appeal cited CIC Insurance to justify looking at an Act’s context, but — referring to Alcan — the Court adopted an interpretation that did ‘not depend on’ and was ‘not influenced by’ extrinsic materials, although they had been used by the judge at first instance.
text_raw:
Thus, in Attorney General of New South Wales v Melco Resorts & Entertainment 
Ltd,50 the New South Wales Court of Appeal cited CIC Insurance to justify looking at an 
Act’s context, but — referring to Alcan — the Court adopted an interpretation that did 
‘not depend on’ and was ‘not influenced by’ extrinsic materials, although they had been 
used by the judge at first instance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: 51 The Court concluded that as the second reading speech in this instance was unclear, it illustrated ‘the dangers and potential pitfalls that resort to extrinsic materials may have’.52 How might the relative weight to be placed on ‘text’ and ‘context’, in particular extrinsic materials, be determined?

speech in this instance was unclear, it illustrated ‘the dangers and potential pitfalls that

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Perhaps one approach lies in a recognition that what is often expressed as a concern about timing — whether context in its widest sense, including extrinsic materials, is considered ‘at the start’, as in CIC Insurance, or ‘after’ the exhaustion of other approaches, as in Saeed — is more readily conceptualised as a concern about importance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The fundamental object of statutory construction is to ascertain legislative intention, understood as the intention that the courts will impute to the legislature by a process of construction, by reference to the language of the statute viewed as a whole.
text_raw:
The fundamental object of statutory construction is to ascertain legislative intention, 
understood as the intention that the courts will impute to the legislature by a process of 
construction, by reference to the language of the statute viewed as a whole.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The starting point for this process of construction is the words of the provision in question read in the context of the statute.
text_raw:
The starting 
point for this process of construction is the words of the provision in question read in the 
context of the statute.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Context is also spoken of in a broader sense as including the general purpose and policy of the legislation, in particular the mischief to which the statute is directed and which the legislature intended to remedy.
text_raw:
Context is also spoken of in a broader sense as including the general 
purpose and policy of the legislation, in particular the mischief to which the statute is 
directed and which the legislature intended to remedy.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It is legitimate to resort to materials outside the statute, but it is necessary to bear in mind the purpose of doing so and the process of construction to which it is directed.
text_raw:
It is legitimate to resort to materials outside the statute, but it is necessary to bear in mind 
the purpose of doing so and the process of construction to which it is directed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: That purpose is, generally speaking, to identify the policy of the statute in order to better understand the language and intended operation of the statute.

text: Section 15AB provides:
text_raw: Section 15AB provides:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (1) Subject to sub-section (3), in the interpretation of a provision of an Act, if any material not forming part of the Act is capable of assisting in the ascertainment of the meaning of the provision, consideration may be given to that material — (a) to confirm that the meaning of the provision is the ordinary meaning conveyed by the text of the provision taking into account its context in the Act and the purpose or object underlying the Act; or (b) to determine the meaning of the provision when — (i) the provision is ambiguous or obscure; or (ii) the ordinary meaning conveyed by the text of the provision taking into account its context in the Act and the purpose or object underlying the Act leads to a result that is manifestly absurd or is unreasonable.
text_raw:
(1) Subject to sub-section (3), in the interpretation of a provision of an Act, if any material 
not forming part of the Act is capable of assisting in the ascertainment of the meaning 
of the provision, consideration may be given to that material —
(a) to confirm that the meaning of the provision is the ordinary meaning conveyed by 
the text of the provision taking into account its context in the Act and the purpose 
or object underlying the Act; or
(b) to determine the meaning of the provision when —
(i) the provision is ambiguous or obscure; or
(ii) the ordinary meaning conveyed by the text of the provision taking into account 
its context in the Act and the purpose or object underlying the Act leads to a 
result that is manifestly absurd or is unreasonable.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (2) Without limiting the generality of sub-section (1), the material that may be considered in accordance with that sub-section in the interpretation of a provision of an Act includes — (a) all matters not forming part of the Act that are set out in the document containing the text of the Act as printed by the Government Printer;
text_raw:
(2) Without limiting the generality of sub-section (1), the material that may be considered 
in accordance with that sub-section  in the interpretation of a provision of an Act 
includes —
(a) all matters not forming part of the Act that are set out in the document containing 
the text of the Act as printed by the Government Printer;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (b) any relevant report of a Royal Commission, Law Reform Commission, committee of inquiry or other similar body that was laid before either House of the Parliament before the time when the provision was enacted;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (c) any relevant report of a committee of the Parliament or of either House of the Parliament that was made to the Parliament or that House of the Parliament before the time when the provision was enacted;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (d) any treaty or other international agreement that is referred to in the Act;
text_raw: (d) any treaty or other international agreement that is referred to in the Act;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (e) any explanatory memorandum relating to the Bill containing the provision, or any other relevant document, that was laid before, or furnished to the members of, either House of the Parliament by a Minister before the time when the provision was enacted;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (f) the speech made to a House of the Parliament by a Minister on the occasion of the moving by that Minister of a motion that the Bill containing the provision be read a second time in that House;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (g) any document (whether or not a document to which a preceding paragraph applies) that is declared by the Act to be a relevant document for the purposes of this section; and (h) any relevant material in the Journals of the Senate, in the Votes and Proceedings of the House of Representatives or in any official record of debates in the Parliament or either House of the Parliament.
text_raw:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (3) In determining whether consideration should be given to any material in accordance with sub-section (1), or in considering the weight to be given to any such material, regard shall be had, in addition to any other relevant matters, to — (a) the desirability of persons being able to rely on the ordinary meaning conveyed by the text of the provision taking into account its context in the Act and the purpose or object underlying the Act; and (b) the need to avoid prolonging legal or other proceedings without compensating advantage.
text_raw:
(3) In determining whether consideration should be given to any material in accordance 
with sub-section (1), or in considering the weight to be given to any such material, 
regard shall be had, in addition to any other relevant matters, to —
(a) the desirability of persons being able to rely on the ordinary meaning conveyed by 
the text of the provision taking into account its context in the Act and the purpose 
or object underlying the Act; and
(b) the need to avoid prolonging legal or other proceedings without compensating 
advantage.

reference to extrinsic materials to have the potential to change an interpretation which 
would otherwise have been arrived at, it is necessary for a court to conclude that one of 
the conditions in s 15AB(1)(b)(i) or (ii) is present; that is, there is a ‘threshold test’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The court must conclude, ignoring any extrinsic materials, that the provision in question is ‘ambiguous’ or ‘obscure’ or, taking account of its context and the underlying purpose or object of the Act, that the ordinary meaning leads to a result that is ‘manifestly absurd’ or ‘unreasonable’.61 The word ‘ambiguous’ is broadly interpreted. ‘It extends to circumstances in which the intention of the legislature is, for whatever reason, doubtful.’62 The ‘threshold test’ described above is a limitation on the operation of s 15AB compared with s 15AA of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901.

text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 378 Another limitation is that extrinsic materials should not be taken into account when they merely indicate a view as to the meaning of legislation in existence at the time when the view is expressed.66 This latter limitation applies equally under the common law.67 It is important to remember that s 15AB and its equivalents empower courts to have recourse to extrinsic materials under certain circumstances, rather than obligating them to do so pursuant to certain criteria.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
378
Another limitation is that extrinsic materials should not be taken into account when 
they merely indicate a view as to the meaning of legislation in existence at the time when 
the view is expressed.66 This latter limitation applies equally under the common law.67
It is important to remember that s 15AB and its equivalents empower courts to 
have recourse to extrinsic materials under certain circumstances, rather than obligating 
them to do so pursuant to certain criteria.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Therefore, even where the ‘threshold test’ is met, the courts are not compelled to refer to extrinsic materials.
text_raw:
Therefore, even where the ‘threshold test’ 
is met, the courts are not compelled to refer to extrinsic materials.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Section 15AB(3) requires the courts, in determining whether recourse to extrinsic materials is justified, to have regard to the desirability of being able to rely on the text of the statute itself, without needing to have recourse to extrinsic materials, and the desirability of avoiding prolonged litigation without ‘compensating advantage’.
text_raw:
Section  15AB(3) 
requires the courts, in determining whether recourse to extrinsic materials is justified, 
to have regard to the desirability of being able to rely on the text of the statute itself, 
without needing to have recourse to extrinsic materials, and the desirability of avoiding 
prolonged litigation without ‘compensating advantage’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A similar provision exists in the corresponding sections of other legislation.

corresponding sections of other legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It is also important to remember that the ‘modern approach’, permitting recourse to extrinsic materials at common law as part of the context ‘in its widest sense’ of the statute, exists alongside the provisions of interpretation legislation, and there is no ‘threshold test’ to be met before it can be applied: see 11.12.
text_raw:
It is also important to remember that the ‘modern approach’, permitting recourse to 
extrinsic materials at common law as part of the context ‘in its widest sense’ of the statute, 
exists alongside the provisions of interpretation legislation, and there is no ‘threshold test’ 
to be met before it can be applied: see 11.12.

text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 380 Here we can see that the judge first determined that the threshold test was met, namely, the absurdity and unreasonableness that flowed from giving the phrase ‘constant care and attention’ its ordinary, literal meaning, which would render the primary care provider ineligible to receive the allowance in question if the child attended a day school.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
380
Here we can see that the judge first determined that the threshold test was met, 
namely, the absurdity and unreasonableness that flowed from giving the phrase ‘constant 
care and attention’ its ordinary, literal meaning, which would render the primary care 
provider ineligible to receive the allowance in question if the child attended a day school.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: This enabled the judge, under Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth) s 15AB(1)(b)(ii), to have reference to extrinsic materials — in this particular instance the Minister’s second reading speech, which explicitly provided that attendance at a day school would not affect eligibility.
text_raw:
This enabled the judge, under Acts Interpretation Act  1901 (Cth) s  15AB(1)(b)(ii), to 
have reference to extrinsic materials — in this particular instance the Minister’s second 
reading speech, which explicitly provided that attendance at a day school would not affect 
eligibility.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Section 35 provides:
text_raw: Section 35 provides:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: In the interpretation of a provision of an Act or subordinate instrument — (a) a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act or subordinate instrument (whether or not that purpose or object is expressly stated in the Act or subordinate instrument) shall be preferred to a construction that would not promote that purpose or object; and (b) consideration may be given to any matter or document that is relevant including but not limited to — (i) all indications provided by the Act or subordinate instrument as printed by authority, including punctuation;
text_raw:
In the interpretation of a provision of an Act or subordinate instrument —
(a) a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act or 
subordinate instrument (whether or not that purpose or object is expressly stated in 
the Act or subordinate instrument) shall be preferred to a construction that would not 
promote that purpose or object; and
(b) consideration may be given to any matter or document that is relevant including but 
not limited to —
(i) all indications provided by the Act or subordinate instrument as printed by 
authority, including punctuation;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (ii) reports of proceedings in any House of the Parliament;
text_raw: (ii) reports of proceedings in any House of the Parliament;

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: (iii) explanatory memoranda or other documents laid before or otherwise presented to any House of the Parliament; and (iv) reports of Royal Commissions, Parliamentary Committees, Law Reform Commissioners and Commissions, Boards of Inquiry or other similar bodies.
text_raw:
(iii) explanatory memoranda or other documents laid before or otherwise presented to 
any House of the Parliament; and
(iv) reports of Royal Commissions, Parliamentary Committees, Law Reform 
Commissioners and Commissions, Boards of Inquiry or other similar bodies.

text: 381 In the Appeal Division of the Supreme Court of Victoria, Crockett and Southwell JJ stated that s 35(a) requires a construction to be given to legislation ‘that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act’.
text_raw:

In the Appeal Division of the Supreme Court of Victoria, Crockett and Southwell JJ 
stated that s 35(a)
requires a construction to be given to legislation ‘that would promote the purpose or object 
underlying the Act’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 11 ExTRinsiC Aids To inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Accordingly, the better view would appear to be that, even if it be thought that the language is clear and unambiguous, it was not improper to have had recourse to the parliamentary debates in order to ensure that to apply the ordinary and grammatical meaning of the words would not give the statute a meaning which obviously was not intended.71 Despite an early view that, in the absence of ambiguity or doubt on the face of the statute, reference should not be made to extrinsic materials, there is general support for the contrary view expressed by Crockett and Southwell JJ.
text_raw:
Accordingly, the better view would appear to be that, even if 
it be thought that the language is clear and unambiguous, it was not improper to have had 
recourse to the parliamentary debates in order to ensure that to apply the ordinary and 
grammatical meaning of the words would not give the statute a meaning which obviously 
was not intended.71
Despite an early view that, in the absence of ambiguity or doubt on the face of the 
statute, reference should not be made to extrinsic materials, there is general support for 
the contrary view expressed by Crockett and Southwell JJ.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: 387 Introduction In Chapter 11 the role of ‘context’ in statutory interpretation was discussed with reference to the permissible uses of extrinsic materials.
text_raw:
387
Introduction
In Chapter 11 the role of ‘context’ in statutory interpretation was discussed with reference 
to the permissible uses of extrinsic materials.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: This chapter considers several other ways in which context is relevant to interpretation, including: • the use of syntactical presumptions to construe terms in legislation; • the effects of reading a provision within the context of other provisions of the legislation under consideration, including the use of definition sections; • the use of aids outside the legislation, such as dictionaries to find ordinary meaning of terms in legislation, a jurisdiction’s interpretation legislation, and technical or trade meanings of terms; • whether to consider a word’s meaning at the time the legislation was drafted or its current meaning; and • the assumptions that words carry consistent meanings, that the deliberate omission of terms may be meaningful, and that all words carry meaning.
text_raw:
This chapter considers several other ways in 
which context is relevant to interpretation, including:
• the use of syntactical presumptions to construe terms in legislation; 
• the effects of reading a provision within the context of other provisions of the 
legislation under consideration, including the use of definition sections; 
• the use of aids outside the legislation, such as dictionaries to find ordinary 
meaning of terms in legislation, a jurisdiction’s interpretation legislation, and 
technical or trade meanings of terms;
• whether to consider a word’s meaning at the time the legislation was drafted or 
its current meaning; and 
• the assumptions that words carry consistent meanings, that the deliberate 
omission of terms may be meaningful, and that all words carry meaning.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: In a leading decision of the High Court, Project Blue Sky Inc v Australian Broadcasting Authority (‘Project Blue Sky ’),2 McHugh, Gummow, Kirby and Hayne JJ observed that ‘the process of construction must always begin by examining the context of the provision that is being construed’.3 To support this observation the Justices referred to these comments of Mason J in K & S Lake City Freighters Pty Ltd v Gordon & Gotch Ltd :4 Problems of legal interpretation are not solved satisfactorily by ritual incantations which emphasise the clarity of meaning which words have when viewed in isolation, divorced from their context.
text_raw:
In a leading decision of the High Court, Project Blue Sky Inc v Australian Broadcasting 
Authority (‘Project Blue Sky ’),2 McHugh, Gummow, Kirby and Hayne JJ observed that 
‘the process of construction must always begin by examining the context of the 
provision that is being construed’.3 To support this observation the Justices referred to 
these comments of Mason J in K & S Lake City Freighters Pty Ltd v Gordon & Gotch Ltd :4
Problems of legal interpretation are not solved satisfactorily by ritual incantations which 
emphasise the clarity of meaning which words have when viewed in isolation, divorced 
from their context.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The modern approach to interpretation insists that the context be considered in the first instance, especially in the case of general words, and not merely at some later stage when ambiguity might be thought to arise.
text_raw:
The modern approach to interpretation insists that the context be 
considered in the first instance, especially in the case of general words, and not merely 
at some later stage when ambiguity might be thought to arise.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: 5 As stated in 10.28 , context may be conceptualised in three different ways, or at three different levels.
text_raw:
5
As stated in 10.28 , context may be conceptualised in three different ways, or at three 
different levels.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The first, and narrowest, is the context of the provision itself; the next level is that of the Act as a whole; the third is the context of the legislation in its widest sense, including a broader statutory scheme, the legislative history of the enactment and the purpose for which the legislation was enacted.
text_raw:
The first, and narrowest, is the context of the provision itself; the next 
level is that of the Act as a whole; the third is the context of the legislation in its widest 
sense, including a broader statutory scheme, the legislative history of the enactment and 
the purpose for which the legislation was enacted.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Summary of principles The implications of the principle that a provision should be interpreted in context include the following, progressing from narrow to wider meanings of ‘context’: • Words should be interpreted with reference to accompanying words — in particular, general words can be ‘read down’ or given a more narrow meaning 2 (1998) 194 CLR 355 (‘Project Blue Sky’) (extracted in 14.9).

LAYING DOWN THE LAW
388
by more specific words that accompany them (following the maxims noscitur a 
sociis or ejusdem generis): see 12.4–12.5.
• Although once not given great weight, today punctuation is regarded as relevant 
to interpretation: see 12.8.
• All words in a provision are assumed to carry meaning, so an interpretation 
should be favoured that gives effect to all the words: see 12.10.
• Words should be interpreted with reference to other parts of the legislation in 
which they appear, including titles, preambles, headings, notes and schedules.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Depending on jurisdiction, some of these form part of the legislation; others, for example section headings, may be extrinsic materials: see 12.11–12.23; see also 9.32ff. • Consistent use of words is assumed throughout a statute — thus a term or phrase will generally be given the same meaning in different parts of the statute: see 12.24. • The express mention of something may draw attention to the absence of something else that might be expected, or which is included elsewhere in the statute (following the maxim expressio unius est exclusio alterius): see 12.25. • Specific provisions can take precedence over general provisions (following the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant): see 12.27. • Words should be interpreted with reference to the interpretation legislation of the relevant jurisdiction: see 12.28–12.29. • Dictionaries may be consulted to obtain the ordinary meaning of words: see 12.30. • Words should be interpreted in accordance with their current meaning, which may change over time: see 12.31. • Provisions may be interpreted with reference to other legislation that is either on the same material (in pari materia) or part of the same legislative scheme: see 12.32–12.36. • Provisions may be interpreted with reference to the audience to which they are primarily directed, in order to give a term its technical or trade meaning rather than its ordinary meaning: see 12.37–12.38. • Provisions may be interpreted with reference to prior or other existing law, which may result in a term being given a legal, rather than ordinary, meaning or being interpreted in accordance with prior judicial interpretation: see 12.39–12.40.
text_raw:
Depending on jurisdiction, some of these form part of the legislation; others, for 
example section headings, may be extrinsic materials: see  12.11–12.23; see also 
9.32ff.
• Consistent use of words is assumed throughout a statute — thus a term or 
phrase will generally be given the same meaning in different parts of the statute: 
see 12.24.
• The express mention of something may draw attention to the absence of 
something else that might be expected, or which is included elsewhere in the 
statute (following the maxim expressio unius est exclusio alterius): see 12.25.
• Specific provisions can take precedence over general provisions (following the 
maxim generalia specialibus non derogant): see 12.27.
• Words should be interpreted with reference to the interpretation legislation of 
the relevant jurisdiction: see 12.28–12.29.
• Dictionaries may be consulted to obtain the ordinary meaning of words: 
see 12.30.
• Words should be interpreted in accordance with their current meaning, which 
may change over time: see 12.31.
• Provisions may be interpreted with reference to other legislation that is either 
on the same material (in pari materia) or part of the same legislative scheme: 
see 12.32–12.36.
• Provisions may be interpreted with reference to the audience to which they are 
primarily directed, in order to give a term its technical or trade meaning rather 
than its ordinary meaning: see 12.37–12.38.
• Provisions may be interpreted with reference to prior or other existing law, which 
may result in a term being given a legal, rather than ordinary, meaning or being 
interpreted in accordance with prior judicial interpretation: see 12.39–12.40.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The principle that words should be interpreted with reference to accompanying words is exemplified in two ancient maxims of interpretation: • noscitur a sociis — the meaning of a word is known from the words that accompany it; and • ejusdem (or eiusdem) generis — if words of particular meaning are followed by general words, the general words are limited to the same kind as the particular words.
text_raw:
The principle that words should be interpreted with reference to accompanying 
words is exemplified in two ancient maxims of interpretation:
• noscitur a sociis — the meaning of a word is known from the words that 
accompany it; and
• ejusdem (or eiusdem) generis — if words of particular meaning are followed by 
general words, the general words are limited to the same kind as the particular 
words.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: It is an Act ‘to make provision for the adjustment of boundaries where buildings encroach on adjoining land; to facilitate the determination of boundaries; and for purposes connected therewith’.
text_raw:
It is an Act ‘to 
make provision for the adjustment of boundaries where buildings encroach on adjoining 
land; to facilitate the determination of boundaries; and for purposes connected therewith’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The twin purposes of the Act are to facilitate the determination of existing boundaries when, but only when, buildings encroach on adjoining land (provided for by s 3).30 A good example of the use of the long title is in R v White ,31 where it was argued that the Evidence Act 1898 (NSW) was intended to codify the law on evidence, and thus the interpretative principles applicable to a code ought to apply: see 9.68.
text_raw:
The twin purposes of the Act are to facilitate the determination of existing boundaries 
when, but only when, buildings encroach on adjoining land (provided for by s 3).30
A good example of the use of the long title is in R v White ,31 where it was argued that 
the Evidence Act 1898 (NSW) was intended to codify the law on evidence, and thus 
the interpretative principles applicable to a code ought to apply: see  9.68.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: However, the court held that as the long title stated that the statute was ‘An Act to consolidate the statute law relating to evidence’, rather than a code, it ought to be interpreted as a consolidating statute, rather than a code.
text_raw:

court held that as the long title stated that the statute was ‘An Act to consolidate 
the statute law relating to evidence’, rather than a code, it ought to be interpreted as a 
consolidating statute, rather than a code.

legislation.32 In Bowtell v Goldsbrough, Mort & Co Ltd Griffith CJ said:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: [W]here the words of a Statute are plain and clear, their meaning cannot be cut down by reference to the preamble.
text_raw:
[W]here the words of a Statute are plain and clear, their meaning cannot be cut down by 
reference to the preamble.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: But, if the words are uncertain as applied to the subject matter, and may bear more than one meaning, then you may, in a proper case, refer to the preamble to ascertain what was the occasion for the alteration of the law.33 In Wacando v Commonwealth Mason J amplified and explained this view:
text_raw:
But, if the words are uncertain as applied to the subject matter, 
and may bear more than one meaning, then you may, in a proper case, refer to the preamble 
to ascertain what was the occasion for the alteration of the law.33
In Wacando v Commonwealth Mason J amplified and explained this view:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: It has been said that where the enacting part of a statute is clear and unambiguous it cannot be cut down by the preamble.
text_raw:
It has been said that where the enacting part of a statute is clear and unambiguous it 
cannot be cut down by the preamble.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: But this does not mean that a court cannot obtain assistance from the preamble in ascertaining the meaning of an operative provision.
text_raw:
But this does not mean that a court cannot obtain 
assistance from the preamble in ascertaining the meaning of an operative provision.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The particular section must be seen in its context; the statute must be read as a whole and recourse to the preamble may throw light on the statutory purpose and object.
text_raw:
The 
particular section must be seen in its context; the statute must be read as a whole and 
recourse to the preamble may throw light on the statutory purpose and object.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: There is, however, one difficulty in seeking to restrict the generality of the operative provision by reference to a suggested restriction expressed in the preamble: it is that Parliament may intend to enact a provision which extends beyond the actual problem sought to be remedied.
text_raw:

text: 41 sECTIon HEADIngs AnD no TEs The interpretation legislation of New South Wales, South Australia, Tasmania and Western Australia provides that headings to sections, marginal notes, footnotes or endnotes are generally not part of legislation.42 However, the equivalent provisions in the Australian Capital T erritory, Northern T erritory, Queensland and Victoria provide that while headings to sections are part of the Act (if the Act has been passed after a certain date), footnotes and endnotes are not.43 There are some exceptions to this in relation to certain notes that are considered part of legislation, such as those expressly referred to in an Act as part of it.

41 
sECTIon HEADIngs AnD no TEs
The interpretation legislation of New  South  Wales, South  Australia, Tasmania and 
Western Australia provides that headings to sections, marginal notes, footnotes or 
endnotes are generally not part of legislation.42 However, the equivalent provisions in the 
Australian Capital T erritory, Northern T erritory, Queensland and Victoria provide that 
while headings to sections are part of the Act (if the Act has been passed after a certain 
date), footnotes and endnotes are not.43 There are some exceptions to this in relation to

in an Act as part of it.
