text: 397 Where section headings and notes are part of an Act on account of interpretation legislation, they are perhaps on the same level as a title: see 12.13.46 Thus, it was recently stated that while ‘a note cannot govern the text of an [A]ct, it can be used as an aid in interpretation’.47 In the absence of statutory provisions governing the issue, Australian courts used to take the view that marginal notes (and, by implication, other notes) could not be taken into account in the interpretation of legislation.
text_raw:
397
Where section headings and notes are part of an Act on account of interpretation 
legislation, they are perhaps on the same level as a title: see 12.13.46 Thus, it was recently 
stated that while ‘a note cannot govern the text of an [A]ct, it can be used as an aid in 
interpretation’.47
In the absence of statutory provisions governing the issue, Australian courts used to 
take the view that marginal notes (and, by implication, other notes) could not be taken 
into account in the interpretation of legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: 48 There was, however, authority for the view that a marginal note may be consulted to the extent that it shows the ‘drift of the section’.49 Stephen J commented in Dugan v Mirror Newspapers Ltd that marginal notes were at most ‘only a quite minor aid’.50 In Ombudsman v Moroney Street CJ took a different view from that taken in the earlier cases:
text_raw:
48 There was, however, authority for the 
view that a marginal note may be consulted to the extent that it shows the ‘drift of the 
section’.49 Stephen J commented in Dugan v Mirror Newspapers Ltd that marginal notes 
were at most ‘only a quite minor aid’.50
In Ombudsman v Moroney Street CJ took a different view from that taken in the 
earlier cases:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: If a clause in a Bill accompanied by a marginal note passes through Parliament unamended and that marginal note is printed on the formal Bill to which Royal assent is in due course given, I see every reason to regard it as a legitimate source upon which to draw as an aid to construction of the section … Whilst asserting, as I do, the permissibility of turning to an authenticated marginal note to assist in resolving the interpretation of a doubtful or ambiguous section, I fully recognize that, not being part of the Act, it cannot control the meaning of the section.
text_raw:
If a clause in a Bill accompanied by a marginal note passes through Parliament unamended 
and that marginal note is printed on the formal Bill to which Royal assent is in due 
course given, I see every reason to regard it as a legitimate source upon which to draw 
as an aid to construction of the section … Whilst asserting, as I do, the permissibility 
of turning to an authenticated marginal note to assist in resolving the interpretation 
of a doubtful or ambiguous section, I fully recognize that, not being part of the Act, it 
cannot control the meaning of the section.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: It may well be only rarely that such doubt or ambiguity will arise as will result in useful reference to an authenticated marginal note for its resolution.

ambiguity will arise as will result in useful reference to an authenticated marginal note

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The interpretation legislation provides that a schedule is part of an Act in all jurisdictions 54 except New South Wales where it is implied.
text_raw:
The interpretation legislation provides that a schedule is part of 
an Act in all jurisdictions 54 except New South Wales where it is implied.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: 55 This means that schedules are not to be regarded as an inferior part of the Act and so, generally speaking, the ordinary principles of interpretation apply to their interpretation.
text_raw:
55 This means 
that schedules are not to be regarded as an inferior part of the Act and so, generally 
speaking, the ordinary principles of interpretation apply to their interpretation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: In Inland Revenue Commissioners v Gittus 56 Lord Sterndale MR set out the principles to be applied in the event of a possible inconsistency between the enabling sections of an Act and a schedule:
text_raw:
In 
Inland Revenue Commissioners v Gittus 56 Lord Sterndale MR set out the principles to 
be applied in the event of a possible inconsistency between the enabling sections of an 
Act and a schedule:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: It seems to me there are two principles or rules of interpretation which ought to be applied to the combination of Act and schedule.
text_raw:
It seems to me there are two principles or rules of interpretation which ought to be applied 
to the combination of Act and schedule.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: If the Act says that the schedule is to be used for a certain purpose and the heading of the part of the schedule in question shows that it is prima facie at any rate devoted to that purpose, then you must read the Act and the schedule as though the schedule were operating for that purpose, and if you can satisfy the language of the section without extending it beyond that purpose you ought to do it.
text_raw:
If the Act says that the schedule is to be used 
for a certain purpose and the heading of the part of the schedule in question shows that 
it is prima facie at any rate devoted to that purpose, then you must read the Act and the 
schedule as though the schedule were operating for that purpose, and if you can satisfy the 
language of the section without extending it beyond that purpose you ought to do it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: But if in spite of that you find in the language of the schedule words and terms that go clearly outside that purpose, then you must give effect to them and you must not consider them as limited by the heading of that part of the schedule or by the purpose mentioned in the Act for which the schedule is prima facie to be used.
text_raw:
But 
if in spite of that you find in the language of the schedule words and terms that go clearly 
outside that purpose, then you must give effect to them and you must not consider them 
as limited by the heading of that part of the schedule or by the purpose mentioned in the 
Act for which the schedule is prima facie to be used.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Y ou cannot refuse to give effect to clear words simply because prima facie they seem to be limited by the heading of the schedule and the definition of the purpose of the schedule contained in the Act.57 The comments in 12.12 concerning interpretation by reference to underlying purpose or object and context apply to schedules as well as to long titles, preambles and headings to parts and divisions.
text_raw:
Y ou cannot refuse to give effect to 
clear words simply because prima facie they seem to be limited by the heading of the 
schedule and the definition of the purpose of the schedule contained in the Act.57
The comments in 12.12 concerning interpretation by reference to underlying purpose 
or object and context apply to schedules as well as to long titles, preambles and 
headings to parts and divisions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: However, it must be remembered that scheduling an international agreement in a statute does not necessarily incorporate it as part of domestic law: see 3.37.

text: 62 Consistent use of words is assumed A further aspect of interpreting a provision within the context of the Act as a whole is considering whether a word or phrase can be found elsewhere in the legislation in a place where its meaning is more apparent.
text_raw:
62
Consistent use of words is assumed
A further aspect of interpreting a provision within the context of the Act as a whole is 
considering whether a word or phrase can be found elsewhere in the legislation in a 
place where its meaning is more apparent.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Unlike poets and novelists, drafters attempt to communicate meaning as directly and briefly as possible.
text_raw:
Unlike poets and novelists, drafters attempt 
to communicate meaning as directly and briefly as possible.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: One of the ways to do this is to repeat the same word or phrase when precisely the same meaning is intended.
text_raw:
One of the ways to do this 
is to repeat the same word or phrase when precisely the same meaning is intended.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: When interpreting a particular piece of legislation, therefore, it may be assumed that the meaning of a word that is repeated is consistent.
text_raw:
When interpreting a particular piece of legislation, therefore, it may be assumed that 
the meaning of a word that is repeated is consistent.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: In Wilson v Commissioner of Stamp Duties, Lee J said:
text_raw:
In Wilson v Commissioner of Stamp 
Duties, Lee J said:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Although there is no absolute requirement that the same words in a statute must be given the same meaning, the need to give different meanings should be clearly apparent and should lead to a result which is consonant with the purpose of the statute.63 The obverse of this principle of interpretation is that, where different words have been used, a different meaning must have been intended.
text_raw:
Although there is no absolute requirement that the same words in a statute must be given 
the same meaning, the need to give different meanings should be clearly apparent and 
should lead to a result which is consonant with the purpose of the statute.63
The obverse of this principle of interpretation is that, where different words have 
been used, a different meaning must have been intended.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: However, drafting styles can change, so it is possible that a different form of words has been used merely for clarity.
text_raw:
However, drafting styles 
can change, so it is possible that a different form of words has been used merely for

text: 401 General provisions do not override specific provisions When considering an Act as a whole, the question can arise as to the relationship between general provisions and specific provisions that are inconsistent with one another, with respect to current provisions within the same Act, and also whether later general provisions repeal earlier specific provisions.
text_raw:
401
General provisions do not override specific 
provisions
When considering an Act as a whole, the question can arise as to the relationship between 
general provisions and specific provisions that are inconsistent with one another, with 
respect to current provisions within the same Act, and also whether later general provisions 
repeal earlier specific provisions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The general presumption as to the approach to adopt is expressed by the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant — ‘general things do not derogate from special things’.
text_raw:
The general presumption as to the approach to adopt is 
expressed by the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant — ‘general things do not derogate 
from special things’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: The ‘things’ referred to are statutory provisions, so that an earlier provision which deals with a particular matter may not be impliedly repealed by a later, more general, provision.
text_raw:
The ‘things’ referred to are statutory provisions, so that an earlier 
provision which deals with a particular matter may not be impliedly repealed by a later, 
more general, provision.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Thus, in South Australia v T anner,70 Wilson, Dawson, T oohey and Gaudron JJ held that the provisions of the later Planning Act 1982 (SA) did not impliedly repeal the earlier Waterworks Regulations 1974 (SA) made under the specific Waterworks Act 1932 (SA), as the Planning Act was concerned with general planning permission, whereas the Waterworks Act dealt with the specific problem of water pollution.
text_raw:
Thus, in South Australia v T anner,70 Wilson, Dawson, T oohey and 
Gaudron JJ held that the provisions of the later Planning Act 1982 (SA) did not impliedly 
repeal the earlier Waterworks Regulations 1974 (SA) made under the specific Waterworks 
Act  1932 (SA), as the Planning Act was concerned with general planning permission, 
whereas the Waterworks Act dealt with the specific problem of water pollution.

text: Statutes may be interpreted on the basis that the connotation of the language remains the same whereas its denotation may differ over time … So the word ‘gas’ was interpreted to include the supply of liquefied petroleum gas [in 1970], whereas only coal gas could have been in the contemplation of the Parliament at the time the legislation was adopted [in 1906] … Similarly [in 1971] ‘mining operations’ was extended to encompass a novel technological procedure for bringing subterranean pockets of brine to the surface to produce salt, which procedure was not in existence at the time the Income T ax Assessment Act (Cth) was enacted [in 1936].86 Spigelman CJ’s distinction between ‘connotation’ and ‘denotation’ here is a distinction between a broad concept ‘connoted’ or ‘suggested’ by a term (here, ‘gas’) and the specific things ‘denoted’, ‘indicated’ or ‘embraced’ by that concept over time (in this case, ‘coal gas’, ‘liquefied petroleum gas’).
text_raw:
Statutes may be interpreted on the basis that the connotation of the language remains the 
same whereas its denotation may differ over time … So the word ‘gas’ was interpreted 
to include the supply of liquefied petroleum gas [in 1970], whereas only coal gas could 
have been in the contemplation of the Parliament at the time the legislation was adopted 
[in 1906] … Similarly [in 1971] ‘mining operations’ was extended to encompass a novel 
technological procedure for bringing subterranean pockets of brine to the surface to 
produce salt, which procedure was not in existence at the time the Income T ax Assessment 
Act (Cth) was enacted [in 1936].86
Spigelman CJ’s distinction between ‘connotation’ and ‘denotation’ here is a distinction 
between a broad concept ‘connoted’ or ‘suggested’ by a term (here, ‘gas’) and the 
specific things ‘denoted’, ‘indicated’ or ‘embraced’ by that concept over time (in this 
case, ‘coal gas’, ‘liquefied petroleum gas’).

text: There is a principle of statutory interpretation supporting a presumption that a legislature intends to attach the same meaning to the same words when used in a subsequent statute in a similar connection.90 This principle can even apply across jurisdictions.
text_raw:
There is a principle of statutory interpretation supporting a presumption that a legislature 
intends to attach the same meaning to the same words when used in a subsequent statute 
in a similar connection.90
This principle can even apply across jurisdictions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: For example, in Kernn v Verran it was held that the term ‘seniority’ in the Commonwealth public service Acts was in pari materia with an Australian Capital Territory ordinance dealing with Territory public servants.91 Where the context is different or dissimilar, the principle cannot be applied.

pari materia with an Australian Capital Territory ordinance dealing with Territory public 
servants.91 Where the context is different or dissimilar, the principle cannot be applied.

text: Because of the nature and purpose of the Prisoners (Interstate Transfer) Acts of New South Wales and Queensland, the court should prefer that construction of the legislation which secures harmony of operation, avoids apparent injustice and obviates the necessity of clarifying amendments where the achievement of such amendments would be more difficult even than ordinarily because of the reciprocal nature of the legislation enacted in all States and T erritories.97 As noted previously, where a statute forms part of a national or cooperative legislative scheme such as that of movie and video game classification (see 9.70), courts will strive for uniform interpretation of national uniform legislation across the different jurisdictions: see 8.36ff.98 Despite these considerations, the definition of a term in an Act does not necessarily determine the meaning of that term in another Act in which it is not defined.
text_raw:
Because of the nature and purpose of the Prisoners (Interstate Transfer) Acts of 
New  South  Wales and Queensland, the court should prefer that construction of the 
legislation which secures harmony of operation, avoids apparent injustice and obviates the 
necessity of clarifying amendments where the achievement of such amendments would 
be more difficult even than ordinarily because of the reciprocal nature of the legislation 
enacted in all States and T erritories.97
As noted previously, where a statute forms part of a national or cooperative legislative 
scheme such as that of movie and video game classification (see  9.70), courts will 
strive for uniform interpretation of national uniform legislation across the different 
jurisdictions: see  8.36ff.98
Despite these considerations, the definition of a term in an Act does not necessarily 
determine the meaning of that term in another Act in which it is not defined.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: I confess that I think most lay people and, indeed, I myself when I first read the papers, would be inclined to the view that to say that if a knife was displayed in a window like that with a price attached to it was not offering it for sale was just nonsense.

that I think most lay people and, indeed, I myself when I first read the papers, would

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Not only is that so, but it is to be observed that in many statutes and orders which prohibit selling and offering for sale of goods it is very common when it is so desired to insert the words ‘offering or exposing for sale’ , ‘exposing for sale’ being clearly words which would cover the display of goods in a shop window.
text_raw:

orders which prohibit selling and offering for sale of goods it is very common when it 
is so desired to insert the words ‘offering or exposing for sale’ , ‘exposing for sale’ being 
clearly words which would cover the display of goods in a shop window.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 12 InTERPRETATIon of LEgIsLATIon In ConTExT
text: Not only that, but it appears that under several statutes — we have been referred in particular to the Prices of Goods Act 1939, and the Goods and Services (Price Control) Act 1941 — Parliament, when it desires to enlarge the ordinary meaning of those words, includes a definition section enlarging the ordinary meaning of ‘offer for sale’ to cover other matters including, be it observed, exposure of goods for sale with the price attached.

415
Introduction
When courts interpret legislation they do so against the background of a series of common 
law presumptions, or assumptions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Presumptions of interpretation are called into service because they are accepted as part of the body of principles used in the interpretation of legislation.
text_raw:
Presumptions of interpretation are called into 
service because they are accepted as part of the body of principles used in the interpretation 
of legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: These presumptions can be broadly classified into three groups.
text_raw: These presumptions can be broadly classified into three groups.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: First are what we might term ‘syntactical’ presumptions, that certain practices will be followed in drafting statutes — the principles ejusdem generis and noscitur a sociis, discussed at 12.4– 12.7, are examples of this type of presumption.
text_raw:
First are 
what we might term ‘syntactical’ presumptions, that certain practices will be followed in 
drafting statutes — the principles ejusdem generis and noscitur a sociis, discussed at  12.4–
12.7, are examples of this type of presumption.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: 2 Second are presumptions that facilitate interpretation, such as the presumption that re-enactment of a provision that has been judicially interpreted constitutes the legislature’s approval of that interpretation.
text_raw:
2 Second are presumptions that facilitate 
interpretation, such as the presumption that re-enactment of a provision that has been 
judicially interpreted constitutes the legislature’s approval of that interpretation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Finally, a number of presumptions are grounded in the liberal values based on the abstract concepts of freedom and the sanctity of private property, which are generally held by people living in parliamentary democracies under the rule of law, including lawyers, legislators and members of the broader community.
text_raw:
Finally, a 
number of presumptions are grounded in the liberal values based on the abstract concepts 
of freedom and the sanctity of private property, which are generally held by people living 
in parliamentary democracies under the rule of law, including lawyers, legislators and 
members of the broader community.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It is presumed that Parliament intends to legislate in accordance with these values.
text_raw:
It is presumed that Parliament intends to legislate in 
accordance with these values.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The application of any of these presumptions in an individual case is theoretically not dependent on the personal views of the judge deciding the case.
text_raw:
The application of any of these presumptions in an individual 
case is theoretically not dependent on the personal views of the judge deciding the case.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: This particular body of presumptions is sometimes said to form a ‘common law Bill of Rights’.
text_raw:
This particular body of presumptions is sometimes said to form a ‘common law Bill of 
Rights’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The approach of interpretation where it is presumed Parliament does not intend to abrogate fundamental rights and freedoms is also termed the ‘principle of legality’.3 Importantly, an intrinsic feature of presumptions of interpretation is that they are presumptions, rather than rules.
text_raw:
The approach of interpretation where it is presumed Parliament does not intend 
to abrogate fundamental rights and freedoms is also termed the ‘principle of legality’.3 
Importantly, an intrinsic feature of presumptions of interpretation is that they are 
presumptions, rather than rules.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: As such, they can be ‘rebutted’ — that is, shown not to apply, when the language of the legislation either explicitly states this to be the case, or it is a necessary implication: the legislation and the presumption cannot operate side by side.
text_raw:
As such, they can be ‘rebutted’ — that is, shown not to 
apply, when the language of the legislation either explicitly states this to be the case, or it 
is a necessary implication: the legislation and the presumption cannot operate side by side.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: This chapter looks at the presumptions underlying statutory interpretation, including: • the view that certain presumptions of interpretation form a common law Bill of Rights; • the circumstances in which a presumption may be rebutted; • which rights are presumed to be protected as being fundamental; and • the particular presumptions that are in operation under the common law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The main focus is on those presumptions derived from shared values, rather than syntactical presumptions (some of which are addressed in Chapter 12 ).
text_raw:
The main focus is on those presumptions derived from shared values, rather than 
syntactical presumptions (some of which are addressed in Chapter 12 ).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Summary of principles Here are the key principles discussed in this chapter in relation to presumptions of interpretation: • Courts interpret legislation against a background of series of presumptions about the intention of the legislature.
text_raw:
Summary of principles
Here are the key principles discussed in this chapter in relation to presumptions of 
interpretation:

about the intention of the legislature.

text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 416 • These presumptions form part of an Act’s context and include those that are syntactical and those that derive from shared values: see 13.1. • Those presumptions that derive from values shared by the courts, community and legislature are sometimes said to form a ‘common law Bill of Rights’ and the approach of interpreting legislation so that it is presumed Parliament does not intend to abrogate fundamental rights is part of the ‘principle of legality’: see 13.1, 13.4 and 13.9–13.13. • No definitive list of fundamental rights exists.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
416
• These presumptions form part of an Act’s context and include those that are 
syntactical and those that derive from shared values: see 13.1.
• Those presumptions that derive from values shared by the courts, community 
and legislature are sometimes said to form a ‘common law Bill of Rights’ and 
the approach of interpreting legislation so that it is presumed Parliament does 
not intend to abrogate fundamental rights is part of the ‘principle of legality’: 
see 13.1, 13.4 and 13.9–13.13.
• No definitive list of fundamental rights exists.

text: The presumption that Parliament does not intend to deprive people of access to the courts, for example, is a ‘strong’ presumption: see 13.20. • Generally speaking, a presumption can be rebutted either by explicit language in the statute, or by implication.

presumption that Parliament does not intend to deprive people of access to the

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: 417 Common LAW PREsumPTions of inTERPRETATion Here are some of the more important common law presumptions of interpretation discussed in this chapter:6 • statutes do not operate retrospectively; • Parliament does not interfere with common law rights; • Parliament does not abrogate the privilege against self-incrimination; • Parliament does not abrogate legal professional privilege; • Parliament does not deprive people of access to the courts; • legislation does not bind the Crown; • penal provisions are strictly construed; • property rights are not taken away without compensation; • re-enactment of a provision constitutes approval of a previous judicial interpretation of the provision; • legislation does not have extraterritorial effect; and • Parliament intends to legislate in conformity with international law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

that if Parliament had wanted to do something as important as repeal an earlier law it

text_raw:
As Kiefel CJ has stated, in relation to abrogating or restricting a ‘fundamental freedom’ 
(see  13.9–13.12), ‘it will usually require that it be manifest from the statute in question 
that the legislature has directed its attention to the question whether to so abrogate or 
restrict and has determined to do so’.7
Over the years the courts have used various phrases as tests of rebuttal, such as ‘clear 
and unambiguous words’ and ‘express words of plain intendment’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Spigelman CJ collected many of these phrases in Durham Holdings Pty Ltd v New South Wales:8 • ‘clear and unambiguous words’; • ‘unambiguously clear’; • ‘irresistible clearness’; • ‘express words of plain intendment’; • ‘clear words or by necessary implication’; • ‘unmistakable and unambiguous’; • ‘expressly stated or necessarily to be implied’; • ‘clearly emerges whether by express words or necessary implication’; and • ‘with a clearness which admits no doubt’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Sometimes it is said that a presumption about legislative intention can be displaced only by necessary implication but that statement does little more than emphasise that the test is a very stringent one. … [I]n some circumstances the presumption may be displaced by an implication if it is necessary to prevent the statutory provisions from becoming inoperative or meaningless.

implication but that statement does little more than emphasise that the test is a very

inoperative or meaningless.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The rule at common law is that a statute ought not be given a retrospective operation where to do so would affect an existing right or obligation unless the language of the statute expressly or by necessary implication requires such construction.
text_raw:
The rule at common law is that a statute ought not be given a retrospective operation 
where to do so would affect an existing right or obligation unless the language of 
the statute expressly or by necessary implication requires such construction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It is said that statutes dealing with procedure are an exception to the rule and that they should be given a retrospective operation.

said that statutes dealing with procedure are an exception to the rule and that they 
should be  given a retrospective operation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It would, we think, be more accurate to say that there is no presumption against retrospectivity in the case of statutes which affect mere matters of procedure.

It would, we think, be more accurate to 
say that there is no presumption against retrospectivity in the case of statutes which 
affect mere matters of procedure.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Indeed, strictly speaking, where procedure alone is involved, a statute will invariably operate prospectively and there is no room for the application of such a presumption.
text_raw:
Indeed, strictly speaking, where procedure alone 
is involved, a  statute will invariably operate prospectively and there is no room for 
the application of such a presumption.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It will operate prospectively because it will prescribe the manner in which something may or must be done in the future, even if what is to be done relates to, or is based upon, past events.
text_raw:
It will operate prospectively because it will 
prescribe the manner in which something may or must be done in the future, even if 
what is to be done relates to, or is based upon, past events.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A statute which prescribes the manner in which the trial of a past offence is to be conducted is one instance.
text_raw:
A statute which prescribes 
the manner in which the trial of a past offence is to be conducted is one instance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: But the difference between substantive law and procedure is often difficult to draw and statutes which are commonly classified as procedural — statutes of limitation, for example — may operate in such a way as to affect existing rights or obligations.
text_raw:
But the difference between substantive law and procedure is often difficult to draw 
and statutes which are commonly classified as procedural — statutes of limitation, 
for example — may operate in such a way as to affect existing rights or obligations.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: When they operate in that way they are not merely procedural and they fall within the presumption against retrospective operation.
text_raw:
When they operate in that way they are not merely procedural and they fall within the 
presumption against retrospective operation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: But when they deal only with procedure they are apt to be regarded as an exception to the rule and, if their application is related to or based upon past events, they are said to be given a retrospective operation provided that they do not affect existing rights or obligations.
text_raw:
But when they deal only with procedure 
they are apt to be regarded as an exception to the rule and, if their application is related 
to or based upon past events, they are said to be given a retrospective operation 
provided that they do not affect existing rights or obligations.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 426 Where a period is limited by statute for the taking of proceedings and the period is subsequently abridged or extended by an amending statute, the amending statute should not, unless it is clearly intended, be given a retrospective operation to revive a cause of action which has become barred or to deprive a person of the opportunity of instituting an action which is within time.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
426
Where a period is limited by statute for the taking of proceedings and the period 
is subsequently abridged or extended by an amending statute, the amending statute 
should not, unless it is clearly intended, be given a retrospective operation to revive 
a cause of action which has become barred or to deprive a person of the opportunity 
of instituting an action which is within time.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: If it were given a retrospective operation, the amending legislation would operate so as to impair existing, substantive rights — either the right to be free of a claim or the right to bring a claim — and such an operation could not be said to be merely procedural.
text_raw:
If it were given a retrospective operation, 
the amending legislation would operate so as to impair existing, substantive rights — 
either the right to be free of a claim or the right to bring a claim — and such an 
operation could not be said to be merely procedural.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

by Williams  J in Maxwell v  Murphy (1957) 96 CLR 261, 278, and his remarks were 
adopted by the Privy Council in Yew Bon Tew v Kenderaan Bas Mara [1983] 1 AC 553,

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Limitations may be regarded as being only of a procedural nature and, therefore, unless a contrary intention appears, retrospective in operation, if, being an amendment enlarging time, it took effect before the right sought to be enforced had become finally barred by lapse of time, and if, being an amendment reducing time, it left time after its commencement within which an action might be brought.
text_raw:
Limitations may be regarded as being only of a procedural nature and, therefore, 
unless a contrary intention appears, retrospective in operation, if, being an amendment 
enlarging time, it took effect before the right sought to be enforced had become finally 
barred by lapse of time, and if, being an amendment reducing time, it left time after its 
commencement within which an action might be brought.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It was recognition of the fact that the simple classification of a statute as either procedural or substantive does not necessarily determine whether it may have a retrospective operation which no doubt led Dixon CJ in Maxwell v Murphy to formulate the general rule in terms which did not rest simply upon that classification.
text_raw:
It was recognition of the fact that the simple classification of a statute as either 
procedural or substantive does not necessarily determine whether it may have 
a retrospective operation which no doubt led Dixon  CJ in Maxwell v  Murphy to 
formulate the general rule in terms which did not rest simply upon that classification.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The general rule of the common law is that a statute changing the law ought not, unless the intention appears with reasonable certainty, to be understood as applying to facts or events that have already occurred in such a way as to confer or impose or otherwise affect rights or liabilities which the law had defined by reference to the past events.
text_raw:
The general rule of the common law is that a statute changing the law ought not, unless 
the intention appears with reasonable certainty, to be understood as applying to facts 
or events that have already occurred in such a way as to confer or impose or otherwise 
affect rights or liabilities which the law had defined by reference to the past events.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: But, given rights and liabilities fixed by reference to past facts, matters or events, the law appointing or regulating the manner in which they are to be enforced or their enjoyment is to be secured by judicial remedy is not within the application of such a presumption.
text_raw:
But, 
given rights and liabilities fixed by reference to past facts, matters or events, the law 
appointing or regulating the manner in which they are to be enforced or their enjoyment 
is to be secured by judicial remedy is not within the application of such a presumption.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Changes made in practice and procedure are applied to proceedings to enforce rights and liabilities, or for that matter to vindicate an immunity or privilege, notwithstanding that before the change in the law was made the accrual or establishment of the rights, liabilities, immunity or privilege was complete and rested on events or transactions that were otherwise past and closed.
text_raw:
Changes made in practice and procedure are applied to proceedings to enforce rights 
and liabilities, or for that matter to vindicate an immunity or privilege, notwithstanding 
that before the change in the law was made the accrual or establishment of the rights, 
liabilities, immunity or privilege was complete and rested on events or transactions that 
were otherwise past and closed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The basis of the distinction was stated by Mellish LJ in Republic of Costa Rica v Erlanger (1876) 3 Ch D 62, 69. ‘No suitor has any vested interest in the course of procedure, nor any right to complain, if during the litigation the procedure is changed, provided, of course, that no injustice is done’ . … [O]rdinarily an amendment to the practice or procedure of a court, including the admissibility of evidence and the effect to be given to evidence, will not operate retrospectively so as to impair any existing right.
text_raw:
The basis of the distinction was stated by Mellish LJ in 
Republic of Costa Rica v Erlanger (1876) 3 Ch D 62, 69. ‘No suitor has any vested interest in 
the course of procedure, nor any right to complain, if during the litigation the procedure 
is changed, provided, of course, that no injustice is done’ .
…
[O]rdinarily an amendment to the practice or procedure of a court, including the 
admissibility of evidence and the effect to be given to evidence, will not operate 
retrospectively so as to impair any existing right.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It may govern the way in which the right is to be enforced or vindicated, but that does not bring it within the presumption against retrospectivity.
text_raw:
It may govern the way in which the 
right is to be enforced or vindicated, but that does not bring it within the presumption 
against retrospectivity.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A person who commits a crime does not have a right to be tried in any particular way; merely a right to be tried according to the practice and procedure prevailing at the time of trial.
text_raw:
A person who commits a crime does not have a right to be 
tried in any particular way; merely a right to be tried according to the practice and 
procedure prevailing at  the time of trial.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The principle is sometimes succinctly, if somewhat sweepingly, expressed by saying, as did Mellish LJ in the passage cited by Dixon CJ in Maxwell v Murphy, that no-one has a vested right in any form of procedure.
text_raw:
The principle is sometimes succinctly, if 
somewhat sweepingly, expressed by saying, as did Mellish LJ in the passage cited by 
Dixon CJ in Maxwell v Murphy, that no-one has a vested right in any form of procedure.

Practices Commission (‘Pyneboard’),36 where it was held that the language and the purpose

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A key factor here was that, without the Commission’s being able to obtain documents and evidence from those who had participated in contraventions of the Act, the Commission would have found it nearly impossible to establish the existence of those contraventions and enforce the Act.

A  key 
factor here was that, without the Commission’s being able to obtain documents and 
evidence from those who had participated in contraventions of the Act, the Commission 
would have found it nearly impossible to establish the existence of those contraventions 
and enforce the Act.

text: 429 Presumption that Parliament does not deprive people of access to the courts The presumption that Parliament does not deprive people of access to the courts is sometimes seen as a specific application of the presumption that Parliament does not interfere with common law rights: see 13.9–13.10.
text_raw:
429
Presumption that Parliament does not deprive 
people of access to the courts
The presumption that Parliament does not deprive people of access to the courts is 
sometimes seen as a specific application of the presumption that Parliament does not 
interfere with common law rights: see 13.9–13.10.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A provision in legislation that purports to deprive access to the courts is commonly called a privative clause or an ouster clause.
text_raw:
A provision in legislation that purports 
to deprive access to the courts is commonly called a privative clause or an ouster clause.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Courts can be relied on to interpret such a provision strictly.
text_raw: Courts can be relied on to interpret such a provision strictly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: In Plaintiff S157/2002 v Commonwealth (‘Plaintiff S157/2002’)40 the High Court upheld the validity of a privative clause contained in s 474 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), at the same time holding that s 474 did not prevent judicial review of decisions that involved jurisdictional error, despite the very lengthy list of explicit exclusions from review contained in the section.
text_raw:
In Plaintiff S157/2002 
v Commonwealth (‘Plaintiff S157/2002’)40 the High Court upheld the validity of a privative 
clause contained in s 474 of the Migration Act 1958 (Cth), at the same time holding that 
s 474 did not prevent judicial review of decisions that involved jurisdictional error, 
despite the very lengthy list of explicit exclusions from review contained in the section.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: The Court reached this conclusion on the basis that such decisions were not protected from review because s 474 applied only to valid decisions made under the Act.
text_raw:
The Court reached this conclusion on the basis that such decisions were not protected 
from review because s 474 applied only to valid decisions made under the Act.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A decision that involved jurisdictional error was not a valid decision but invalid from the start (ab initio), because the decision-maker lacked the ‘jurisdiction’ to make that decision — either because the decision-maker lacked the power to do so, or prerequisites for making the decision had not been satisfied.
text_raw:
A decision 
that involved jurisdictional error was not a valid decision but invalid from the start 
(ab initio), because the decision-maker lacked the ‘jurisdiction’ to make that decision — 
either because the decision-maker lacked the power to do so, or prerequisites for making 
the decision had not been satisfied.

text_raw:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Accordingly, privative clauses are strictly construed.41 The High Court endorsed this rule in Fish v Solution 6 Holdings Ltd .42 The presumption also applies to state parliaments.
text_raw:
Accordingly, privative clauses are strictly construed.41
The High Court endorsed this rule in Fish v Solution 6 Holdings Ltd .42 The presumption 
also applies to state parliaments.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: 43 The interpretation of privative clauses, a complex topic, is studied as part of administrative law.44 Presumption that penal provisions are construed strictly and beneficial provisions construed broadly The presumption that penal provisions should be construed ‘strictly’ — that is, as narrowly as possible, to apply to as few people as possible — is one that has reduced in weight over the years.
text_raw:
43 
The interpretation of privative clauses, a complex topic, is studied as part of 
administrative law.44
Presumption that penal provisions are 
construed strictly and beneficial provisions 
construed broadly 
The presumption that penal provisions should be construed ‘strictly’ — that is, as narrowly 
as possible, to apply to as few people as possible — is one that has reduced in weight over 
the years.

of construction, as Gibbs CJ commented in Beckwith v The Queen:

text_raw:

has lost much of its importance in modern times.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 432 Presumption that re-enactment constitutes approval of previous judicial interpretation Moving beyond presumptions associated with fundamental rights, to one that aids in judicial interpretation, there is a presumption that re-enactment of a provision that has previously been interpreted by the courts in the same terms constitutes legislative approval of that judicial interpretation.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
432
Presumption that re-enactment constitutes 
approval of previous judicial interpretation
Moving beyond presumptions associated with fundamental rights, to one that aids in 
judicial interpretation, there is a presumption that re-enactment of a provision that has 
previously been interpreted by the courts in the same terms constitutes legislative approval 
of that judicial interpretation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: This position was stated clearly in Public Service Association of New South Wales v Industrial Commission of New South Wales where Kirby P said:
text_raw:
This position was stated clearly in Public Service Association of 
New South Wales v Industrial Commission of New South Wales where Kirby P said:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: There is a presumption, useful in statutory interpretation, that where a provision of legislation has been passed upon by authoritative decisions of the courts and is later reenacted, Parliament can be taken, in the absence of a clear intention to the contrary, to know and accept the interpretations given to the legislation.63 As the legislative history of a provision can be considered as part of the context of an enactment in the widest sense, this presumption can also be expressed as part of the modern, contextual approach to interpretation.
text_raw:
There is a presumption, useful in statutory interpretation, that where a provision of 
legislation has been passed upon by authoritative decisions of the courts and is later 
reenacted, Parliament can be taken, in the absence of a clear intention to the contrary, to 
know and accept the interpretations given to the legislation.63
As the legislative history of a provision can be considered as part of the context of an 
enactment in the widest sense, this presumption can also be expressed as part of the 
modern, contextual approach to interpretation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

text: [The] modern contextual approach ordinarily requires that statutory language re-enacted in an identical form after it has acquired a settled judicial meaning be taken to have the same meaning.
text_raw:
[The] modern contextual approach ordinarily requires that statutory language re-enacted 
in an identical form after it has acquired a settled judicial meaning be taken to have the 
same meaning.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: It equally requires that, changes of drafting style aside, statutory language re-enacted in an altered form after it has acquired a settled judicial meaning be taken to have a different meaning.
text_raw:
It equally requires that, changes of drafting style aside, statutory language 
re-enacted in an altered form after it has acquired a settled judicial meaning be taken to 
have a different meaning.

text: In Australia, this question is complicated by the presence of state and territorial Crowns as well as a Commonwealth Crown.76 The weakening of this presumption over time was noted by the High Court in Bropho v Western Australia (‘Bropho’).77 In a joint judgment with which Brennan J was in broad agreement, Mason CJ and Deane, Dawson, T oohey, Gaudron and McHugh JJ commented that earlier judicial statements to the effect that it must be manifest from the very terms of the statute itself that it was the legislative intent that the general words of a statute should bind the Crown, or that it must be apparent that the purposes of the statute would be wholly frustrated unless the Crown were bound, should be read as applying to the context of the particular statutory provisions involved in the cases in which they were made.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: In Queensland and Tasmania, interpretation legislation provides that legislation does not bind the Crown unless it is expressly declared to do so.80 For an example of reliance on the Queensland provision, s 13 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1954 (Qld), see Re Northbuild Construction Pty Ltd.81 The majority of the High Court stated in Bropho that provisions such as those in the Queensland and Tasmanian interpretation legislation would necessarily give way to the provisions of a subsequent enactment which, notwithstanding the earlier provision, disclosed a contrary legislative intent since the subsequent enactment would represent a pro tanto repeal or amendment of the earlier provision.82 That is, despite these provisions, if it is a necessary implication (that is, not expressly stated, just implied) that the statute does not bind the Crown, the courts will interpret the legislation so that the Crown is not bound.
text_raw:
In Queensland and Tasmania, interpretation legislation provides that legislation does 
not bind the Crown unless it is expressly declared to do so.80 For an example of reliance on 
the Queensland provision, s 13 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1954 (Qld), see Re Northbuild 
Construction Pty Ltd.81 The majority of the High Court stated in Bropho that provisions 
such as those in the Queensland and Tasmanian interpretation legislation
would necessarily give way to the provisions of a subsequent enactment which, 
notwithstanding the earlier provision, disclosed a contrary legislative intent since the 
subsequent enactment would represent a pro tanto repeal or amendment of the earlier 
provision.82
That is, despite these provisions, if it is a necessary implication (that is, not expressly 
stated, just implied) that the statute does not bind the Crown, the courts will interpret 
the legislation so that the Crown is not bound.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: Most Statutes, if their general words were taken literally in their widest sense, would apply to the whole world, but they are always read as being prima facie restricted in their operation with territorial limits.86 The presumption is enacted in the interpretation legislation 87 of the Commonwealth, the states, except for South Australia and Western Australia, and the territories, as well as existing at common law.

Most Statutes, if their general words were taken literally in their widest sense, would apply 
to the whole world, but they are always read as being prima facie restricted in their operation 
with territorial limits.86

the states, except for South Australia and Western Australia, and the territories, as well 
as existing at common law.

text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
438
Suggested answer
This particular situation appears, at first blush, to involve the retrospective operation of a 
statute — Nasem’s actions were in 2008, yet in 2012 an apparently additional consequence 
has been applied.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: However, it is important to remember an important distinction between the retrospective operation of an Act and the using of past events as a basis for future action.
text_raw:
However, it is important to remember an important distinction between 
the retrospective operation of an Act and the using of past events as a basis for future 
action.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: This distinction can be difficult to get one’s head around.
text_raw: This distinction can be difficult to get one’s head around.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: These circumstances are using past actions as a basis for future actions, rather than retrospective operation: the prohibition is prospective as it only applies from 2012 onwards, even though it uses past actions as a basis for the disqualification.
text_raw:
These circumstances 
are using past actions as a basis for future actions, rather than retrospective operation: the 
prohibition is prospective as it only applies from 2012 onwards, even though it uses past 
actions as a basis for the disqualification.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A retrospective operation of the statute would penalise anyone who had employed Nasem from 2008–2011, before the Act came into force, or declaring anything done by Nasem as a clerk in this period (2008–2011) void or voidable.

penalise anyone who had employed Nasem from 2008–2011, before the Act came into

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: We can also examine the purpose of the statute itself.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion
text: A conviction for fraud, whether occurring in, say, 2010 (before the Act) or in 2012 (after the Act), would appear to carry the same implications for the integrity or honesty of the person concerned.
text_raw:
A conviction for fraud, whether occurring in, say, 2010 (before the Act) or 
in 2012 (after the Act), would appear to carry the same implications for the integrity or 
honesty of the person concerned.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 13 PREsumPTions usEd in THE inTERPRETATion of LEgisLATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: 443 Introduction It is not uncommon for legislation to empower a particular person or agency — often someone holding a particular office — to make a decision or perform an action.
text_raw:
443
Introduction
It is not uncommon for legislation to empower a particular person or agency — often 
someone holding a particular office — to make a decision or perform an action.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: It is important to know whether, under legislation, that person or agency is obliged, or has a duty, to do something or whether the office-holder has a discretion, or a choice, to do or not to do it.
text_raw:
It is 
important to know whether, under legislation, that person or agency is obliged, or has 
a duty, to do something or whether the office-holder has a discretion, or a choice, to 
do or not to do it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: Another way of putting this is to ask whether a legislative provision is obligatory or discretionary.
text_raw:
Another way of putting this is to ask whether a legislative provision is 
obligatory or discretionary.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: If an office-holder has an unfettered discretion as to whether to do something, failure to do the thing cannot be the subject of a legitimate complaint at law.
text_raw:
If an office-holder has an unfettered discretion as to whether 
to do something, failure to do the thing cannot be the subject of a legitimate complaint 
at law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: However, if there has been a failure to perform an obligation imposed by legislation, quite apart from possible consequences for the person or agency that failed to fulfil the obligation, there may be an issue as to the legal consequences of that breach of the law.
text_raw:
However, if there has been a failure to perform an obligation imposed by legislation, 
quite apart from possible consequences for the person or agency that failed to fulfil the 
obligation, there may be an issue as to the legal consequences of that breach of the law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: In particular, there may be implications for the legal status of that decision or action — in essence, is the decision or action still legally valid?
text_raw:
In particular, there may be implications for the legal status of that decision or action — in 
essence, is the decision or action still legally valid?

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: The outcome of this determination in turn has an impact on those potentially affected by that decision or action.
text_raw:
The outcome of this determination 
in turn has an impact on those potentially affected by that decision or action.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: This chapter focuses on the two main questions that arise in relation to statutory obligations and discretions: • how to determine whether a legislative provision imposes an obligation or confers a discretion; and • how to determine whether failure to comply with a statutory obligation renders the action or decision invalid.
text_raw:
This chapter focuses on the two main questions that arise in relation to statutory 
obligations and discretions:
• how to determine whether a legislative provision imposes an obligation or 
confers a discretion; and
• how to determine whether failure to comply with a statutory obligation renders 
the action or decision invalid.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: The answers to these questions are arrived at by applying the principles of interpretation discussed in the previous four chapters.
text_raw:
The answers to these questions are arrived at by applying the principles of interpretation 
discussed in the previous four chapters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: The next chapter considers the application of these principles to complex problems.
text_raw:
The next chapter considers the application of

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: 445 Section 33 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth) makes provision in relation to the word ‘may’ creating a discretion, although does not explicitly provide for obligatory language:
text_raw:
445
Section 33 of the Acts Interpretation Act 1901 (Cth) makes provision in relation to 
the word ‘may’ creating a discretion, although does not explicitly provide for obligatory 
language:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: (1) Where an Act confers a power or function or imposes a duty, then the power may be exercised and the function or duty must be performed from time to time as occasion requires.
text_raw:
(1) Where an Act confers a power or function or imposes a duty, then the power may be 
exercised and the function or duty must be performed from time to time as occasion 
requires.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: (2A) Where an Act assented to after the commencement of this subsection provides that a person, court or body may do a particular act or thing, and the word may is used, the act or thing may be done at the discretion of the person, court or body.
text_raw:
(2A) Where an Act assented to after the commencement of this subsection provides that a 
person, court or body may do a particular act or thing, and the word may is used, the 
act or thing may be done at the discretion of the person, court or body.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: Section 33(2A) commenced on 18 December 1987 and is thus applicable to Commonwealth Acts passed after that date.
text_raw:
Section  33(2A) commenced on 18  December 1987 and is thus applicable to 
Commonwealth Acts passed after that date.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: The Commonwealth provision is more helpful than the somewhat circular provision contained in s 9 of the Interpretation Act 1987 (NSW), which provides:
text_raw:
The Commonwealth provision is more helpful 
than the somewhat circular provision contained in s  9 of the Interpretation Act  1987 
(NSW), which provides:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: (1) In any Act or instrument, the word ‘may’, if used to confer a power, indicates that the power may be exercised or not, at discretion.
text_raw:
(1) In any Act or instrument, the word ‘may’, if used to confer a power, indicates that the 
power may be exercised or not, at discretion.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: (2) In any Act or instrument, the word ‘shall’, if used to impose a duty, indicates that the duty must be performed.
text_raw:
(2) In any Act or instrument, the word ‘shall’, if used to impose a duty, indicates that the 
duty must be performed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: The circularity here lies in the fact that before one can determine that ‘may’ confers a discretion, one must determine whether it confers a power — that is, whether the provision confers a discretion.
text_raw:
The circularity here lies in the fact that before one can determine that ‘may’ confers 
a discretion, one must determine whether it confers a power — that is, whether the 
provision confers a discretion.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: Similarly, before one can determine that ‘shall’ creates an obligation, one must determine whether the provision imposes a duty — that is, whether it creates an obligation.
text_raw:
Similarly, before one can determine that ‘shall’ creates 
an obligation, one must determine whether the provision imposes a duty — that is, 
whether it creates an obligation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: As Basten JA said of the New South Wales provision in Coffs Harbour and District Local Aboriginal Land Council v Lynwood :
text_raw:
As Basten JA said of the New South Wales provision 
in Coffs Harbour and District Local Aboriginal Land Council v Lynwood :

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: The statement in s 9(2) of the Interpretation Act, namely, that ‘shall’, if used to impose a duty, indicates that the duty must be performed is question begging; the real issue will usually be whether the word imposes a duty.3 Compare the provisions in the interpretation legislation of other jurisdictions: the Legislation Act 2001 (ACT) s 146 and Acts Interpretation Act 1931 (Tas) s 10A treat the use of ‘may’ or ‘must’ as prima facie determinative, whereas the Acts Interpretation Act 1954 (Qld) s 32CA, Acts Interpretation Act 1984 (SA) s 34, Interpretation of Legislation Act 1984 (Vic) s 45 and Interpretation Act 1984 (WA) s 56 have similar wording to the New South Wales provision.
text_raw:
The statement in s 9(2) of the Interpretation Act, namely, that ‘shall’, if used to impose 
a duty, indicates that the duty must be performed is question begging; the real issue will 
usually be whether the word imposes a duty.3
Compare the provisions in the interpretation legislation of other jurisdictions: the 
Legislation Act  2001 (ACT) s  146 and Acts Interpretation Act  1931 (Tas) s  10A treat 
the use of ‘may’ or ‘must’ as prima facie determinative, whereas the Acts Interpretation 
Act 1954 (Qld) s 32CA, Acts Interpretation Act 1984 (SA) s 34, Interpretation of Legislation 
Act 1984 (Vic) s 45 and Interpretation Act 1984 (WA) s 56 have similar wording to the 
New South Wales provision.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: JudiCiAl APPRoACHES As Dennis Pearce has shown, the courts have not always treated the use of ‘shall’ and ‘may’ as conclusive, either under statutory provisions or the common law.4 Instead, the courts have sought to go beyond those words and have attempted, by considering the possible effects of alternative interpretations, to reach a conclusion that is in accordance with the purpose or object underlying the provision.
text_raw:
JudiCiAl APPRoACHES
As Dennis Pearce has shown, the courts have not always treated the use of ‘shall’ and ‘may’ 
as conclusive, either under statutory provisions or the common law.4 Instead, the courts 
have sought to go beyond those words and have attempted, by considering the possible 
effects of alternative interpretations, to reach a conclusion that is in accordance with the 
purpose or object underlying the provision.

text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 450 In our opinion, the Court of Appeal of New South Wales was correct in Tasker v Fullwood [1978] 1 NSWLR 20, 23–4; see also Victoria v Commonwealth and Connor (1975) 7 ALR 1 (Gibbs J) in criticising the continued use of the ‘elusive distinction between directory and mandatory requirements’ … The classification of a statutory provision as mandatory or directory records a result which has been reached on other grounds.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
450
In our opinion, the Court of Appeal of New South Wales was correct in Tasker 
v  Fullwood [1978] 1 NSWLR 20, 23–4; see  also Victoria v  Commonwealth and Connor 
(1975) 7 ALR 1 (Gibbs  J) in criticising the continued use of the ‘elusive distinction 
between directory and mandatory requirements’ … The classification of a statutory 
provision as mandatory or directory records a result which has been reached on other 
grounds.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 14 STATuToR y obligATionS And diSCRETionS
text: The classification is the end of the inquiry, not the beginning … That being so, a court, determining the validity of an act done in breach of a statutory provision, may easily focus on the wrong factors if it asks itself whether compliance with the provision is mandatory or directory … A better test for determining the issue of validity is to ask whether it was a purpose of the legislation that an act done in breach of the provision should be invalid.
text_raw:
The classification is the end of the inquiry, not the beginning … That being so, 
a court, determining the validity of an act done in breach of a statutory provision, may 
easily focus on the wrong factors if it asks itself whether compliance with the provision 
is mandatory or directory … A better test for determining the issue of validity is to ask 
whether it was a purpose of the legislation that an act done in breach of the provision 
should be invalid.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Sam Keen is a law student doing voluntary work at the Broken Hill Legal Advice Centre in New South Wales.
text_raw:
Sam Keen is a law student doing voluntary work at the Broken Hill Legal Advice 
Centre in New South Wales.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: The duty solicitor has asked him for a report on the following matter:
text_raw:
The duty solicitor has asked him for a report on the following 
matter:

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Last year Bill Blake purchased a small Crown pastoral lease a few kilometres out of Broken Hill.
text_raw:
Last year Bill Blake purchased a small Crown pastoral lease a few kilometres out of Broken 
Hill.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Several months ago he found a dingo pup on his property.
text_raw: Several months ago he found a dingo pup on his property.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Bill took it home and telephoned the Wild Dog Destruction Board, asking for permission to keep it.
text_raw:
Bill took it home and 
telephoned the Wild Dog Destruction Board, asking for permission to keep it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: A few days later he received a letter from the Board, authorising him to keep the dingo, but advising him to ensure that it was tied up.
text_raw:
A few days 
later he received a letter from the Board, authorising him to keep the dingo, but advising 
him to ensure that it was tied up.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: A month ago it got off the chain and since then Bill has been unable to catch it.
text_raw:
A month ago it got off the chain and since then Bill has 
been unable to catch it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Bill’s neighbours saw the dingo wandering around on Bill’s property.
text_raw: Bill’s neighbours saw the dingo wandering around on Bill’s property.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: They complained about it to the Wild Dog Destruction Board.
text_raw:
They complained 
about it to the Wild Dog Destruction Board.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Last week Arch Huggins, a Board member (the nominee of the Broken Hill Rural Lands Protection Board), went out to take a look.
text_raw:
Last week Arch Huggins, a Board member (the 
nominee of the Broken Hill Rural Lands Protection Board), went out to take a look.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: The dingo walked over and licked Arch’s hand, but Bill’s blue heeler dog viciously attacked Arch, knocking him to the ground and biting his leg.
text_raw:
The 
dingo walked over and licked Arch’s hand, but Bill’s blue heeler dog viciously attacked Arch, 
knocking him to the ground and biting his leg.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Later that day the neighbours told Arch that the dingo was quiet and friendly but that recently the blue heeler had attacked them several times and was now very dangerous.
text_raw:
Later that day the neighbours told Arch that 
the dingo was quiet and friendly but that recently the blue heeler had attacked them several 
times and was now very dangerous.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: The following day, Arch gave a full report on the visit at a meeting of the Board, as a result of which the Board prepared a notice addressed to Bill, requiring him to arrange for both the dingo and the blue heeler dog to be destroyed.
text_raw:
The following day, Arch gave a full report on the visit at a meeting of the Board, as a 
result of which the Board prepared a notice addressed to Bill, requiring him to arrange for 
both the dingo and the blue heeler dog to be destroyed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: The notice specified that this was to be done within 24 hours of receipt of the notice.
text_raw:
The notice specified that this was 
to be done within 24 hours of receipt of the notice.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Arch drove out to Bill’s property later that day and gave the notice to him.
text_raw:
Arch drove out to Bill’s property later 
that day and gave the notice to him.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: That evening, Bill telephoned Vince Dunn, a veterinary surgeon, asking him to come out and destroy the animals.
text_raw:
That evening, Bill telephoned Vince Dunn, a veterinary 
surgeon, asking him to come out and destroy the animals.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Vince said that he was very busy, but that he would get out there as soon as he could.
text_raw:
Vince said that he was very busy, 
but that he would get out there as soon as he could.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Y esterday, two days after his last visit, Arch called in again at Bill’s place and saw both the dingo and the blue heeler.
text_raw:
Y esterday, two days after his last visit, Arch called in again at Bill’s place and saw both 
the dingo and the blue heeler.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: Bill explained to Arch what Vince had said.
text_raw: Bill explained to Arch what Vince had said.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: This morning, after receiving a report of these events from Arch, the Board resolved that, in the exercise of authority granted by s 8 of the Wild Dog Destruction Act 1921 (NSW), Bill would be required to pay a fine of $500 unless he informed the Board in writing forthwith after receiving written notice of the Board’s resolution that he had complied with the Board’s original notice.
text_raw:
This morning, 
after receiving a report of these events from Arch, the Board resolved that, in the exercise 
of authority granted by s 8 of the Wild Dog Destruction Act 1921 (NSW), Bill would be 
required to pay a fine of $500 unless he informed the Board in writing forthwith after 
receiving written notice of the Board’s resolution that he had complied with the Board’s 
original notice.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: When Arch delivered the notice of this resolution to Bill, Bill told Arch that Vince had just destroyed the animals.
text_raw:
When Arch delivered the notice of this resolution to Bill, Bill told Arch 
that Vince had just destroyed the animals.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 15 APPlying lEgislATion To ComPlEx PRoblEms
text: When Arch reported this back to the Board it decided that Bill should be fined because he had not shown in writing that he had complied with the notice.
text_raw:
When Arch reported this back to the Board 
it decided that Bill should be fined because he had not shown in writing that he had 
complied with the notice.
