chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: However, an assertion that ‘summers are getting hotter every year’ would still need some reference to research that establishes this as an empirical fact.
text_raw:
However, an assertion that ‘summers are getting hotter every 
year’ would still need some reference to research that establishes this as an empirical fact.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: T o strengthen an argument in an essay, a writer will want to find empirical research and other opinions, and what the reader learns from these other sources must be referenced.
text_raw:
T o strengthen an argument in an essay, a writer will want to find empirical research and

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: For specific points made by others, and certainly for quotations that are used, a pinpoint reference needs to be provided.
text_raw:
For specific points made by others, and certainly for quotations that are used, a pinpoint

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: A simple example serves to illustrate these points about what and when to reference.
text_raw: A simple example serves to illustrate these points about what and when to reference.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Suppose you were required to write an essay about whether the default speed limit on Australian roads should be increased.
text_raw:
Suppose you were required to write an essay about whether the default speed limit on 
Australian roads should be increased.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: One of the first questions you would need to answer and assert in your essay is the current limit.
text_raw:
One of the first questions you would need to answer 
and assert in your essay is the current limit.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: An assertion that the default speed limit on Australian urban roads is 50 kilometres per hour is a statement of what the law currently is.
text_raw:
An assertion that the default speed limit on 
Australian urban roads is 50 kilometres per hour is a statement of what the law currently 
is.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: This statement of the law requires a reference to a primary source, which would be a statute.6 However, to explore arguments for and against changing this limit, a student would need to research the history or the implications of such a change, and reference any empirical data or opinions relied on.
text_raw:
This statement of the law requires a reference to a primary source, which would be 
a statute.6 However, to explore arguments for and against changing this limit, a student

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: An assertion that ‘most people drive above the speed limit’ would need support from an empirical study about driving habits; personal or anecdotal experience is rarely ever sufficient.

text: Similarly, the work of other authors on this topic would need to be referenced.
text_raw:

this topic would need to be referenced.

text: In a well-written legal essay there will be some description of the law, which must be supported by reference to primary sources, and then arguments about how the law operates, could operate, should be changed or otherwise, and these latter points need to be supported with reference to empirical research and the views of experts, appropriately referenced.

appropriately referenced.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The AGLC style is to use ‘ibid’.10 For example, suppose that in note 4 of a document, you refer to Martin Loughlin, Public Law and Political Theory (Clarendon Press, 1992) 164.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In the example with the first reference to page 164, any subsequent reference to a different page — for example, page 182 — would be noted as ‘ibid 182’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The second qualification is that ‘ibid’ cannot be used if there is more than one source listed in the preceding reference, because ‘ibid’ would not distinguish between the different sources in the preceding note and thus the reference would be ambiguous.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Citing cases The term ‘citation’, when used in relation to a case, includes the name of the case and a unique alphanumeric reference, which is the information needed to locate it.13 There are two types of case citations: law reports and medium neutral citations: see 7.66ff.
text_raw:
Citing cases
The term ‘citation’, when used in relation to a case, includes the name of the case and a 
unique alphanumeric reference, which is the information needed to locate it.13 There are 
two types of case citations: law reports and medium neutral citations: see 7.66ff.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: REPoRTEd CASES And MEdiUM nEUTRAL CiTATion The most legally significant cases are published as part of one or more series of authorised reports, which are available in hard copy volumes and now also electronically.
text_raw:
REPoRTEd CASES And MEdiUM nEUTRAL CiTATion
The most legally significant cases are published as part of one or more series of authorised 
reports, which are available in hard copy volumes and now also electronically.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: A complete case citation for reported cases includes: • the name of the case, italicised; • the year of the decision (or publication, where the report series is published in annual volumes); • the volume number of the report series (if there is one); • the abbreviated title of the report series; • the page in the report volume at which the case begins; and • if a pinpoint reference is called for, the specific page being referred to within the case (a paragraph reference can also be given).14 Usually the name of the court that decided the case is not shown, but where this is important and is not obvious from the report series, the court name should be given in parentheses after the citation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: When the citation is to reference a specific part of a judgment, especially in cases where there was more than one judge, the name of the judge who wrote that part of the judgment should also be shown in parentheses after the pinpoint reference.
text_raw:
When the citation is to reference a specific part of a 
judgment, especially in cases where there was more than one judge, the name of the 
judge who wrote that part of the judgment should also be shown in parentheses after 
the pinpoint reference.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The system was adopted due to the difficulty of reproduction of pagination in an electronic file and the adoption of a numbered paragraph system instead.
text_raw:
The 
system was adopted due to the difficulty of reproduction of pagination in an electronic file

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The medium neutral system is intended to operate in conjunction with, not in lieu of, traditional citation methods.
text_raw:
The medium neutral system 
is intended to operate in conjunction with, not in lieu of, traditional citation methods.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Remembering that only the most legally significant cases are published in law reports, for most judgments there will be only a medium neutral citation.
text_raw:
Remembering that only the most legally significant cases are published in law reports, for 
most judgments there will be only a medium neutral citation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: However, medium neutral citations are only used if the citation ‘was allocated by the court itself’;15 all other cases that have not been included in a law report are cited as ‘unreported’.16 The basic components of a medium neutral citation system are: • the name of the case; • the year the judgment is handed down by a court or tribunal, in square brackets; • a unique court or tribunal identifier in abbreviated form; • the judgment number (issued by the court or tribunal); and • a pinpoint reference to the relevant paragraph(s), shown in square brackets (where required).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: As with authorised report case citations, the name of the judge may also be shown in parentheses after the citation.
text_raw:
As with authorised report case citations, the name of the judge may also be shown in 
parentheses after the citation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In tribunal decisions, the names of the parties are often preceded by ‘Re’ and the names of the other parties are separated by ‘and’ (used in speech as well), not ‘v’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Example Re Bongioletti and Veterans’ Review Board If a case has more than two parties, the additional party or parties are sometimes acknowledged by the use of ‘and Another’, or ‘and Others’ (shortened to ‘and Anor’ or ‘and Ors’); however, AGLC style is to cite cases solely by reference to the main parties.17 When the parties include a corporate body, the full corporate title should be used, although abbreviations such as ‘Pty’, ‘Ltd’ and ‘&’ are employed.
text_raw:
Example
Re Bongioletti and Veterans’ Review Board
If a case has more than two parties, the additional party or parties are sometimes 
acknowledged by the use of ‘and Another’, or ‘and Others’ (shortened to ‘and Anor’ 
or ‘and Ors’); however, AGLC style is to cite cases solely by reference to the main 
parties.17
When the parties include a corporate body, the full corporate title should be used, 
although abbreviations such as ‘Pty’, ‘Ltd’ and ‘&’ are employed.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: If the name of a case is given in the text and the citation is footnoted, it is not necessary to repeat the name in the footnote.18 The following sections outline a few more specific details about the naming of parties and how the names are to appear in citations. description of parties The parties at first instance are usually called the ‘plaintiff’ and the ‘defendant’ or, particularly if the hearing is before a tribunal, the ‘applicant’ and the ‘respondent’.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Re proceedings Even though it is common to speak of the common law as an ‘adversarial system’, many court proceedings have only one named party.
text_raw:
Re proceedings
Even though it is common to speak of the common law as an ‘adversarial system’, many 
court proceedings have only one named party.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Common examples are cases dealing with the interpretation of a deed of trust, the disposition of an estate under a will, or the winding up of a company.
text_raw:
Common examples are cases dealing with 
the interpretation of a deed of trust, the disposition of an estate under a will, or the 
winding up of a company.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: These cases are usually titled Re or In re, followed by the name of the trust, testator or company.
text_raw:
These cases are usually titled Re or In re, followed by the name 
of the trust, testator or company.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: An example is Re Huon V alley Springs Pty Ltd.22 These cases should be distinguished from decisions of tribunals which are also reported as Re [party names].
text_raw:
An example is Re Huon V alley Springs Pty Ltd.22
These cases should be distinguished from decisions of tribunals which are also 
reported as Re [party names].

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Here, too, the reason for use of this form of citation is that the proceedings are supposedly not adversarial.
text_raw:

the proceedings are supposedly not adversarial.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The government agency against which the action is brought is represented at the hearing to assist the tribunal, rather than to oppose the application.
text_raw:
The government agency against which 
the action is brought is represented at the hearing to assist the tribunal, rather than to 
oppose the application.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: An example is Re McDonald and Secretary, Department of Family and Community Services.23 Cases in which the identity of the parties is kept confidential In an increasing number of cases the law may require,24 or the court or tribunal may order, that the name of a party or a witness to certain proceedings not be published or broadcast.
text_raw:
An example is Re McDonald and Secretary, Department of Family and 
Community Services.23
Cases in which the identity of the parties is kept confidential
In an increasing number of cases the law may require,24 or the court or tribunal may order, 
that the name of a party or a witness to certain proceedings not be published or broadcast.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: This can happen in cases involving children, people with intellectual disability, sensitive issues of family law, applicants for protection visas, or other cases in which the identity of the party is not disclosed for reasons of confidentiality.
text_raw:
This can happen in cases involving children, people with intellectual disability, sensitive 
issues of family law, applicants for protection visas, or other cases in which the identity of 
the party is not disclosed for reasons of confidentiality.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In such an instance, the case may be reported using the party’s initials or an acronym of random initials.
text_raw:
In such an instance, the case may 
be reported using the party’s initials or an acronym of random initials.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In many older English cases the actual title has been all but forgotten, and the convention is to cite the case using the popular name.
text_raw:
In many older English cases the actual title has been all but forgotten, and the 
convention is to cite the case using the popular name.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In newer cases, the convention is to cite the full reference followed by the common name in parentheses.
text_raw:
In newer cases, the convention is to 
cite the full reference followed by the common name in parentheses.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: So, for example, the Engineers’ Case27 should be cited as Amalgamated Society of Engineers v Adelaide Steamship Company (‘Engineers’ Case’).
text_raw:
So, for example, the 
Engineers’ Case27 should be cited as Amalgamated Society of Engineers v Adelaide Steamship 
Company (‘Engineers’ Case’).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Similarly, you often see a reference to the T asmanian Dam Case,28 although the correct form is Commonwealth v T asmania (‘T asmanian Dam Case’).
text_raw:
Similarly, you often see a reference to the T asmanian Dam 
Case,28 although the correct form is Commonwealth v T asmania (‘T asmanian Dam Case’).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Another example is Re Judiciary and Navigation Acts29 (‘Advisory Opinions Case’).
text_raw: Another example is Re Judiciary and Navigation Acts29 (‘Advisory Opinions Case’).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: YEAR And V oLUME nUMBER of REPoRT SERiES When cases are collated into published report series they are numbered and identified in one of two ways: by volumes numbered consecutively; or by year.
text_raw:
YEAR And V oLUME nUMBER of REPoRT SERiES
When cases are collated into published report series they are numbered and identified 
in one of two ways: by volumes numbered consecutively; or by year.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In most Australian series of law reports, there are consecutively numbered volumes.
text_raw:
In most Australian 
series of law reports, there are consecutively numbered volumes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The Commonwealth Law Reports, for example, comprise primarily the decisions of the High Court of Australia from volume 1 in 1903 to volume 265 in 2018, and beyond.
text_raw:
The Commonwealth Law 
Reports, for example, comprise primarily the decisions of the High Court of Australia from 
volume 1 in 1903 to volume 265 in 2018, and beyond.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The year of decision is included in the citation (in round brackets), but it is the volume number, not the year, which is critical to identifying and locating particular decisions.
text_raw:
The year of decision is included 
in the citation (in round brackets), but it is the volume number, not the year, which is 
critical to identifying and locating particular decisions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Volume 162 of the Commonwealth Law Reports, for example, covers cases decided by the High Court in 1986–87.
text_raw:
Volume 162 of the Commonwealth 
Law Reports, for example, covers cases decided by the High Court in 1986–87.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The case of Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko-Wallsend Ltd is found at page 24.
text_raw:
The case 
of Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko-Wallsend Ltd is found at page 24.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Oral argument in the case was heard in November 1985, but the decision was not handed down until July 1986.
text_raw:
Oral argument in 
the case was heard in November 1985, but the decision was not handed down until July 
1986.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Accordingly, the proper citation for the case is Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko- Wallsend Ltd (1986) 162 CLR 24.
text_raw:
Accordingly, the proper citation for the case is Minister for Aboriginal Affairs v Peko-
Wallsend Ltd (1986) 162 CLR 24.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In other series, cases (and the report in which they can be found) are identified by the year in which they were published, usually shown in square brackets.
text_raw:
In other series, cases (and the report in which they can be found) are identified 
by the year in which they were published, usually shown in square brackets.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The current series of the authorised reports for Queensland, England and New Zealand are published this way.
text_raw:
The current 
series of the authorised reports for Queensland, England and New Zealand are published 
this way.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Where there is more than one volume in a year, then the volume number must also be identified.
text_raw:
Where there is more than one volume in a year, then the volume number must 
also be identified.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: For example, [2013] 2 All ER refers to the second volume of the All England Reports for the year 2013.
text_raw:
For example, [2013] 2 All ER refers to the second volume of the All 
England Reports for the year 2013.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Medium neutral citations by definition do not refer to a bound or published series and thus do not have volume numbers.
text_raw:
Medium neutral citations by definition do not refer to a bound or published series 
and thus do not have volume numbers.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The year of the decision is included, inside square brackets, and is a critical part of the citation.
text_raw:
The year of the decision is included, inside square 
brackets, and is a critical part of the citation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: TiTLE of REPoRT SERiES If a case is reported in more than one series, the writer should always cite the authorised report in preference to an unauthorised series (see 21.26).
text_raw:
TiTLE of REPoRT SERiES
If a case is reported in more than one series, the writer should always cite the authorised 
report in preference to an unauthorised series (see  21.26).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: There is sometimes an exception to this in the case of those who practise before tribunals (such as the Fair Work Commission or the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal).
text_raw:
There is sometimes an 
exception to this in the case of those who practise before tribunals (such as the Fair 
Work Commission or the Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In such cases, the custom is sometimes to cite an unofficial, but highly authoritative, report series specific to that commission or tribunal.
text_raw:
In such cases, the 
custom is sometimes to cite an unofficial, but highly authoritative, report series specific 
to that commission or tribunal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The abbreviations for commonly used law reports, and a guide to the various report series, including the authorised reports for all Australian, British, New Zealand, and key Canadian and United States jurisdictions, are set out in Essential Legal Toolkit B and C.
text_raw:
The abbreviations for commonly used law reports, and a guide to the various report 
series, including the authorised reports for all Australian, British, New Zealand, and key 
Canadian and United States jurisdictions, are set out in Essential Legal Toolkit B and C.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: PAgE And PARA gRAPH REfEREnCES Each case citation needs to include the page at which the report of the case begins; for medium neutral citation, the equivalent of the first page is the judgment number.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: In addition, if quoting from a case, or referring to a specific portion of a judgment, the citation must include a pinpoint reference.
text_raw:
In addition, if quoting from a case, or referring to a specific portion of a judgment, 
the citation must include a pinpoint reference.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: For citations to law reports, this specific reference must be to the relevant page (and can also include the paragraph number).31 Examples Commonwealth v Western Australia (1999) 196 CLR 392, 398 Re Culleton [2017] HCA 3 [38]–[43] Failure to include pinpoint references is one of the more common errors made by new law students.

reference must be to the relevant page (and can also include the paragraph number).31

Re Culleton [2017] HCA 3 [38]–[43]

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Reports in the Commonwealth Law Reports, the authorised series, should be cited in preference to reports in the unauthorised Australian Law Reports, the Australian Law Journal Reports or the Federal Law Reports; and citation of Federal Court decisions should be to the Federal Court Reports, the authorised series, rather than the Australian Law Reports or the Administrative Appeal Reports series.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Citing statutes The conventional method of citing an Australian statute is as follows:34 • the statute’s short title or name, including the year of enactment, in italics; • the jurisdiction in which the statute was enacted, in round brackets (unless it is obvious from the context); and • if appropriate, the specific part being referred to (for example, section, subsection, paragraph or subparagraph).
text_raw:
Citing statutes
The conventional method of citing an Australian statute is as follows:34
• the statute’s short title or name, including the year of enactment, in italics;
• the jurisdiction in which the statute was enacted, in round brackets (unless it is 
obvious from the context); and
• if appropriate, the specific part being referred to (for example, section, subsection, 
paragraph or subparagraph).

580
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
Statutory provisions are broken down into sections, subsections and paragraphs (and

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: The current practice in Australia is to use the written abbreviation ‘s’ or ‘section’ to refer to any part of a statutory provision.

The current practice 
in Australia is to use the written abbreviation ‘s’ or ‘section’ to refer to any part of a statutory

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: For example, ‘s 20’ refers to section 20 of a given Act, while ‘s 20(3)(a)(ii)’ refers to section 20 subsection (3) paragraph (a) and sub-paragraph (ii).

to section 20 subsection (3) paragraph (a) and sub-paragraph (ii).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 21 REfEREnCing And CiTATion
text: Occasionally, when you need to distinguish between parts of the same provision, more detailed reference can be given; for example, ‘sub-paras (ii) and (iii)’ of s 20(3)(a).

text: When referring to two or more sections of the same Act, use ‘ss’; for example, ‘ss 33(1) and 37(2)’, ‘ss 46–52’.35 CiTing BRiTiSH And iMPERiAL STATUTES As with modern Australian statutes, the AGLC says that British legislation is cited using the short title, together with the year of enactment, using the standard practice of italicisation.36 The British practice, using their standard style guide, is to put the short titles of domestic statutes in roman (that is, not italicised).37 Work to be submitted or published in Australia should comply with the AGLC.
text_raw:

sections of the same Act, use ‘ss’; for example, ‘ss 33(1) and 37(2)’, ‘ss 46–52’.35 
CiTing BRiTiSH And iMPERiAL STATUTES
As with modern Australian statutes, the AGLC says that British legislation is cited 
using the short title, together with the year of enactment, using the standard practice of 
italicisation.36 The British practice, using their standard style guide, is to put the short titles 
of domestic statutes in roman (that is, not italicised).37 Work to be submitted or published 
in Australia should comply with the AGLC.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: 589 Introduction This chapter deals with two related topics — study skills and exam-taking.
text_raw:
589
Introduction
This chapter deals with two related topics — study skills and exam-taking.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: It provides advice on how to: • develop key study skills, including reading, note-taking and organising time; • participate effectively both in and out of the classroom; • find the right study methods; • prepare for exams; • create summaries as part of exam preparation; • get the most out of study groups; and • structure a response to a typical issue-spotting law school exam.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Good study skills are a key component of success at university.
text_raw: Good study skills are a key component of success at university.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Most of the study problems faced by students are common to all, but they are faced and overcome in many different ways.
text_raw:
Most of the study 
problems faced by students are common to all, but they are faced and overcome in many 
different ways.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: So while it is not possible to prescribe a fail-safe method that is useful to everyone, this chapter starts with suggestions that should be helpful to most students.
text_raw:
So while it is not possible to prescribe a fail-safe method that is useful to 
everyone, this chapter starts with suggestions that should be helpful to most students.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Generally teachers make clear to students the expected learning outcomes for a particular unit or course.
text_raw:
Generally teachers make clear to students the expected learning outcomes for a 
particular unit or course.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The outcomes will usually include both an understanding of the particular doctrinal field and the ability to apply the law correctly to hypothetical scenarios.
text_raw:
The outcomes will usually include both an understanding of 
the particular doctrinal field and the ability to apply the law correctly to hypothetical 
scenarios.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: These outcomes are often tested through ‘issue-spotting’ exams.
text_raw: These outcomes are often tested through ‘issue-spotting’ exams.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: In this type of exam a factual scenario is provided and the student is asked to write a response that is akin to a legal advice about whether, for example, someone in the scenario has breached the contract, committed a crime or could be liable in tort.
text_raw:
In this type of 
exam a factual scenario is provided and the student is asked to write a response that is akin 
to a legal advice about whether, for example, someone in the scenario has breached the 
contract, committed a crime or could be liable in tort.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: This type of assessment is different from legal essay writing (discussed in 20.47ff).
text_raw:
This type of assessment is different 
from legal essay writing (discussed in 20.47ff).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: It mainly relies on primary sources and requires the student to provide an objective, rather than persuasive, conclusion about the likelihood of success in a court if the matter was pursued.
text_raw:
It mainly relies on primary sources and 
requires the student to provide an objective, rather than persuasive, conclusion about the 
likelihood of success in a court if the matter was pursued.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: However, most teachers will also expect students to develop a wider, contextual understanding of how the law operates to address a social ill or promote particular behaviours.
text_raw:
However, most teachers will also expect students to develop a wider, contextual 
understanding of how the law operates to address a social ill or promote particular behaviours.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Achieving these outcomes requires more than merely learning the rules of law; it requires critical thinking and reading beyond legislation and cases.
text_raw:
Achieving these outcomes requires more than merely learning the rules of law; it requires 
critical thinking and reading beyond legislation and cases.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There may be some scope for assessing these outcomes in the standard issue-spotting exam, but class participation and essays often perform this role.
text_raw:
There may be some scope for 
assessing these outcomes in the standard issue-spotting exam, but class participation and 
essays often perform this role.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Critical thinking is discussed further at 22.20ff.
text_raw: Critical thinking is discussed further at 22.20ff.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Focusing on the enumerated learning outcomes is important, but it is essential to remember that studying is not an end in itself.
text_raw:
Focusing on the enumerated learning outcomes is important, but it is essential to 
remember that studying is not an end in itself.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The ultimate purpose of study is education and understanding.
text_raw:
The ultimate purpose of study is education 
and understanding.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: As Paul Vinogradoff, one of the world’s best-known legal historians, once said, ‘study is knowledge coordinated by reflection’.2 This is important to bear in mind while studying law.
text_raw:
As Paul Vinogradoff, one of the world’s best-known legal historians, 
once said, ‘study is knowledge coordinated by reflection’.2 This is important to bear in 
mind while studying law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The mere acquisition of detailed information is not enough.
text_raw: The mere acquisition of detailed information is not enough.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: In addition there must be reflection — a period of contemplation about what has been learned and how it fits into a particular subject area and the broader framework of the legal system.
text_raw:
In addition there must be reflection — a period of contemplation about what has been 
learned and how it fits into a particular subject area and the broader framework of the 
legal system.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Students who do best in law school are those who are not only familiar with the law’s constituent parts — individual subjects such as torts, contracts and the like — but who can also see the wider picture of the law in its entirety, as a system, and as part of our culture.
text_raw:
Students who do best in law school are those who are not only familiar with 
the law’s constituent parts — individual subjects such as torts, contracts and the like — 
but who can also see the wider picture of the law in its entirety, as a system, and as part 
of our culture.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: What are study skills?
text_raw: What are study skills?

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There are a number of skills students need at least some competence in to enjoy, and excel at, tertiary study.
text_raw:
There are a number of skills students need at least some competence in to enjoy, and 
excel at, tertiary study.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There are, of course, personal skills which include: managing uncertainty — academic, vocational, personal and family; dealing with anxiety and tension; and managing relationships, particularly with fellow students, teachers, family and colleagues.
text_raw:
There are, of course, personal skills which include: managing 
uncertainty  — academic, vocational, personal and family; dealing with anxiety and 
tension; and managing relationships, particularly with fellow students, teachers, family 
and colleagues.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: These are beyond the scope of this book.
text_raw: These are beyond the scope of this book.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There are also legal writing skills, which are explained in Chapter 20.
text_raw:
There are also legal writing skills, 
which are explained in Chapter 20.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Other skills can be grouped as study skills to be used throughout the course and these are dealt with at 22.5–22.22.
text_raw:
Other skills can be grouped as study skills to be used 
throughout the course and these are dealt with at 22.5–22.22.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Skills more specific to preparing for exams are outlined later in the chapter at 22.23–22.36.
text_raw:
Skills more specific to 
preparing for exams are outlined later in the chapter at 22.23–22.36.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The study skills covered in this chapter include: • planning and organising study time effectively; • reading actively and efficiently; • actively listening and taking notes in classes; • participating in classes; • engaging with teachers and other students outside of the classroom; and • critical thinking.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: We provide here some guidance on how to study and develop these skills, but ultimately, to study effectively, students need to understand for themselves how they learn best.
text_raw:
We provide here some guidance on how to study and develop these skills, but ultimately, 
to study effectively, students need to understand for themselves how they learn best.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: After looking at the skills listed above, we provide suggestions on how a student can help to develop and use such awareness to improve their study performance.
text_raw:
After looking at the skills listed above, we provide suggestions on how a student can 
help to develop and use such awareness to improve their study performance.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Organising study time It is common sense that to do anything efficiently and effectively it is necessary to be well organised.
text_raw:
Organising study time
It is common sense that to do anything efficiently and effectively it is necessary to be 
well organised.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: This is particularly true of tertiary study where there is little externally imposed discipline and students are left to themselves to plan their work schedules, ensure adherence to deadlines and prepare properly for exams.
text_raw:
This is particularly true of tertiary study where there is little externally 
imposed discipline and students are left to themselves to plan their work schedules, ensure 
adherence to deadlines and prepare properly for exams.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: A study plan can be a useful organisational tool.
text_raw: A study plan can be a useful organisational tool.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From the beginning of a program of study, students need to find out what they are required to cover and understand, in each course or unit.
text_raw:
From the beginning of a program of 
study, students need to find out what they are required to cover and understand, in each 
course or unit.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: This information can be used to draw up a study plan, identifying how and when time will be allocated to cover the material, complete assessments and prepare for any exams.
text_raw:
This information can be used to draw up a study plan, identifying how 
and when time will be allocated to cover the material, complete assessments and prepare 
for any exams.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: It is a good idea to note important dates and deadlines, so that you can conceptualise the course of a program and how much time you have for assessments and study.
text_raw:
It is a good idea to note important dates and deadlines, so that you can 
conceptualise the course of a program and how much time you have for assessments and 
study.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: No plan should be completely inflexible.
text_raw: No plan should be completely inflexible.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: And all plans should factor in non-study activities, including those things that enable study to be sustainable over the long term, such as work, relaxation, exercise and social engagement.
text_raw:
And all plans should factor in non-study 
activities, including those things that enable study to be sustainable over the long term, 
such as work, relaxation, exercise and social engagement.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The challenge is to balance these.
text_raw: The challenge is to balance these.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: It is important to remember that adequate relaxation can help you to study efficiently; being disciplined and diligent is good, but unreasonably extending the hours of study is unlikely to help.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: 591 Reading efficiently Law students are required to do a large amount of reading, so it is important to work out how to do this efficiently and effectively.
text_raw:
591
Reading efficiently
Law students are required to do a large amount of reading, so it is important to work 
out how to do this efficiently and effectively.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: In some units the reading will consist mainly of judgments but other readings include journal articles, texts and other books, legislative material, case commentaries and reports.
text_raw:
In some units the reading will consist 
mainly of judgments but other readings include journal articles, texts and other books, 
legislative material, case commentaries and reports.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The specific skills involved in reading and analysing cases are discussed in Chapter 7.
text_raw:
The specific skills involved in reading 
and analysing cases are discussed in Chapter 7.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Here are four important points to remember in relation to reading generally. • Skim-read.
text_raw:
Here are four important points to remember in relation to reading generally.
• Skim-read.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: It is often useful to skim-read a piece first to determine whether it will be relevant, helpful and worth reading thoroughly.
text_raw:
It is often useful to skim-read a piece first to determine whether 
it will be relevant, helpful and worth reading thoroughly.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Cases may also be skimmed in order to identify the important or relevant points, using the key elements of the cases identified at 7.10ff. • Read what is relevant.
text_raw:
Cases may also be 
skimmed in order to identify the important or relevant points, using the key 
elements of the cases identified at 7.10ff.
• Read what is relevant.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There are many resources available to students and a challenge is to identify which ones are worth reading at any given time.
text_raw:
There are many resources available to students and a 
challenge is to identify which ones are worth reading at any given time.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Be guided by your teachers and your goals.
text_raw:
Be 
guided by your teachers and your goals.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Unit outlines will generally distinguish between required readings (those which the student is expected to read for a class), and recommended readings (which are suggested for further depth or as a lead for research).
text_raw:
Unit outlines will generally distinguish 
between required readings (those which the student is expected to read for a 
class), and recommended readings (which are suggested for further depth or as a 
lead for research).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Even the required readings can be lengthy and cover a variety of issues.
text_raw:
Even the required readings can be lengthy and cover a variety 
of issues.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Students should focus their attention on the parts that are most relevant.
text_raw: Students should focus their attention on the parts that are most relevant.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Use headings, table of contents, introductions and conclusions to identify what a particular resource covers and be guided by the course outline or a specific research goal in allocating your time and attention in reading the resource. • Read actively.
text_raw:
Use headings, table of contents, introductions and conclusions to identify what 
a particular resource covers and be guided by the course outline or a specific 
research goal in allocating your time and attention in reading the resource. 
• Read actively.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Reading actively means asking questions and thinking critically about the material being read (see 22.20–22.22) in order to understand it.
text_raw:
Reading actively means asking questions and thinking critically 
about the material being read (see 22.20–22.22) in order to understand it.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Reading can very easily become a passive occupation.
text_raw: Reading can very easily become a passive occupation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: For this reason it is important, where possible, to read when fresh and wide awake, and to take breaks at regular intervals.
text_raw:
For this reason it is 
important, where possible, to read when fresh and wide awake, and to take 
breaks at regular intervals.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Significant words or passages should be underlined or highlighted, and notes taken for revision purposes.
text_raw:
Significant words or passages should be underlined or 
highlighted, and notes taken for revision purposes.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The student should ensure that the substance of the material is constantly in mind and is being understood.
text_raw:
The student should ensure 
that the substance of the material is constantly in mind and is being understood.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Students should seek to develop a sense of what reading habits and methods work best for them.
text_raw:
Students should seek to develop a sense of what reading habits and methods work 
best for them.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Sometimes it is best to read the materials before class so that the classes build on a basic level of understanding.
text_raw:
Sometimes it is best to read the materials before class so that the classes 
build on a basic level of understanding.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: For other students or other courses, it might be better to skim the materials or focus on key readings before class, and then read them with greater diligence after the class.
text_raw:
For other students or other courses, it might be 
better to skim the materials or focus on key readings before class, and then read them with 
greater diligence after the class.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: This might also be shaped by what teachers expect in the classroom.
text_raw:
This might also be shaped by what teachers expect in the 
classroom.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: For some, lecturing is designed to convey information and provide guidance for subsequent reading.
text_raw:
For some, lecturing is designed to convey information and provide guidance 
for subsequent reading.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Other teachers conduct classes, even large classes, in an interactive questioning style, expecting students to have read materials in advance to use class time for testing, clarifying and deepening understanding.
text_raw:
Other teachers conduct classes, even large classes, in an interactive 
questioning style, expecting students to have read materials in advance to use class time 
for testing, clarifying and deepening understanding.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Taking notes and making the most of lectures Lectures are intended to impart ideas, theories and concepts, and to put in context, expand upon, enliven and update information contained in cases, legislation, articles and textbooks.
text_raw:
Taking notes and making the most of lectures 
Lectures are intended to impart ideas, theories and concepts, and to put in context, 
expand upon, enliven and update information contained in cases, legislation, articles 
and textbooks.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: T o absorb and retain this information it is generally best for students to take notes; learning often occurs through the process of making notes.
text_raw:
T o absorb and retain this information it is generally best for students 
to take notes; learning often occurs through the process of making notes.

text: PRACTiCAl TiPS FOR WRiTinG Ex AmS Here are some practical tips for writing exams, particularly for sit-down, handwritten exams, that may help you in developing your response and guide your reader: • Do not start with a recitation of the facts; this takes up valuable time and words, and adds nothing.
text_raw:
PRACTiCAl TiPS FOR WRiTinG Ex AmS
Here are some practical tips for writing exams, particularly for sit-down, handwritten 
exams, that may help you in developing your response and guide your reader: 
• Do not start with a recitation of the facts; this takes up valuable time and words, 
and adds nothing.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Note the facts if and when they are relevant within your analysis. • Clearly note the number of the examination question at the start of the answer. • Leave a line space between paragraphs and, if possible, between each line of the answer. • Do not let a page look like an unbroken, un-signposted, mass of verbiage without structure.
text_raw:
Note the facts if and when they are relevant within your 
analysis. 
• Clearly note the number of the examination question at the start of the answer. 
• Leave a line space between paragraphs and, if possible, between each line of the 
answer. 
• Do not let a page look like an unbroken, un-signposted, mass of verbiage without 
structure.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Underline headings and, if it helps communicate a list or steps, you might even use point form. • Do not rewrite passages to correct minor errors.
text_raw:
Underline headings and, if it helps communicate a list or steps, you 
might even use point form. 
• Do not rewrite passages to correct minor errors.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Add corrected material to the existing text; this is where a spare line between each line of text can be useful. • If time is getting short, finish the answer in note form rather than leaving it unfinished or attempting complete sentences. • Provide authority, whether from case law or legislation, for all propositions of law.
text_raw:
Add corrected material to the 
existing text; this is where a spare line between each line of text can be useful. 
• If time is getting short, finish the answer in note form rather than leaving it 
unfinished or attempting complete sentences. 
• Provide authority, whether from case law or legislation, for all propositions of 
law.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: In short-release or sit-down exams, generally there is no requirement to give full citations, just enough detail to ensure that the case or legislation is identified. • Answer each question as concisely as possible.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: In addition to its courts, each jurisdiction has a plethora of specialist tribunals that review decisions of bodies ranging from private professional disciplinary boards like the Physiotherapy Board of Australia, to public bodies such as parole boards and industrial relations commissions.
text_raw:

of specialist tribunals that review decisions of bodies ranging from private professional 
disciplinary boards like the Physiotherapy Board of Australia, to public bodies such 
as parole boards and industrial relations commissions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Tribunals have great practical importance because they decide a large percentage of the matters which are litigated, but it is not practical to cover them all here.

importance because they decide a large percentage of the matters which are litigated, but 
it is not practical to cover them all here.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There is usually a right of appeal from tribunals to the courts.

text: For further discussion of tribunals, see Chapter 6.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Federal hierarchy The following are the courts and tribunals in the federal system: • High Court of Australia, which has general appellate jurisdiction and original jurisdiction in certain matters including constitutional cases.
text_raw:
Federal hierarchy
The following are the courts and tribunals in the federal system:
• High Court of Australia, which has general appellate jurisdiction and original 
jurisdiction in certain matters including constitutional cases.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There are seven Justices on the High Court. • Federal Court of Australia, which may be constituted by a single judge or a Full Court (at least three judges and, in significant cases, five judges).
text_raw:
There are seven 
Justices on the High Court.
• Federal Court of Australia, which may be constituted by a single judge or 
a Full Court (at least three judges and, in significant cases, five judges).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Single judges have original and some appellate jurisdiction and the Full Court has appellate jurisdiction, including jurisdiction to hear appeals from state and territory courts on some matters. • Family Court of Australia.
text_raw:
Single 
judges have original and some appellate jurisdiction and the Full Court has 
appellate jurisdiction, including jurisdiction to hear appeals from state and 
territory courts on some matters.
• Family Court of Australia.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The Appeal Division of the Family Court has appellate jurisdiction, while a single judge has original jurisdiction and may hear appeals on family matters from the Magistrates Courts of the territories and the Federal Circuit Court. • Federal Circuit Court of Australia.
text_raw:
The Appeal Division of the Family Court has 
appellate jurisdiction, while a single judge has original jurisdiction and may hear 
appeals on family matters from the Magistrates Courts of the territories and the 
Federal Circuit Court.
• Federal Circuit Court of Australia.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Established in 1999 as the Federal Magistrates Court, its name was changed in 2013 and its judicial officers are now referred to as judges.
text_raw:
Established in 1999 as the Federal 
Magistrates Court, its name was changed in 2013 and its judicial officers are 
now referred to as judges.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: It has wide jurisdiction over family law and federal law, and was established to determine less complex matters. • Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) is the foremost national tribunal.
text_raw:
It has wide jurisdiction over family law and federal 
law, and was established to determine less complex matters.
• Administrative Appeals Tribunal (AAT) is the foremost national tribunal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The AAT conducts merits review of decisions by government under more than 400 pieces of legislation.
text_raw:
The AAT conducts merits review of decisions by government under more 
than 400 pieces of legislation.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From 1 July 2015 former specialist tribunals (the Migration and Refugee Review Tribunals, and the Social Security Appeals Tribunal) were brought into the AAT as divisions of the Tribunal.
text_raw:

The High Court of Australia, headed by the Chief Justice of Australia, is at the apex

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: It has two classes of original jurisdiction conferred directly by s 75 of the Australian Constitution and arising by federal legislation made under s 76 of the Constitution.
text_raw:
It has two classes of original jurisdiction conferred 
directly by s 75 of the Australian Constitution and arising by federal legislation made under 
s 76 of the Constitution.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: For matters within the Court’s original jurisdiction, parties have a right to apply to the High Court, a right exercised in particular by people claiming refugee status.
text_raw:
For matters within the Court’s original jurisdiction, parties have 
a right to apply to the High Court, a right exercised in particular by people claiming 
refugee status.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The Court has comprehensive jurisdiction, under s 73 of the Constitution, as the final court of appeal from all courts in Australia.
text_raw:
The Court has comprehensive jurisdiction, under s 73 of the Constitution, 
as the final court of appeal from all courts in Australia.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: However, litigants generally do not have an automatic right of appeal to the High Court but require the High Court’s special leave.
text_raw:
However, litigants generally do not 
have an automatic right of appeal to the High Court but require the High Court’s special 
leave.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The High Court establishes the common law for all Australians.
text_raw: The High Court establishes the common law for all Australians.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Court HierarCHies 611 State courts are included in the diagram since, under s 39 of the Judiciary Act 1903 (Cth), state courts can exercise federal jurisdiction.
text_raw:
Court HierarCHies
611
State courts are included in the diagram since, under s 39 of the Judiciary Act 1903 
(Cth), state courts can exercise federal jurisdiction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Depending on the Commonwealth legislation under which a case is being heard, appeals from single judges of state supreme courts exercising federal jurisdiction may be made either to the Full Court of the Federal Court or to the appellate court of the relevant state supreme court.
text_raw:
Depending on the Commonwealth 
legislation under which a case is being heard, appeals from single judges of state supreme 
courts exercising federal jurisdiction may be made either to the Full Court of the Federal 
Court or to the appellate court of the relevant state supreme court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From this intermediate appellate court, appeal lies by special leave to the High Court.
text_raw:
From this intermediate 
appellate court, appeal lies by special leave to the High Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Federal Court appeals go to the Full Court of the Federal Court, and then to the High Court with special leave.
text_raw:
Federal Court appeals go 
to the Full Court of the Federal Court, and then to the High Court with special leave.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Family Court appeals go to the Full Court of the Family Court and then to the High Court with special leave.
text_raw:
Family Court appeals go to the Full Court of the Family Court and then to the High 
Court with special leave.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From the Federal Circuit Court, appeals may be taken to the Federal Court or the Family Court depending on the nature of the matter.
text_raw:
From the Federal Circuit Court, appeals may be taken to the 
Federal Court or the Family Court depending on the nature of the matter.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: An appeal from the Federal Circuit Court may be to a single judge of the Federal Court but is regarded as an appeal to the Full Court of the Federal Court.
text_raw:
An appeal 
from the Federal Circuit Court may be to a single judge of the Federal Court but is 
regarded as an appeal to the Full Court of the Federal Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There is a right of appeal on a question of law from the AAT to the Federal Court, although such an appeal may be remitted by the Federal Court to the Federal Circuit Court.
text_raw:
There is a right of appeal on a question of law from the AAT to the Federal 
Court, although such an appeal may be remitted by the Federal Court to the Federal Circuit 
Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: A single judge of the Federal Court or Family Court has coordinate jurisdiction with a single judge of a state Supreme Court.
text_raw:
A single judge of the Federal Court or Family Court has coordinate jurisdiction with 
a single judge of a state Supreme Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Similarly, the appellate courts of the state Supreme Courts have coordinate jurisdiction with the Full Federal Court and Full Family Court.
text_raw:
Similarly, the appellate courts of the state Supreme 
Courts have coordinate jurisdiction with the Full Federal Court and Full Family Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: With regard to family law, Western Australia is a special case.
text_raw: With regard to family law, Western Australia is a special case.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The Commonwealth has given federal jurisdiction to the Western Australian Family Court and to family law magistrates in the Magistrates Court of Western Australia.
text_raw:
The Commonwealth 
has given federal jurisdiction to the Western Australian Family Court and to family law 
magistrates in the Magistrates Court of Western Australia.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals from the Magistrates Court on non-federal family law go to the Western Australian Family Court, Supreme Court or Court of Appeal.
text_raw:
Appeals from the Magistrates 
Court on non-federal family law go to the Western Australian Family Court, Supreme 
Court or Court of Appeal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals from the Western Australian Family Court on non-federal family law go to the Court of Appeal.
text_raw:
Appeals from the Western Australian Family Court on 
non-federal family law go to the Court of Appeal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals on federal family law from the Magistrates Court go to the (federal) Family Court (the Full Court or a single Judge).
text_raw:
Appeals on federal family law from the 
Magistrates Court go to the (federal) Family Court (the Full Court or a single Judge).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals on federal family law from the Western Australian Family Court go to the Full Court of the (federal) Family Court of Australia.
text_raw:
Appeals on federal family law from the Western Australian Family Court go to the 
Full Court of the (federal) Family Court of Australia.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: LAYING DOWN THE LAW 612 State courts and tribunals In each state court system there is a superior court called the Supreme Court.
text_raw:
LAYING DOWN THE LAW
612
State courts and tribunals
In each state court system there is a superior court called the Supreme Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The supreme courts have appellate and some original jurisdiction, both civil and criminal, and deal with state and also federal matters.
text_raw:
The 
supreme courts have appellate and some original jurisdiction, both civil and criminal, and 
deal with state and also federal matters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Except in Tasmania, below the Supreme Court there are two levels of courts: an intermediate court and lower courts.
text_raw:
Except in Tasmania, below the Supreme Court 
there are two levels of courts: an intermediate court and lower courts.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: In the states with an intermediate court, that court has similar jurisdiction to its Supreme Court but with some financial or other limit in civil matters, and a limit on the types of offence it may try in its criminal jurisdiction.
text_raw:
In the states with 
an intermediate court, that court has similar jurisdiction to its Supreme Court but with 
some financial or other limit in civil matters, and a limit on the types of offence it may 
try in its criminal jurisdiction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: All jurisdictions except Tasmania have a multi-jurisdiction civil and administrative appeals tribunal with authority to make original decisions as well as to review government decisions by others.
text_raw:
All jurisdictions except Tasmania have a multi-jurisdiction 
civil and administrative appeals tribunal with authority to make original decisions as 
well as to review government decisions by others.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: In Tasmania the jurisdiction is in an administrative division of the Magistrates Court but a Tasmanian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (TasCAT) is scheduled for introduction in 2020.
text_raw:
In Tasmania the jurisdiction is in an 
administrative division of the Magistrates Court but a Tasmanian Civil and Administrative 
Tribunal (TasCAT) is scheduled for introduction in 2020.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: 1 In addition, each state has individual specialist tribunals dealing with matters such as industrial relations, mental health, and land and the environment.
text_raw:
1 In addition, each state has 
individual specialist tribunals dealing with matters such as industrial relations, mental 
health, and land and the environment.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: A significant limit on the powers of the state civil and administrative tribunals is that they are prohibited by s 75(iv) of the Constitution from hearing matters involving parties outside their own state — commonly described as the diversity jurisdiction.
text_raw:
A significant limit on the powers of the state civil and administrative tribunals is 
that they are prohibited by s 75(iv) of the Constitution from hearing matters involving 
parties outside their own state — commonly described as the diversity jurisdiction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: 2 This has the capacity to reduce their ability to hear matters in areas such as guardianship, discrimination and some commercial operations.
text_raw:
2 This 
has the capacity to reduce their ability to hear matters in areas such as guardianship, 
discrimination and some commercial operations.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The effect of the decision has been addressed legislatively in most jurisdictions.
text_raw:
The effect of the decision has been 
addressed legislatively in most jurisdictions.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The state court hierarchies are illustrated in simplified form in the diagram below with a description of each jurisdiction’s court system following.

The state court hierarchies are illustrated in simplified form in the diagram below

text: (The federal jurisdiction of the state courts has been considered at A2.) The diagram makes no distinction between civil and criminal cases.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Criminal trials in the supreme and intermediate courts are generally heard with a jury, but juries are uncommon in civil trials.
text_raw:
Criminal trials in the supreme and intermediate courts are 
generally heard with a jury, but juries are uncommon in civil trials.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There are significant differences between jurisdictions, particularly in criminal matters, as to rights of appeal from lower and intermediate courts to the Supreme Court.
text_raw:
There are significant 
differences between jurisdictions, particularly in criminal matters, as to rights of appeal 
from lower and intermediate courts to the Supreme Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: There are rights of appeal to the court systems from state and territory tribunals and specialist courts.
text_raw:
There are rights of appeal to the court systems from state and territory tribunals and 
specialist courts.

text: NeW soutH W aLes • The Supreme Court of New South Wales has two divisions: the Common Law Division (including criminal and some civil matters), and the Equity Division (including many commercial matters).
text_raw:
NeW soutH W aLes
• The Supreme Court of New South Wales has two divisions: the Common Law 
Division (including criminal and some civil matters), and the Equity Division 
(including many commercial matters).

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Within the Supreme Court there is a Court of Appeal and a Court of Criminal Appeal, each of which sits with three or more judges.
text_raw:
Within the Supreme Court there is a 
Court of Appeal and a Court of Criminal Appeal, each of which sits with three 
or more judges.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Judges of Appeal are specially appointed to the Court of Appeal. • The District Court of New South Wales is an intermediate court with extensive civil and criminal jurisdiction. • The Local Court has limited civil and criminal jurisdiction within local areas. • The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT) has broad civil and administrative jurisdiction.
text_raw:
Judges of Appeal are specially appointed to the Court of Appeal.
• The District Court of New South Wales is an intermediate court with extensive 
civil and criminal jurisdiction.
• The Local Court has limited civil and criminal jurisdiction within local areas.
• The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT) has broad civil and 
administrative jurisdiction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals from the Local Court can be made to the District Court, or directly to the New South Wales Supreme Court or, where appropriate, to the Federal Court.
text_raw:
Appeals from the Local Court can be made to the District Court, or directly to the 
New South Wales Supreme Court or, where appropriate, to the Federal Court.

614
a limited right of appeal from the District Court to the Court of Appeal or to the Court

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From the appellate courts, and, in some circumstances, from a single judge, appeals can be taken to the High Court with the Court’s special leave.
text_raw:
From the appellate courts, and, in some circumstances, from a 
single judge, appeals can be taken to the High Court with the Court’s special leave.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Parties may appeal from NCAT decisions to an Internal Appeal Panel, or, in some circumstances, to the Supreme Court or to the District Court.
text_raw:
Parties may appeal from NCAT decisions to an Internal Appeal Panel, or, in some 
circumstances, to the Supreme Court or to the District Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: QueeNsLaND • The Supreme Court of Queensland has appellate and original jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters.
text_raw:
QueeNsLaND
• The Supreme Court of Queensland has appellate and original jurisdiction in civil 
and criminal matters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The Trial Division, constituted by a single judge, may exercise original or appellate jurisdiction, while the Court of Appeal hears only appeals. • The District Court of Queensland has extensive civil and criminal jurisdiction and hears appeals from the Magistrates Court. • The Magistrates Court has a limited civil and criminal jurisdiction. • The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) has broad civil and administrative jurisdiction.
text_raw:
The Trial Division, constituted by a single judge, may exercise 
original or appellate jurisdiction, while the Court of Appeal hears only appeals.
• The District Court of Queensland has extensive civil and criminal jurisdiction 
and hears appeals from the Magistrates Court.
• The Magistrates Court has a limited civil and criminal jurisdiction.
• The Queensland Civil and Administrative Tribunal (QCAT) has broad civil and 
administrative jurisdiction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals from the Magistrates Court are to the District Court and, where appropriate, to the Federal Court.
text_raw:
Appeals from the Magistrates Court are to the District Court and, where appropriate, 
to the Federal Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From the District Court appeals go to the Court of Appeal.
text_raw: From the District Court appeals go to the Court of Appeal.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals also lie to the Court of Appeal from a single judge of the Supreme Court.
text_raw: Appeals also lie to the Court of Appeal from a single judge of the Supreme Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals lie from the Court of Appeal, and, in certain circumstances, the Trial Division, to the High Court with the Court’s special leave.
text_raw:
Appeals lie from the Court of Appeal, and, in certain circumstances, the Trial Division, 
to the High Court with the Court’s special leave.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeals from the QCAT go to the Tribunal’s appeal tier, or to the Court of Appeal. soutH austraLia • The Supreme Court of South Australia has original and general appellate jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters.
text_raw:
Appeals from the QCAT go to the Tribunal’s appeal tier, or to the Court of Appeal.
soutH austraLia
• The Supreme Court of South Australia has original and general appellate 
jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: A single judge may exercise original or appellate jurisdiction while the Full Court exercises appellate jurisdiction only.
text_raw:
A single judge may exercise original or 
appellate jurisdiction while the Full Court exercises appellate jurisdiction only.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From January 2021, there will be a South Australian Court of Appeal, with five judges dedicated to hearing matters on appeal.3 • The District Court of South Australia has extensive civil and criminal jurisdiction exercised in a Civil Division, a Criminal Division and a Criminal Injuries Division. • The Magistrates Court has a limited civil and criminal jurisdiction. • The South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) resolves a broad range of civil and administrative appeals and disciplinary matters, formerly dealt with by a division of the District Court.
text_raw:
From January 2021, there will be a South Australian Court of Appeal, with five 
judges dedicated to hearing matters on appeal.3
• The District Court of South Australia has extensive civil and criminal 
jurisdiction exercised in a Civil Division, a Criminal Division and a Criminal 
Injuries Division.
• The Magistrates Court has a limited civil and criminal jurisdiction.
• The South Australian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (SACAT) resolves a 
broad range of civil and administrative appeals and disciplinary matters, formerly 
dealt with by a division of the District Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From the Magistrates Court, appeals may be taken to the District Court or directly to the Supreme Court.
text_raw:
From the Magistrates Court, appeals may be taken to the District Court or directly 
to the Supreme Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: From the District Court an appeal lies to the Supreme Court.
text_raw: From the District Court an appeal lies to the Supreme Court.

text: Court HierarCHies 615 There is a right of internal appeal to an appeal panel of the SACAT, as well as a right to appeal to a single judge or the Court of Appeal. tasMaNia Tasmania has only two tiers of courts. • The Supreme Court of Tasmania has original and general appellate jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters.
text_raw:
Court HierarCHies
615
There is a right of internal appeal to an appeal panel of the SACAT, as well as a right 
to appeal to a single judge or the Court of Appeal.
tasMaNia
Tasmania has only two tiers of courts.
• The Supreme Court of Tasmania has original and general appellate jurisdiction 
in civil and criminal matters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The Full Court and the Court of Criminal Appeal have appellate jurisdiction only, while a single judge may exercise original or appellate jurisdiction. • The Magistrates Court of Tasmania has divisions with civil and criminal jurisdiction, and an administrative appeals jurisdiction which will be transferred to the general jurisdiction tribunal (TasCAT) when it is established in 2020.
text_raw:
The Full Court and the Court of Criminal Appeal 
have appellate jurisdiction only, while a single judge may exercise original or 
appellate jurisdiction.
• The Magistrates Court of Tasmania has divisions with civil and criminal 
jurisdiction, and an administrative appeals jurisdiction which will be transferred 
to the general jurisdiction tribunal (TasCAT) when it is established in 2020.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeal from the Magistrates Court may be made to a single judge of the Supreme Court or, where appropriate, to the Federal Court of Australia.
text_raw:
Appeal from the Magistrates Court may be made to a single judge of the Supreme 
Court or, where appropriate, to the Federal Court of Australia.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeal from a single judge of the Supreme Court is usually to three judges sitting as the Full Court or the Court of Criminal Appeal or, where appropriate, to the Federal Court.
text_raw:
Appeal from a single 
judge of the Supreme Court is usually to three judges sitting as the Full Court or the 
Court of Criminal Appeal or, where appropriate, to the Federal Court.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: Appeal also lies in certain circumstances from a single judge of the Supreme Court, and from appellate courts, to the High Court with the Court’s special leave.
text_raw:
Appeal also lies 
in certain circumstances from a single judge of the Supreme Court, and from appellate 
courts, to the High Court with the Court’s special leave.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: ViCtoria • The Supreme Court of Victoria has original and appellate jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters.
text_raw:
ViCtoria
• The Supreme Court of Victoria has original and appellate jurisdiction in civil 
and criminal matters.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: A single judge may exercise both jurisdictions while the Court of Appeal functions as a civil and a criminal court of appeal. • The County Court of Victoria is an intermediate court with extensive civil and criminal jurisdiction at first instance and, in certain circumstances, on appeal. • The Magistrates’ Court has a limited jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters. • The Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) has broad civil and administrative jurisdiction.
text_raw:
A single judge may exercise both jurisdictions while the 
Court of Appeal functions as a civil and a criminal court of appeal.
• The County Court of Victoria is an intermediate court with extensive civil and 
criminal jurisdiction at first instance and, in certain circumstances, on appeal.
• The Magistrates’ Court has a limited jurisdiction in civil and criminal matters.
• The Victorian Civil and Administrative Tribunal (VCAT) has broad civil and 
administrative jurisdiction.

chapter_title: CHAPTER 22 STudy And Ex Am SkillS
text: The Magistrates’ Court is at the base of the Victorian court hierarchy.
text_raw: The Magistrates’ Court is at the base of the Victorian court hierarchy.
